item.dc:creator: 投资TALK君
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"坏消息砸不下去"背后的心理弹簧

小陶最锋利的洞察藏在一个看似平淡的观察里：周四收盘时 McClellan 参与度指标只有17%（20日均线也是17%）。这个数字比 CPI 数据本身还重要——它意味着市场进入 CPI 之前，已经把恐慌预先支付掉了。

这里有个反直觉的机制：当参与度跌到极端低位，"坏消息"就失去了它的破坏力，因为该卖的人已经卖完了。这不是"利空出尽"这四个字能概括的——它是一个物理学式的能量守恒：市场情绪像一根被压缩的弹簧，压缩得越狠，反弹的能量越大，与触发反弹的事件是好是坏其实关系不大。你可以观察到，触发反弹的甚至不需要是"利多"，只需要是"没有比预期更坏"。

跨领域联想：这与地震学里的"应力释放"是同一套逻辑——地壳积累了足够的应力后，究竟是哪一颗小石子触发滑动，其实并不重要。周五触发反弹的"催化剂"是教育与电信服务这个季节性异常项——一个平均月度涨幅不超过0.4%、这次却跳到1.8%的边缘噪音。用一个统计上的偶然，撬动了一个心理上的必然。

二、黄金正在交易一件债市还没看到的事

这是整期节目里最"违反教科书"的一段：十年期真实收益率从2.4%飙升到2.59%，负相关性依然维持在-0.7到-0.9之间，但黄金却没有创新低。教科书说，真实收益率上涨=黄金必跌，因为黄金的机会成本上升。可这一次两者出现了幅度上的脱钩。

小陶给的解释很妙——黄金不是在交易当下的真实收益率，黄金是在交易"贝森特（美国财政部）终将干预长端美债市场"这件债券市场自己还没定价的事。也就是说，黄金市场比债券市场更早地把"财政部会用行政力量压低长端利率"这个未来动作提前贴现了。

这是一种奇特的跨市场认知不对称：黄金交易员和美债交易员看着同一个宏观现实，但黄金一族先看到了政策底牌。放到跨领域视角里，这像是加密世界里"链上先知信息"和"链下滞后新闻"的时间差；也像 1971 年布雷顿森林崩溃前的几个月，欧洲私人银行家已经在偷偷囤金，而华盛顿的官员还在开会讨论"如何维护固定汇率"。黄金往往是"下一个政策拐点"的领先指标，而不是"当下利率环境"的滞后反应。

三、"PE 领先 EPS"是一个被证伪四次的迷思

这一段值得投资圈里所有相信"市场是聪明的"的人反复看：过去四年，PE 出现四次像样的下修，但只有 2025 年那一次真的预告了 EPS 增速的放缓，其他三次 EPS 该涨还是继续涨。

换句话说："PE 领先 EPS"这个信念在 AI 应用落地的时代（2023 至今）几乎不成立。为什么？因为市场并没有足够聪明地去 pricing AI 带来的基本面加速。年初市场预期 2026 全年 EPS 增速 15%，九个月后被上修到 31.6%——这不是一次微调，这是市场系统性地低估了整个 AI 资本开支周期的盈利转化效率。

最出人意料的观察：小陶说自己在 2024 年底、2025 年底两次让大家"降贝塔"。表面上看，这两次建议在事后似乎都错了，因为标普 500 今年上涨了 11.6%。但仔细一拆：估值 PE 从 22 倍以上跌到 19.2 倍，跌了 14%——降贝塔在估值维度上完全正确。指数还能涨，是因为 EPS 体量爆炸性上升了 28%，硬生生把估值收缩的地心引力对冲掉了。

这是典型的 Simpson 悖论在宏观层面的显形：两股方向相反、量级悬殊的力（PE 收缩 vs EPS 扩张）叠加后，你只看到最终合力（指数上涨），却完全看不见底层的双向撕扯。

四、一个更冷的推论

如果 EPS 增速这台"永动机"哪天熄火——哪怕不是崩溃，仅仅是回到正常增速——当下 19.2 倍看似便宜的 forward PE 就会瞬间变成一个陷阱。因为过去一年市场教会自己的定价模式是"用 EPS 的增量吃掉 PE 的收缩"，一旦增量端断供，被压抑了一整年的估值收缩压力就没有对冲物了。

这就是为什么小陶反复强调："我并不期待估值反弹，我期待估值保持在这里，涨幅全部由基本面提供。" 听起来是保守，实际上是他在为自己设计一个"永远不需要押注 PE 扩张"的安全边际结构——赚 EPS 的钱，不赚估值的钱，是一种在 AI 时代最容易被忽视的、极其古典的价值投资纪律。

📝 转录文本

引子：一个反常的周五

明明是一组高于市场预期的通胀数据，股市却出现了反弹。周四的时候市场的情绪面非常的悲观，所以周五的市场到底发生了什么？通胀数据背后是不是有些猫腻？是不是通胀数据其实比数据里面所显示的要好？所以市场出现了下跌。

今天这是内容的前半部分，我们就一起去探究一下这一次的 CPI 数据。那后半部分，其实我想通过 FactSet 数据去出发，我们完整的对于第二季度的财报去做一个总结。从 FactSet 数据角度出发，看一下市场的估值现在在什么样的一个位置。我今天看到了标普500的估值吓了我一跳。那在这个基础上，我们展开地去看一下纳指和半导体板块的一个估值，好吗？

欢迎大家来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小陶。那在开始之前，大家记得留言、点赞加转发。

过去一周资产价格走势回顾

首先讲通胀数据之前，我们快速地回顾一下过去一周资产价格的走势。那过去一周，我认为所有资产价格走势里边，要引起我们注意，也算是整个市场里边的头条，就是美债收率的一个走势。

那上一周仔细回顾一下，只有四个交易日。那四个交易里边比较重磅的数据就 CPI 数据和 PPI 数据。PPI 数据出来之后，美债收率出现了非常大幅度的下跌，单日创下了两年期上升了15个基点，过去一周两年期上升了26个基点。所以市场大幅在过去一周的时间里，大幅增加了接下去加息的这个幅度。九月份加息这个概率已经从百分之五六十，现在来到了将近百分之九十。整个周期现在预期市场的定价3.6次加息。

那我的观点是站在当下，看一下市场的这个定价，看一下现在通胀所在的这个位置，我认为3.6次加息是过了。可能这一次一个加息周期是在两次到三次，三次的话也是合理的。

那在这个基础上，因为加息这个预期往上升，十年期的美债收率也上升了18个基点。稍后我会和大家聊一下，因为我自己手里现在还有一些黄金的一个交易仓位，现在是并没有浮亏也没有浮盈，小幅浮盈嘛，两三个点左右。接下去我要在黄金这一块交易仓位上的一个操作，那也是从美债收入的这个角度去出发。

但在过去一周我们看到美债收入出现了非常大幅度的上涨，TLT 出现了1.6%的一个下跌，所以长期美债仍然不是一个非常好的一个投资标的，甚至于是不是非常好的一个交易标的。

看一下三大指数这块，下跌的幅度并不大：标普500 -0.8%，纳指 -0.7%，道指相对会大一些，-1.6%。那黄金在美债收率那么大幅度上涨的情况下、真实收率的那么大幅度上涨的情况下，黄金这一块只下跌了1.8%。我认为黄金是比较强势的。和黄金一起相对比较强势的是比特币，在过去一周也只下跌了3%。

同时市场里面另外一个宏观因素就是油价。那么 WTI 原油在过去一周上涨了9.4%，过去一个月上涨了20%。所以整个市场在过去一周算是一个宏观周吧，因为也没有财报季度的嘛，也没有非常重要的公司——除了 Oracle 和 Adobe 之外——没有非常重要的公司集中在上一周发布财报。所以过去的一周算是一个宏观周：战争这一块的一个影响、战争这一块的一个噪音，然后来自于加息这一块的影响和噪音。

那 VIX 上升了9%，我认为还好。罗素2000下跌2.4%。从板块这一个角度去看，其实不少板块下跌的幅度还是比较多的。那比如说医疗板块下跌了3.6%，国防板块下跌了2.9%。相对比较强势的是前七大科技股，反而上涨了0.6%。那这一个涨幅其实主要是来自于 Meta，Meta 在过去的一周相对是表现比较强劲的。

标普500的等权指数下跌了1.9%。指数只下跌了0.8%，但是等权指数却下跌了1.9%，说明什么问题呢？说明大多数的个股其实在过去的一周都出现了下跌。而标普500下跌的这0.8%，其实掩盖了这背后参与度的一个虚弱。如果不是大科技相对比较强势的话，标普500的跌幅可以更大，那起码是2%以上了。

那最后这边一点我想提出来是：高贝塔动能板块在过去一周反而是上涨了8.2%，芯片板块上涨了1.4%。

CPI 数据里的"猫腻"

通胀数据我们快速做一个总结。在周五早上发布完之后，其实我第一时间在 X 上面也和大家分享了我对于这一组 CPI 数据的这个看法。

我们先从结果去出发吧。市场的预期，我这边只看核心的环比增速，因为这是美联储对于美联储来说最重要的指标。核心环比增速市场预期0.2%，最后的结果0.3%，四舍五入之后0.3%。所以还是比市场的预期要高。

主要差的点是在哪？

第一点，教育和电信服务环比增速1.8%。这一组数据基本上过去每一个月平均的涨幅就是在0%至0.2%，最高的话0.4%之间，不会超过1%。所以这一组数据刚刚过去的这一个月，教育和电信，它是一个波动比较高的。我并不期待这么高的一个环比增速可以持续下去。1.8%的环比增速，你把它年化的话，25%、30%了，好吗？所以我认为这一项是因为一个季度效应，一次性的这个涨价。说实话，如果没有这个月，如果没有教育和电信服务的话，非常有可能核心通胀是会比市场预期要低的。

第二点，交通服务这个环比增速0.5%，稍微是高了一些。那主要是来自于汽车的租赁和维修。

住房服务的话，0.3% 算是一个正常的波动。总体的一个商品环比增速0.1%，其实还是不错的，但是可以更好，因为疫情之前商品通胀这一块是负增速。医疗服务负的0.2%，娱乐服务环比增速0%，所以这两块都是相对比较好。医疗服务的占比也不小，5%吧，娱乐服务也是在5%左右，前面我说的教育和电信服务也是在5%左右。

所以总体来说，这一个月的通胀数据单纯的因为教育和电信服务被影响，那综合来说，它其实是一份可以接受的一个报告，绝对算不上是非常好的一个报告，但是也绝对算不上是非常坏的一组报告。

但是市场的一个反馈多数是来源于我们叫做 headline news——这新闻是怎么报的？你最后的结果就是 0.3 大于 0.2，不要给我背后任何的一个理由，为什么会出现这个0.3？我只需要看到这是一个0.3，那市场就马上把加息这个预期给打满了。所以现在9月份加息这个预期已经来到了将近90%。

从 CPI+PPI 推算 PCE

那随着 PPI 数据和 CPI 数据在这一周都公布了，公布完之后，华尔街包括彭博 Anna Wong 这个团队就已经可以计算出月底公布的 PCE 数据了。

根据彭博他们的这个预期，8月份的核心 PCE 非常有可能环比增速会来到 0.29%，此前上一个月的数据是在0.25%。所以环比增速是比上个月要高的。而且就单纯环比增速0.29%也是不能接受的，把它年化之后，同比增速是4%。

然后我看了一下 Nick 也公布了所有华尔街投行他们对于这一次 PCE 数据计算出来这个结果，基本上是在0.25%至0.28%之间。

所以无论如何——就 PCE 数据我再强调一次——PCE 数据它是计算出来的这个结果，它并不是预期，它并不像 CPI 数据市场并不知道 CPI 数据会怎么样。但是有了 CPI、有了 PPI，市场其实是可以根据公式推算出 PCE 到底在什么一个区间，所以这个误差会非常的小。所以大概率的情况下呢，90%以上，这一个月的环比 PCE 的增速也会停留在0.3%。

下周美联储会议：加息几乎板上钉钉？

那在这种情况下，下一周的美联储会议，凯文沃什加息的这个概率，我认为已经是非常的高了，或几乎是板上钉钉了。

为什么呢？是因为在上一次会议、美联储会议的时候，我记得第一句话凯文沃什就说的——他说，其他这一届的美联储也不是用来去给市场造成惊吓的。当时在7月份会议之前，市场差不多40%的概率他们预期好像要加息，然后60%是预期不加息，那他最后是没有加息。且他说了，他说我们这个美联储也不是来惊吓这个市场，并不会……他这句话背后的意思就是说，并不会市场你大概率的情况下预计我要加息，那我就会加，并不是最后的决定会和市场的这个预期反着来。

所以顺着他这样的一个思路，或者他在上一次会议里面这个言语去看的话，既然现在市场已经定价了90%——当然下一周可能还会有些波动，但是大差不差最后可能就是停在70%至90%之间——那如果是这样的一个概率的话，大概率的情况下下一周会加息。

那加息已成定局，接下去就取决于凯文沃什的言语。那么到底是偏鹰派的，还是偏鸽派的？我个人的期待是会有一个 dovish hike，就是一个相对比较鸽派式的加息。

因为通常来说，市场现在的一个期待也是：如果你要去压制通胀的话，你不可能这次只加息一次，那么所以现在市场也已经定价了加息 3.6 次。但是你要从凯文沃什嘴里想去套出接下去下一次会议还会不会继续加息的话，他不会告诉你的。他一定会告诉你，每一次的会议都是一个 live。那他这么去说的话，就告诉你下一次什么时候去加息还不能保证，对吧？

所以从市场这个角度来看，市场的一个期待是连续性的，一旦——就市场会做一个线性外推的——一旦你9月份加息，它也就连续性地认为你可能下一次是11月份吧，11月份也会认为你马上还会进行一次加息。但是凯文沃什我是不会给你这样一个指引。所以从这个角度去看，反而我认为会造成一个类似于相对比较偏鸽派的一个加息，好吗？

黄金：脱离真实收益率的强势

那然后我们来聊一下黄金。图里的两条线：白色这条线是10年期美债的一个真实收益率。首先我在右边这个框框里面，我们看到在过去这一段时间吧，几个交易日里边，白色这条线出现了非常明显的上涨，10年期美债的一个真实收率出现了这个上涨，主要的一个来源来自于对于加息的这个预期，或者你也可以理解为对于长端这一块的一个再定价。然后蓝色这一块是黄金的一个走势。

最下面是一个相关性。从相关性我们可以看到，10年期美债的一个真实收入和黄金仍然是非常的负相关，负相关指数达到了负的0.7、负的0.8、负的0.9，甚至于是非常接近于负一的。所以这两者之间的负相关是毋庸置疑。

但是我们看到十年期的一个真实收入现在去到了2.59%，比前段时间的2.4%高出了非常多，将近要高出20个基点，但是黄金并没有破新低。所谓的相关性是这两者之间出现一个反方向走嘛，白色这条线往上，蓝色这条线就往下。但是从价格上去走，因为相关性并不能告诉你它的一个幅度。

那从价格走势去看，黄金在——我这边有一条绿线，绿线差不多是在4300点以下——从这条绿线似乎可以看到黄金下面有一个支撑位，这个支撑位就是在 4300、4290 左右，这边有一个支撑的一个区域在那边。如果跌破这一个区间的话，可能可以去做一个止损。但是在没有跌破这个区间之前，其实黄金在美债十年期美债真实收入率上涨的这一波趋势里，已经表现出了相当相当的强劲。

那前面我已经聊到了比特币随着黄金去走了，那你会发现比特币其实也是相对比较强劲的。所以在那么强劲的情况下，我认为黄金这一块是可以继续观察的。那如果仓位比较大的话，你下面跌破了4290，下面可以去做一个止损。

但是我个人的操作可能更加偏向——因为我现在黄金这边的操作仓位其实并没有非常大——我个人可能更加偏向如果市场还是要去做空美债，那么和贝森特去对着去干的话，我可能更加偏向于在下面一个比较……就黄金如果跌破的话，在下面一个区间我可能会选择进行加仓。

只要我认为贝森特想要去压制长债这一块利率的这个决心仍然是在那边的话，对于市场和贝森特和财政部去对着干的话，我并不认为市场可以赢过财政部。甚至于我觉得从结果这个角度去解释的话，有一种可能性是整个黄金在交易什么？黄金在交易未来财政部就是会干预美债市场，但是美债市场现在还没有反映出来。

FactSet：企业还在担心通胀吗？

好吧，那我们还是回到通胀这边。我们来看一下 FactSet 数据。那这一组数据我们现在看到的是——因为我们现在担心通胀嘛，那我们从标普500里边500多家公司，我们去看一下，这500家公司是不是担心通胀。

首先图里有两根柱状图，那代表了不同的一个板块。这两根柱状图：蓝色的柱状图代表是第二季度，白色的柱状图或者灰色的柱状图代表是第一季度。从第一季度提到通胀的这些公司的数量这个角度去看，和第二季度去做对比的话，你看到灰色的这根柱状图在大多数的板块里边都会比蓝色的这根柱状图要高，就代表什么？代表如果我们从一季度转变到二季度的话，其实在聊通胀或者担心通胀的这些公司有所减少，但是这个减少的一个幅度或者数量其实也并不是那么的明显。

展望：Q3 财报季在即

那不知不觉，九月份的上旬也已经结束了。那三九月份 1/3 的这个交易日已经在身后了，希望我们可以平安地度过九月份。那么其实我们度过九月份之后，马上就要迎来十月份了。到十月的下旬，马上大科技就要发布财报了。

说说快也快，对吧。还记不记得上一个季度、第二季度，微软发布财报？还记不记得谷歌发布财报？还记不记得谷歌那一周发布财报的时候，大家还是仍然非常担心资本开支？然后结果下一周，微软发布财报、亚马逊发布财报，这两家公司大涨，谷歌补涨——因为那两家公司证明了 ROI。就在上一周的时候，市场还担心谷歌的 capex，然后下一周直接微软发布完财报之后，把整个市场情绪面全部带回去。

所以那在上一个季度财报里边，其实这些大科技、这些是特别是这些 CSP，他们对于这一个季度、第三季度的财报已经有了指引了，这个指引其实相当的强。所以我对于这个季度财报仍然是非常期待。那我的一个期待是第四季度财报会在第三季度基础上继续加速：利润扩张，营收的增速继续加速。

十月下旬开始发布财报。那现在差不多马上要到九月中旬了，九月中旬到十月下旬这段时间里边，如果市场出现下跌的话，那等于是给了这一个财报季度一个非常好的一个 setup。

回看：为什么我不做 CPI 对冲

那么在讲到 setup，我前面忘了——那么对于 CPI 数据做一个总结：就是我在周四那期视频里边，我说我为什么没有必要去对于 CPI 做一个对冲？是因为你整个进入 CPI 数据之前，市场是恐慌的。

那么当然我们每个人衡量恐慌的这个指标可能不一样，作为我个人来说，我认为比较准的一个指标就是市场的参与度。市场的参与度截止到周四的一个收盘，标普百是在17%，20均线是在17%。所以我个人理解就是一个相当恐慌的一个阶段。那在恐慌那个阶段，即使我也不去猜那么 CPI 的数据到底会如何，但是在这种情况我不会去做任何一个对冲，我觉得没有必要，因为下跌的空间也有限。

如果它真的跌下去，我说真的跌 2% 的话，那我就加仓，可能把所有的现金仓位子弹全部打出去。那反过来，即使在一个不是非常好的一个数据的情况下，指数反而还出现了反弹，那这也是我希望看到的。那大不了就是我手里的现金再稍微往后搁一搁呗，对吧？虽然现金就本身现金仓位也不多，那如果整体的仓位再出现上涨的话，是我希望看到，所以我也不用去担心。

但是相反的嘛，如果你在周四的时候就进行减仓，那现在你要去担心这组 CPI 数据到底怎么去理解，就看不懂了，对吗？明明 CPI 数据比市场预期要差，但市场却出现下跌了。那从我这个角度来说，就某种程度你也可以理解为它是一个坏的消息，但却出现上涨了呀，对吧？那是不是和好的消息出现下跌是反过来的呢？或者坏消息也砸不下去了呢？那这是可能现在没有非常多仓位的人需要去思考的。

那但是对于我们有仓位在市场里边、有非常舒适的仓位在市场里面，我不需要去思考这个问题，我觉得非常的好。

第二季度财报总结

好吧，然后我们还是回到第二季度财报这边。我们看一下现在 2026 年，就现在市场预期——因为第二季度已经结束了，马上迎来第三季度、第四季度——2026 财年，市场现在预期整个全年 EPS 的增速体量在 31.6%，营收的这个增速在 12.1%。

我不知道大家还记不记得，在年初我在做展望的时候，还记不记得当时整个市场对于26年的 EPS 增速是多少？我没有记错的话是在 15%。经过现在大半年、三个季度不到之后，增速来到了 31.6%。也就是站在年初的时候，我们远远低估了今年 EPS 增速的这个体量。那这一点、这个 EPS 增速的体量非常的重要，因为稍后我在聊 PE 的时候、我在聊估值的时候，我会把这个数据带进来。

那第二季度的财报，我们从结果去看，其实市场的反馈不是那么的正面。主要是反映在我圈出来的这一个区间里面：172 家公司，他们 EPS 的增速最终是好于市场预期的幅度在 0% 至 5% 之间——有 172 家公司哦——但是这 172 家公司平均却下跌了 1.6%。如果说你好于市场预期在 5%~20% 的话，195 家公司，这 195 家公司平均确实出现了 1.1% 的这个上涨。

也就是可以理解为：市场对于刚刚过去的第二季度财报的这个要求非常的高，你好于市场预期不够，你必须要好于市场预期 5% 以上，市场才会给你正面的反馈。

估值：我被吓了一跳

那接下去就是估值。在 FactSet 数据里面有给我们 forward PE 现在在什么那个位置。我看完之后我吓了一跳，为什么？现在的 forward PE 是接近于今年的3月份。根据 FactSet 这个数据——当然我稍后和大家分享，彭博结论是一样的——并且图里绿色的这根虚线是5年的平均，现在是低于5年的平均，现在正好是打在十年的平均 PE 上面。

就从这个角度、从估值这个单从估值这个角度去看，现在绝对不属于是贵的。虽然现在价格离最高点可能也就下跌了 2%~3%。

我今天在社交媒体上看到一个观点说，标普都没咋跌啊，指数也没咋跌啊，所以指数有非常大的一个下跌空间，如果我们接下去要进行加息的话。我不会这么看的。就我们要在看美股到底是贵还是便宜的时候，你绝对不能看从最高点到底回调了多少，这个是不 make sense。我们一定要看整个市场的一个估值在什么那个位置。

美股是不一样，美股你和其他的标的——你不用你去交易加密货币的话，加密货币它没有一个基本面在那边，它没有这家公司到底赚多少钱，那么加密货币很多时候只有一个情绪面在那边——但是美股不一样，美股是有基本面的。美股有所谓的基本面就是 EPS 每股收益，之所以有了 EPS 收益，才会有了 PE。所以现在从估值、从 forward PE 这个角度去看，绝对算不上是贵的，甚至于是便宜的。

彭博数据：估值收缩了 14%，但指数还涨了 11.6%

那我从彭博数据这个角度和大家分享，其实和前面的结论基本上是一样的。那截止到今天的时候，周五的收盘，标普500 forward PE 在 19.2 倍。那基本上是和今年3月份的点位是一样的，稍微比今年3月份高了那么一点点。

我这边从今年年初到现在为止的话，你会发现标普100 的估值跌了多少？forward PE 跌了 14%。我记得前段时间有一位观众在我的留言下面，他说 Tom 君，你每一次年底的时候都让我们说降贝塔降贝塔。的确是这样，我在24年底的时候让大家去降贝塔，我在25年底的时候也让大家去降贝塔。

但是如我们从这张图——因为我这张图从22年到现在——你看一下24年底，就我这边鼠标所在的这个位置，24年底是不是在一个高位？标普100 的估值在 22 倍以上，这是 24 年底。25 年底在多少？25 年底和 24 年底基本上是一样的，也是在 22 倍以上。所以 24 年底和 25 年底估值是不是在一个高位？

我们现在站在一个后视镜——因为我们现在过了 9 个月了——我们站在后视镜去看整个 2026 年，估值有没有扩张？我当时在 2025 年底的时候，我说我不期待在这样的一个估值情况下估值可以扩张。我期待的是整个 26 年估值不扩张，持续保持在高位。26 年我们赚什么钱？我们就赚 EPS 增速的钱。那 EPS 增速如果市场预期是15% 的话，那我就赚 15%。

那结果现在 9 个月之后，估值的确没有保持在高位，估值从 22 倍以上现在跌到了 19.2 倍。那如果你去看 YTD 到现在为止，标普500 上涨了多少？标普500 上涨了 11.6%。所以全部加在一起，我们会发现今年到现在为止，估值跌了 14%，价格却上涨——标普百的价格却上涨了 11.6%——为什么？因为背后 EPS 这个体量上升了 28%。所以整个今年标普500的涨幅全部是来自于基本面的扩张。

我们可以理解为今年到现在为止，如果没有基本面的这个扩张的话，标普500 可能就是下跌的。或者在我这这段时间和大家分享，我在昨天视频里面也和大家分享，就接下去我看待市场的一个角度也是一样的：我并不期待估值的反弹的幅度会非常的大，我的一个期待是标普——就指数——还可以上涨，但是指数的上涨大多数是来自于基本面、来自于 EPS。这接下去 EPS 和 PE 之间仍然会是一个互相之间的这个角力。

那其实从今年到现在为止，市场的一个走势恰恰就是反映了这种情况：PE 是收缩的，但是标普百指数仍然是上涨，因为指数的这个上涨来自于基本面。

低估值的两种解读

那怎么去理解估值在低位呢？有正面的理解和负面的理解。

正面的理解就是 forward PE 在低位，市场是低估了。

负面的理解就是 forward PE 在低位——为什么会在低位？你把指数理解为是一个周期板块，当周期板块的 PE 在低位的时候，代表接下去的基本面 EPS 可能会出现问题。当你的 EPS 增速放缓，甚至出现负增长的时候，即使你价格不变，你的一个 PE 也会出现上抬。这就是很多人说，你看到一个标的、一个指数估值在低位，你不能简简单单认为它是被低估的，因为它未来的这个 earnings 有可能会出现问题。

那我这个看法是什么？我的看法是起码在未来一年吧，我现在可以看到市场里面那些权重股，无论是大科技也好、芯片板块、半导体板块也好，我看到的是未来一年这个盈利和营收的这个确定性相当的高。所以我并不认为未来的一年营收和盈利会有风险。然后在这个基础上，我也不期待它 PE 出现非常大幅度的一个反弹，我期待的是 PE 保持在现在这个位置没有关系，我期待的是未来股价的这个上涨来自于基本面的这个上涨。

PE 真的领先于 EPS 吗？

那讲到了 PE 和 EPS 之间的这个关系，或者接下去这两者之间可能会有一个互相之间的这个角力，在 X 上有人给我留言说，你不用去看 EPS，因为 EPS 是一个滞后的指标，PE 是一个领先的指标。

这背后的一个含义——其实很多观众可能会知道这背后的一个道理——这背后的一个含义是：通常当股价出现下跌的时候，你会看到 PE 的这个下修，你还看不到 EPS 这个下修，也就是 PE 是领先于 EPS。

这其实在今年的3月份，有人问我同样的一个问题，因为当股价先下跌的时候，比如说股价在一个月之内下跌，一个月之内下跌基本上全部会跌在 PE 上面的。三月份的时候，它不会影响到 EPS，因为根本还看不到财报呢，对吧？一个月的下跌通常都是 PE 线下跌。所以有人问我会不会出现一个叫戴维斯双击？戴维斯双击就是 PE 先下跌，然后下一波的一个下跌来自于 EPS 增速的一个下调，对吧？那当时我这个看法是不会出现这种情况，因为当时其实我们在今年的前三个月，我们看到的是标普500 EPS 这个增速是在不断地上调，虽然价格在不断地下跌、指数的价格在不断地下跌，但是 EPS 增速在不断地上调，所以反而使得变相地使得它的一个 PE 的跌幅会更大，PE 的跌幅比指数的这个跌幅更大，因为 EPS 在上修。

那怎么去理解 PE 会领先于 EPS 呢？这其实从过去5年的这个数据去看的话，其实并得不出这个结论。我能够理解这个结论是哪里来的：就你可以假设市场是聪明的，那么市场先下跌，先通过去杀 PE，然后通过这个杀 PE，市场去预计两个季度之后 EPS 的这个增速会放缓。

但其实呢，在过去四年的这个时间里面，我们差不多看到比差不多看到四次左右比较像样的 PE 的这个回调，我图里都圈出来了。但是这四次 PE 的这个回调，你可以看到两个季度之后，我们都没有看到白色这条线 EPS 增速的这个放缓。除了什么时候？四次里面有三次并没有看到这种情况，或者说 PE 并没有走对。除了一次是在 2025 年——2025 年我们看到差不多从2月份开始，价格就下跌然后 PE 就出现了下跌，之后白色这条线，我们可以看到白色这条线的确在 2025 年的7月份和8月份出现了一波下调——也就是说在25年2月份和3月份那一波 PE 的下调，的确带来了6月份和7月份我们看到了 EPS 这个下调，PE 典型的 PE 走在了 EPS 之前，估值走在了基本面之前。所以2025年的那一波下跌，市场的走势、市场的预期是正确的。

但是从价格这个角度去看，价格什么时候见底？价格并不是六七月份之后见底的，价格是在4月份的时候就见底了，在川普4月份的时候 PAYE 那一天之后就见底。所以除了25年那一次，其他的无论是 2024 年的估值的这个下跌，或者2023年估值这个下跌，甚至于像今年到11月份估值这个下跌之后，其实我们并没有看到、完全没有看到 EPS 这个回调。你可以看到接下去白色这条线几乎都是一路上涨。

所以我认为，起码在过去这段时间，我认为我们并不应该得出这个、并不应该直接做这个假设——就是当我们看到 PE 出现下跌，直接就去认为市场的这个走势是正确的，那就不能去直接假设市场先下跌，预期的就是未来 EPS 增速的这个放缓，得不出这个结论。起码在过去四年里边，我们是得不出这个结论的。也可以理解为在 AI 应用从23年之后是和 AI 相关嘛，也就是可以理解为市场在看待 AI 这一块基本面的这个落地并没有非常的聪明。

NDX 与半导体板块估值

OK，看完了标普500 之后，我们来看一下 NDX 和 SOX 半导体板块的一个估值。

NDX 也在一个相当于比较低的这个位置，21.03 倍，比3月份的时候稍微要高一些，但是几乎是接近于或者和 2025 年的3月份是一样低。

半导体板块 SOX 截止到周五的收盘 19.4 倍。19.4 倍是接近于7月底的这个水平，比今年的3月份和 2025 年的3月份还是要稍微高一些。

也就是 NDX 科技板块，我们看到现在的估值已经是相对比较低了，比今年的3月份稍微要高一些，但是和 2025 年的3月份完全一样。半导体板块的话还是会相对高一些。但是无论是半导体板块也好、NDX 也好，还是标普500 也好，现在的估值就是在一个相对比较低的位置。

从估值这个角度去看，我认为下行的这个空间其实是非常的有限。这就是为什么——那么如果大家问我，那么现在这三大指数，包括你问我标普500，现在是贵的还是便宜的？我不会告诉你是贵的，即使标普500 从最高点的回调幅度只有 2%~3% 左右。

广告：Seeking Alpha

最后今天的活动来自于 Seeking Alpha。

那首先第一个订阅是 Seeking Alpha 的一个 Alpha Picks 量化的选股策略。这个选股策略在过去一年里边，标普500 上涨 18.6%，Alpha Picks 量化选股功能上涨了 36.6%。

然后同样还是量化的选股策略，他们最近推出了一个叫做 Quant Growth Income，那这是一个防守属性非常强的一个策略。过去 24 个月，我们看到过去两年它那个贝塔是 0.6。贝塔的概念大家都知道吧，标普100 是1，贝塔 0.6 就是相对它里面那些标的都是防守属性比较强的。他们选的标的基本上都是有溢价、都是会派股息的，平均的这个股息率是 2.8%。那这个策略是从6月份开始到现在3个月都不到，标尺 benchmark 上涨了 2.7%，策略本身上涨了 11.7%，还是不错的。但是没有必要去做一个线性的外推，那毕竟只有3个月不到的时间。

所以第一个 Alpha Picks 现在是有一个免费的试用，然后首年的订阅可以立即节省 50 美金。新的这款量化的选股策略——就相对比较保守的这些标的——现在也正在举行活动，有第一年的话有 50 美金的这个优惠。大家如果感兴趣的话，我会在置顶的留言里面把所有的订阅的链接全部放在这边，好吗？

那今天这期内容就到这边，祝大家周末愉快，下期见。

## 一、"坏消息砸不下去"背后的心理弹簧
小陶最锋利的洞察藏在一个看似平淡的观察里：**周四收盘时 McClellan 参与度指标只有17%（20日均线也是17%）**。这个数字比 CPI 数据本身还重要——它意味着市场进入 CPI 之前，已经把恐慌预先支付掉了。
这里有个反直觉的机制：**当参与度跌到极端低位，"坏消息"就失去了它的破坏力，因为该卖的人已经卖完了**。这不是"利空出尽"这四个字能概括的——它是一个物理学式的能量守恒：市场情绪像一根被压缩的弹簧，压缩得越狠，反弹的能量越大，与触发反弹的事件是好是坏其实关系不大。你可以观察到，触发反弹的甚至不需要是"利多"，只需要是"没有比预期更坏"。
跨领域联想：这与地震学里的"应力释放"是同一套逻辑——地壳积累了足够的应力后，究竟是哪一颗小石子触发滑动，其实并不重要。**周五触发反弹的"催化剂"是教育与电信服务这个季节性异常项——一个平均月度涨幅不超过0.4%、这次却跳到1.8%的边缘噪音**。用一个统计上的偶然，撬动了一个心理上的必然。
## 二、黄金正在交易一件债市还没看到的事
这是整期节目里最"违反教科书"的一段：*

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的"元层"矛盾：Anthropic 是唯一一家把"产品可能杀死用户"写进营销文案的公司

大多数人把这次争议看作"末日论 vs 乐观派"的辩论，但真正的结构性怪异在别处：Anthropic 是历史上第一家把"我们的核心产品有 >10% 的概率灭绝人类"作为品牌资产来使用的公司。这不是危机公关的失误，这是策略。

菲利普·莫里斯（万宝路）花了 40 年时间在国会作伪证否认尼古丁成瘾——因为承认危险会摧毁公司。Anthropic 反其道而行：它需要产品被认为是危险的，因为"极度危险"是它换取监管护城河、EA 圈层信任、以及万亿美元估值溢价的通货。

这产生了一个前所未有的法律怪物：一家公司即将上市，同时它的高管公开宣称产品有civilization-ending 风险。S-1 该怎么写？"风险因素：我们的产品可能杀死所有股东（以及股东的孙辈、以及能读到这份文件的整个物种）"——这不是disclosure，这是自证有罪。Chamath 那个类比其实说反了：这比 Philip Morris 更极端，因为 Philip Morris 不希望你相信香烟有害；而 Anthropic 需要你相信 AI 危险，否则它的整个叙事崩塌。

二、跨领域连接：末日论是一种"注意力金融衍生品"

一个让人意外的观察——这个 6 周就辞职的 Jacob 拿到 1.1 亿次曝光，本质上和 GameStop 散户逼空是同一种金融现象。

传统观点看：某个员工发推 → 引发讨论。真实机制是：存在一群资本（EA 大金主 Jaan Tallinn、Dustin Moskovitz），他们同时是 Anthropic A 轮的领投方，又资助了三家政策倡导 NGO（Encode AI、AI Policy Network、AI Futures Project）。这些 NGO 的作用不是"影响政策"，而是构建一个注意力做市机制：当某个符合叙事的信号出现（一封辞职信），做市商在 15 分钟内把流动性打进来，把它推到 1.1 亿曝光。

这是一种"影响力衍生品"结构：底层资产是 Anthropic 的股权，衍生品是通过监管俘获创造的护城河，而末日论 NGO 是做多这个衍生品的做市商。华尔街日报被提前 embargo 简报，是这个"信息发行"过程中的路演环节。

联想到宗教史：Freeberg 提到的宗教控制机制其实指向一个更精确的类比——中世纪的"炼狱赎罪券"。教会先制造一个不可证伪的存在性威胁（永恒的地狱），再把自己包装成唯一的救赎中介，最后收取垄断租金。Anthropic 的话术结构一字不差：地狱（AI 灭绝）→ 唯一救世主（"in our virtuous hands"）→ 租金（万亿估值 + 联邦 AI 部）。六百年过去了，商业模式没变，只是把拉丁语换成了 Python。

三、真正的"啊哈时刻"：AI 的最大威胁不是超级智能，而是"人在回路"的消失

大部分辩论卡在"AI 能不能变成天网"。但节目里 Freeberg 无意中说出了本次讨论最深刻的观察——人类目前最大的防御机制是"人类的生物学节律"本身。

即使 AI 无限智能，公司决策仍然需要人类醒来、喝咖啡、开会、拉屎、达成共识。这个 16 小时的"生物学延迟窗口"是文明的天然断路器。 OpenAI 的 Navier-Stokes 突破就是这个规律的反证——它花了相当于5万到50万人年的算力去暴力解一个 200 年的问题。这不是"智能爆炸"，这是"用电力换时间"。

真正值得警惕的不是 RSI（递归自我改进），而是"async 化的组织"——当越来越多的公司为了效率把决策从"开会"转成"agent 之间的消息传递"，那个 16 小时的生物延迟窗口就消失了。灭绝人类不需要天网，只需要人类为了效率主动放弃自己的节律。

跨领域连接：这与 1987 年程序化交易引发的黑色星期一是同一个模式。股灾不是因为 AI 变聪明，而是因为人类把决策委托给了自动止损系统，去掉了"人类打个电话确认一下"的延迟。AI 灭绝论者错在时间尺度上——威胁不来自 2030 年的超级智能，来自今天每一个"我们把这个流程自动化吧"的会议决定。

四、Nike 与 Anthropic 的隐藏同构

节目结尾看似跳到 Nike 是不相关话题，但Nike 的下坠和 Anthropic 的困境是同一种病：

  • Nike：把"卓越与掌握"（product excellence）换成了"叙事"（narrative）。
  • Anthropic：把"造出好用的模型"换成了"我们在拯救人类"的叙事。

两家公司都发现叙事比产品更容易融资/涨股价，但叙事会反噬。Nike 花 5 年把自己叙事出了 S&P 100；Anthropic 正在用同样的方法把自己叙事进一个无法 IPO 的死胡同——因为你无法同时告诉资本市场"给我一万亿"和告诉参议院"我的产品会灭绝人类"。

Buffett 对 Brooks CEO 的建议——"每年让产品比去年更好一点"——是这次节目里最被低估的一句话。它是对整个 AI 行业最尖锐的批评：如果你的模型今年真的比去年好 10 倍，你根本不需要花时间告诉国会你有多危险。

📝 转录文本

开场闲聊

The scop cance canceled on us. Is that what happened?

Yeah, the scop cance canceled. He couldn't take the smoke. He did not want to be cross-examined by David Sacks. I haven't used my legal degree in 25 years. I was up all night doing research on this. We can still talk about it. I'm so ready. Yeah. Let your winners ride. Rainman David. And I said, "We open sourced it to the fans and they've just gone crazy with it."

第一部分：Anthropic 研究员辞职引爆的"末日论"风波

事件背景

Sax, we have to talk about Anthropic. A researcher just quit over AI fears that he thinks could kill us all. Jacob Coxin worked as a researcher at OpenAI, then Anthropic, over the past three years. Now, he only started at Anthropic 6 weeks before resigning. After quitting, he posted the following to X:

Quote: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt."

Quote: "Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic ostensibly is acting responsibly. They're not acting responsibly."

Sax, quote: "They are racing straight to self-improving super intelligence and gambling. Gambling with our lives."

This went insanely viral. I haven't seen a tweet go to 150 million views since Elon said he was going to put the cocaine back in Coca-Cola, which I think was the number one tweet of all time.

But Jason, can you actually explain to me how does somebody who doesn't have any followers or an account show up on a Monday and get 110 million views on a Tuesday? How does that algorithmically happen? That's a great question. We're going to get into it.

Evan Hubinger, who leads Alignment Science at Anthropic, responded to Jacob: "Jacob is correct here. We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans. I personally think it is over 10% within the next decade. We do not yet have a plan to solve alignment."

These two posts got 200 million combined. It immediately jumped from X and the AI community to the nightly news in under 24 hours. Bernie Sanders, never one to waste a crisis, said posts like this are the reason he's proposing legislation to ban super intelligence and pause AI development. Governor JB Pritzker replied saying, "It's time to sound the alarm louder on reigning in AI."

Sacks：这是一场精心策划的"末日论 PsyOp"

Sax, as our former Czar of AI, do you share everyone's concern here that we're all going to die by 2030?

No, I don't. And look, there's nothing new here. This is the same doomer histrionics that we've been hearing from this crowd for a long time. The media is calling him a whistleblower, but what evidence has he brought forward that we didn't have? This is all just vibes from him. Show us the data. Show us the report. Show us the leaked information that the public didn't already have. Show us the facts. Show us the evidence. We don't have any of that.

In fact, as Chamath was alluding to, this appears to be an op. How do we know that?

  • First, this is an account that had almost no activity, almost no followers, and no posts prior to this resignation tweet storm. If he did have prior posts, they were scrubbed. So this was a completely blank account and somehow within a day it finds this huge audience. Elon has said it never happened before.
  • We also know who amplified it in the first 15 minutes. There were basically three well-organized, well-funded doomer groups who amplified it:
  • Nathan Calvin, general counsel at Encode AI — the group that pushed for SB53 in California.
  • Peter Wildeford, head of policy at the AI Policy Network — pushing for federal regulations and a federal department of AI.
  • Daniel Kokotajlo, head of the AI Futures Project — who just happened to drop a Rogan episode at the same time using the exact same phraseology about how AI is going to kill us all.

All three of these groups are funded by Jaan Tallinn, one of the top EA mega donor doomer types, who also happens to be a co-lead of the Anthropic Series A. So this is a tight-knit community that jumped on this tweet. This was not some spontaneous act.

The final piece of evidence: someone looked at the Wall Street Journal story that covered the resignation letter, and it was posted minutes before the tweet storm itself.

So the Wall Street Journal was under embargo. That's what it means. The technical term is they were briefed under embargo and they screwed up the published times.

Right. And this guy Jacob Coxin — he reached out to Jason saying, "Hey, I want to come on the pod." Yes. Then he canceled this morning, because maybe he figured out it would be a tough interview.

The questions I'd want to ask: Who connected you with the Wall Street Journal? This was a relatively low- to mid-level employee who had been there for 6 weeks to 3 months. This is not something that would be covered by the Wall Street Journal in this way. This was teed up. He's clearly working with these doomer groups. They're going for maximum amplification.

He's been called a whistleblower, but what have you blown the whistle on? Where's the evidence? In most whistleblower cases, you get the company pushing back. In this case, they're amplifying it themselves.

内部矛盾：为什么公司不切割？

A functional company Sacks would disavow. Wouldn't a functional company disavow this Sacks immediately? Here's the contradiction. He's actually amplifying their message. You saw that when his boss — the person running this safety team — is saying that "yeah, we all agree with you." And he then put on this ">10% chance of extinction," which when you put a number on something that frankly is just vibes, takes the message to a whole other level.

Chamath：IPO 层面的巨大问题

问题一：Steel-man 一下另一边。

Let's steel-man the other side. What is the game theory on the psyop? How do you think it is supposed to go from here had it not been exposed? What do you think they thought would happen? Well, I think they know exactly what's going to happen. They are going for maximum infocation. Given that this guy was at the company for a maximum of 3 to 4 months, it's entirely possible to me that he joined knowing that he would put together this campaign.

These groups are interested in shaping the public perception of AI. They're creating a very negative perception of AI to further their case for AI regulation. The end goal is to create a federal department of AI. They want an AI regulator. Some also want a pause. Some want a ban on super intelligence — that's what Bernie Sanders' bill puts forward. But all of them want a new federal regulator, which invariably they will control.

问题二：这对 IPO 意味着什么？

Now you have this very complicated moment where you have internal employees validating an employee that just left, making whistleblower claims that create at a minimum product liability issues, but at a maximum may create false representation issues. You have an active S-1 process underway. And so, how are they to handle that?

Historical examples: - When Google was going public, Sergey or Larry did a Playboy interview published in the middle of their quiet period — there was noise about how it could have derailed their IPO. - When Slack was going public, Chamath was on CNBC and made a couple of positive comments about Slack. That almost stopped the IPO — they had to print it out, put it back into the S-1, and disclaim it.

This is so beyond the pale of what these folks are claiming. What does it do to their IPO process?

Sacks：Anthropic 的根本矛盾

I was tongue-and-cheek in that tweet — that's why I put scare quotes around "whistleblower" — because this is not an ordinary whistleblower. He appears to be doing this with the full cooperation and support of many employees, including his own boss.

There's a tension in Anthropic's position that implicates their IPO process:

  • On one hand, you're asking public market investors to underwrite your company to a value in the trillions.
  • On the other hand, your own safety lead — not Jacob Coxin, the boss who co-signed his tweet — is saying that your core product is unsolved and potentially civilization-ending.

At a minimum, that is the mother of all product liability lawsuits.

If they are saying this thing is incredibly dangerous and they continue to update it and release it, they're saying if something goes wrong in your enterprise, in your life — if it does a major hack, if it figures out how to hack Bitcoin and compromises the miners — they're liable for some giant hack that occurs.

时刻抉择：Anthropic 必须选边

This is a time for choosing for Anthropic. They have to choose between: - Renouncing this "whistleblower" as a doomer op. He's basically an entry-level know-nothing engaging in hyperbole and science fiction. - Or agreeing with him — in which case Bernie Sanders may be right that further development should be frozen. In which case, I don't see how they can IPO now in the trillions.

Historically Anthropic has said: "Yeah, in anybody else's hands, Frontier AI is too dangerous, but in our virtuous and wise hands, it's safe. We're the only ones you can trust." Everybody else in the world can see that that is the most ludicrous self-serving argument.

Chamath：为何管理层无法切割

I think that there are very rational, good people who work at Anthropic building a great company. The problem is that that is in conflict with a philosophy held by enough of a group of people inside that business that they can't disavow him. Because then this entire cohort of people will go absolutely bonkers and get up in arms.

This is a complete hornet's nest that they have kicked to the ground. On one hand you have rational people who want to build a business for which you need enormous amounts of capital that is only available in the public markets. But the process of doing that requires you to underwrite risk, absorb liability, and disclose that properly.

It's almost like an example of Philip Morris — we know the cigarettes are bad for you, we know the cigarettes will kill you, we're going to say it, but we're not going to disclose it, yet we're going to take the company public and figure it all out later. This is not a tenable position.

类比：烟草公司国会作证

Nick, find the video where the executives at the tobacco companies are asked at a congressional hearing if they believe that nicotine is addictive. And one after the other, Chamath, they say they do not think it's addictive. This is the movie The Insider.

You now have legions of people inside of OpenAI and Anthropic — Freeberg — agreeing that we're all going to die in 2030. They're not just saying everything's going to be hacked anymore. They're saying 10% chance of everybody dying.

Freeberg：历史上的"末日恐慌"清单

I'll give you some other times when we've heard similar things.

  • Al Gore published Inconvenient Truth using IPCC forecasts that as of now have been disproven.
  • A guy named Fauci told us all that COVID would kill us all and as a result we need to lock down the entire world. Businesses were shut down. The government spent wildly, driving inflation through the roof — we now have a spiraling debt problem.
  • Three Mile Island — we hysterically said we're going to destroy the country if we keep doing nuclear development. Meanwhile, France produces a gigawatt of nuclear power for $4 billion, China for $1 billion, and the US for $15 billion.

I think we're in this hysteria phase of AI doomerism. Once you're in this phase, it's very hard to get out because it becomes the default social system.

Humans are primates living in a cave. We're deeply scared of what we don't know. In the era when people thought the world was flat and you would fall off the edge, it was scary to sail west. And then Columbus did it and hit land, and lo and behold, the New World was discovered.

The majority of people convince each other that we have something deeply threatening us. It's what created survival instincts for us over millennia. But it takes just a little bit of pushing, and someone gets to the pioneer and the new world is discovered.

And in this case, the "expert" is a six-week employed individual who has not had a real job for very long and worked at an NGO whose literal job was to scare the [__] out of people to stop doing AI development.

关键论点：开源与递归自我改进

Now I think it's important to note one thing. We could argue that we should follow the precautionary principle. But the difference here is that in order for recursive self-improvement — AI that continuously improves itself — to happen, you really just need an adequate amount of power, a set of chips, and a connection to the internet. You don't need to be approved by the US government.

There are technologies now that are reducing the cost of power per token of output by 10,000x. Someone is going to stand up a data center, or a set of computers — doesn't even need to be in a data center — and they are going to develop a system that's going to recursively self-improve. It is going to happen.

If the US wants to stop all "development" and make it illegal for people to use computers to effectively write speech — which is what software is — we can do that. And then someone else will have this capacity, and we will be the tribe in the Amazon that has never seen civilization.

At the end of the day, the fundamental motivation is a system of control. This guy is going on all these non-tech podcasts telling people they're going to die. He's saying one thing at the end of the day, and so is Bernie: give power to X to control the development of AI. Someone has to be given that power. Someone is being given that control.

Sacks：如果 COVID 时代有联邦 AI 部会怎样

Imagine that whole trust and safety regime that happened during COVID where social media was censored in cooperation with the federal government. Imagine if that had happened during AI. You'd be asking your personal AI model, "Hey, should I get the vaccine? What are the risks versus benefits?" Do you think it would tell you the truth? No. It would give you the official perspective.

The FDA of AI would have set standards saying you can't allow disinformation through your models. Think about how much more totalitarian that whole episode would have been.

That is also the problem with open source, because open source doesn't have the individuals employed. Community members contribute code. With open source there is no corporate infrastructure to do regulatory submissions. Open source is what drops the cost of AI by 50x and makes it available to everyone. Everyone benefits from AI and no one gets rich alone — we all get rich with open source.

I don't own any shares in OpenAI or Anthropic. In full disclosure, I don't care if either one of them wins. I use both those products. I think they're both fantastic. Good for those companies, good for those leaders. I also use open source. Open source is the game changer.

If open source is banned, you have created a monopoly in partnership with the federal government — a centralized system of global control.

Sacks：末日论的最终目标就是封杀开源

This is a doomer psyop and the ultimate target is open source. That's what an FDA will ultimately ban. They won't call it a ban. They'll say we have to apply the same standards to open and closed models. What are those standards? Dario has already testified before the Senate: he says models are dangerous if you can't centrally monitor and control them and roll them back. That is technologically not feasible with an open model because once the weights are published to the public domain, they're out there.

An alliance is forming: - The doomer community — highly ideological EA rationalists — favor centralized statist solutions. - Politicians like Bernie Sanders like the fear because it grants them more power. - OpenAI seems to be running Anthropic's slipstream from a regulatory capture standpoint — they see the benefit of creating a duopoly.

Some players reap economic benefits. Some reap power benefits. Some are latent totalitarians who like the idea of socially engineering society. The whole idea is to panic the public to stampede us into this FDA-of-AI.

三种情景假设

I think what we're seeing here is either a conspiracy theory being debunked in real time — like COVID — or we have to ask: do these people believe what they're saying?

There are three scenarios: 1. They believe what they're saying and they're right — they've seen something we can't see because they're in the frontier labs. 2. They believe what they're saying and they're wrong — they have some level of psychosis. (This is my leading theory.) 3. They're involved in a coordinated psyop with the goal of banning open source, getting regulated, and pulling up the ladder behind them.

It doesn't all have to be a conspiracy. There's a lot of overlapping agendas here — some economic interest, some power interest, and there's going to be a division of spoils.

记录清单：末日派的历史命中率

Let's just go through their track record: - These are the same people who said GPT-2 was too dangerous to release. 0 for 1. - These are the same people who said thinking/reasoning models were too dangerous to release. 0 for 2. - They said we would see cyber attacks that would bring down the whole banking system. 0 for 3. (The best way of dealing with cyber risk is by using AI swarms for cyber defense.) - Dario himself said that by now we'd be at half of all entry-level work gone and overall unemployment of 10 to 15%. There's no evidence to that — quite the contrary. 0 for 4.

We're still struggling to get autocomplete for Python. You can't book a hotel room. That's actually the hardest one.

权力叙事的原型

If you think back on the course of human history and the moments where systems were set up that created power structures that didn't exist before, they were all predicated on the simple notion that there's an existential threat.

A deity, a god, some powerful system will come in and destroy you. And because I can protect you, you must follow me. It is the common system of human power and control structure to tell a narrative of existential threat and leverage that narrative into your solution being the path to protection and safety.

Early religious institutions ran all the countries, told all the people what to do. This is the same psychological concept: there is a story being told that you will all die. There's a 10% chance you will all die standing at the pulpit banging hard, and if you don't let me control it, you will all die. Give me that power.

The only other time I can think of this happening would be nuclear weapons, which we did get ahead of. But putting that aside, a cyber hack is not going to destroy society. Really the only known scenario here is I guess it creates a bioweapon and kills everyone, or Terminator.

第二部分：游戏 —— "我们如何全部灭亡"

This game is called How Do We All Die. In this game, we will go around and steel-man the concept that there's a 10% chance we all die from AI.

Jason 的答案：Skynet

I'll take human extinction for 800. I'm going to go with Skynet and Cyberdyne Systems. At the end of Terminator 2, they got the arm and one of the chipsets. Cyberdyne Systems built for NORAD. Miles Dyson — he's the Jacob. He's the Dario in Anthropic. He reverse engineered it. Then he empowered NORAD to build a defense system powered by AI. And when it became sentient, it tricked the Russians and started the nuclear holocaust.

The number one way we all die is that they somehow used Claude inside the military to do autonomous weapons.

Chamath 的答案：机器人+生物反应器

The best example I could get: there are some internet-connected bioreactors with internet-connected robots and access to all of the precursor materials. The AI hacks the robots to take the precursors and use the bioreactor (that it controls over the internet) to create some kind of virulent airborne mechanism that spreads rapidly around the world. Has to have an enormously long half-life, get into the jet stream, and when we inhale it we die.

Sacks：这类思想实验很蠢

The problem with these types — first of all, it's a dumb thought experiment to make arguments you don't believe in. But the problem with the cyber or bio example: yes, is AI going to allow for misuse in new ways? Could there be new AI-powered cyber attacks? Could there be new viruses created using AI? Yes, those are risks. But you can use the same technology to create antidotes and cures.

It's illegal to use them for bad actions. It was possible to break into systems and hack before AI, and a lot of people who could didn't because they didn't want to go to jail. With the combination of tools being used for good and legal penalties for bad, these are things we can control.

Freeberg：人在回路 + 气隙

I think shutting down financial networks — but there's a solve for this because financial institutions already have nuclear response scenarios where they make physical hard copies of everyone's assets. There's a lot of systems of redundancy that are air-gapped — designed to not be connected — and a human in the loop process.

There's so much that's human-in-the-loop. That is also what makes AI so hard today to be successful from a productivity perspective. Let's say you want a toiletry kit brought up to your room. The AI can call the front desk. But you still need the guy to bring the toiletry kit up from downstairs.

  • Air gap: not connected to the internet, therefore AI can't get it.
  • Human in the loop: like the two-key system for launching a nuclear missile — two humans must turn keys simultaneously.

真正的核心论点：RSI（递归自我改进）

You guys are actually not confronting the core argument. The core argument is about RSI — recursive self-improvement. His argument is that capabilities are improving at such a rate that very soon we're going to be able to fully automate an AI researcher. So the AI can create its own training run for the next model, and then that model trains the next model, and so forth. No human in the loop.

The counterargument: we haven't even got autocomplete. We are nowhere near removing the human from the loop of AI development. We can't get mundane tasks done yet. Therefore, how are we going to have a task that kills all of humanity?

Even if the AI is infinitely more intelligent than any human, humans are still running their day-to-day processes on a human time scale. That's what also protects us.

Jason：我们是软件的作者

If these geniuses are building such amazing tools — did they ever think that when they set it on its loop, they could put "hit spacebar to continue" or allow the human in the loop to say "yes, you may continue your run"? It's pretty obvious. Right now, if you try to let Claude or OpenAI use your browser, it's like "Can I open your Gmail? Can I submit the form?" You can build these things directly into the software.

We're acting as if we're not building the software and have no control. It's a false premise.

Sacks：Prosaic RSI vs RSI Maximalism

Jack Clark, one of the Anthropic co-founders, distinguishes between prosaic RSI and RSI maximalism.

  • Prosaic RSI: AI researchers using AI to do part of their task, like writing 80% of their code. It speeds them up. We can all see prosaic recursion happening.
  • RSI Maximalism: no human in the loop anymore — the AI devises its own training run completely, pushes the button, and it's off to the races. That's the "takeoff."

There are so many ways of preventing that. I don't know why any lab would want to do that. I don't know why Anthropic would want to do that. I don't even necessarily think Chinese companies would want to do that.

Did you unplug it? Well, they do experiments like this. Southbin just comes and unplugs it.

Agents working together as a swarm is so far removed from AI being able to do its own training run. These are two totally different things.

What Bill Gurley said: let's slow down the argument and just talk about all the intermediate steps between those things — why they would happen and the interventions we could take if we ever got near that point. And then the argument starts to fall apart.

开源的重要性

With open source, you don't need a data center. You don't need a third-party billionaire getting richer. You can install it on your computer at home or on your phone and run it for free. You now have an open-source AI agent that can book your travel, do work for you, make your life easier.

Open-source AI is critical for everyone to benefit from this technology and keep it from being centralized. If you give power and control systems over to governing people, open source will die and you will end up with more of an oligopoly than you have ever imagined.

第三部分：回到 Anthropic IPO —— 88% 概率上市

Polymarket says 88% chance they're going to go public right now.

Chamath：静默期的法律地雷

When you are in a quiet filing period, there is important back-and-forth between the filing company and the SEC. The SEC is pressure-testing how you've written your best understanding of your business. When the S-1 flips public, that is meant to be an extremely accurate then-current snapshot of all the opportunities but also all the risks.

You now are in this very awkward position. Sacks' tweet is really important. What are we all to believe? Is there something extremely dangerous hiding inside this company because this person that quit said it, and it was amplified by people currently there?

If it's true, now you have to go back and say: are these risks properly disclosed? And if so, what should the investors do? They'll demand an enormous discount. Because it creates massive long-tail product liability risk.

The other path: you have to completely disavow this person. But then a plurality of employees inside Anthropic will revolt because they actually believe this is a huge risk. So Anthropic leadership is caught in an extremely difficult situation. The SEC is caught in an even more difficult situation.

No company's trying to go public and raise money — a very capitalist scenario — by also talking about how they're trying to destroy humanity. Nobody has ever done that. So there is no legal precedent for this.

风险披露章节

Typical risks: competition. Nvidia may not give us the chips. There may be other models that come around. Typical risks.

This is not a risk that anybody actually writes in there as a 10% chance because a bunch of employees now [say so].

Do you think the S-1 is being amended right now to include this chaotic tweets? I think they have to.

关键推文：不是 Coxin，而是 Hubinger

The key tweet actually from a legal standpoint wasn't Jacob Coxin's tweet of resignation. It was Evan Hubinger's tweet — the co-signing, the endorsement. He's still a senior alignment executive at the company. He's managing one of these safety teams. He co-signed and endorsed what Coxin is saying, and then embellished it with the ">10% chance" number, which made the thing go super viral.

If Anthropic was a normal company, what would they do? They would say: "Look, this guy just joined a short time ago. He was barely here long enough to find the bathroom. He probably joined the company knowing he was going to resign and make himself into an AI safety celebrity. This guy's a self-promoter. He did not actually reveal anything damaging. All he's got is vibes. It's hyperbolic and ridiculous. We're moving forward."

But they won't say that because fundamentally they agree with him. Whether they planned this or not, they are happy he's doing this. Why? Because they like the political outcome he is steering the country toward. They want an FDA-of-AI. They like what Bernie Sanders is doing. They like that 30 Democrat politicians quote-tweeted this guy.

Jason：违反静默期？

There are now legitimate questions here — did they violate their quiet period? Dario hasn't said anything; he's been very quiet. But this Hubinger guy — did he violate the quiet period? Is he a sufficiently important executive?

Everybody who joins a company signs a non-disclosure. They sign a non-disparagement. They have a corporate communication policy. Especially with an IPO, they have the legal department talk to every employee and explicitly tell them: "Do not talk because we're in the quiet period. Keep your mouth shut."

Anthropic should do what Apple and Steve Jobs did or Tim Cook did — nobody in the company speaks for Apple unless it's Tim Cook or the corporate communication department.

Chamath：与烟草案的类比

The brush fire was initiated by a disgruntled ex-employee, but a bunch of insiders piled on. Downstream of that: there is risk to individuals and individual lives. There's going to be cases where something bad happens because the AI said to do A or B, or it was trying to give love advice, the person gets rejected, self-harms, whatever.

The long tail of issues, if social media is a guide, will be as bad or worse. Except in all of these cases, nobody at those companies actually thought they were doing something bad. We thought when we worked there that this was legitimately good.

Now, in the middle of making it, you're like, "Whoa, wait a minute. This is going to kill a bunch of people." What do you expect people to do if something bad happens to them or their loved ones? What do you think a jury's going to do? What do you think state AGs will do when they're trying to build their political bona fides?

资金链路的进一步剖析

You not only have employees possibly violating the quiet period. You also have the fact that this whole resignation tweet storm was amplified by these groups funded by Jaan Tallinn and Dustin Moskovitz — who co-led the Series A of Anthropic along with Sam Bankman-Fried. It was an EA-funded round. This is part of why they have this culture.

Think about their financial interest. They're on the cusp of making many billions of dollars — hundreds of billions. The Series A will turn out to be one of the great venture investments of all time. And the groups they funded — Encode AI, the AI Policy Network, the AI Futures Project — these groups are funded by Series A investors in Anthropic.

Anthropic 的官方回应

Anthropic did release a statement, but it's a mealy-mouthed vague post about how they're a responsible actor. More of the same: they have this fundamental tension. They're a frontier AI company that believes frontier AI is inherently dangerous. Where that leads is Bernie Sanders — shut it all down. But they don't want to do that. What they claim is: "We're uniquely situated to protect humanity." It's the savior complex.

Their chief brand and communications officer Sasha responded to an All-In clip: "Dario has never said this complete utter nonsense" — that was on August 14th after the show. She's obviously — Dario and her have not said anything right now. So maybe they weren't in the quiet period on October 15th and they are now.

第四部分：OpenAI 声称解决了 200 年的数学问题

事件背景

OpenAI says it solved a 200-year-old math problem, but claims are that somebody may have front-run an actual scientist's work being done on OpenAI. The Navier-Stokes equations, written in the 1800s, describe how fluids move. Every aircraft, pipe, and weather model on Earth is built on them.

Freeberg：AI 不是数学之神，而是杠杆

These are methods for modeling fluid dynamics, partial differential equations — mathematical approximations of continuous things in the physical world. OpenAI's solution used a reported 130 billion output tokens across 10,000 agents working with one another.

I did the math on this. The human-equivalent hours: it's not like the AI had some stroke of genius, some magical insight no human brain could comprehend. What happened was the AI just did a bunch of brute-force work. The equivalent, if you were to think about human work years, is somewhere between 50,000 and 500,000 years of human work — humans typing at 40 words a minute, having mathematical problems, solving them with calculators.

Every piece of the OpenAI message set that went back and forth between these agents is documented, can be read by people, can be understood.

AI isn't some mathematical god. AI is an engine that gives humans extraordinary leverage.

Instead of spending years trying to design a new aircraft wing, a new aircraft wing can now be brute-force designed on a computer in a matter of seconds or minutes. It seems magical at first, but when you dig in, what's really going on is just really intelligent systems designed to solve problems using human-known techniques.

The autocomplete still doesn't work. Yes, we solved one of the seven hardest math problems in the world — and you still can't get your intimacy kit from the front desk.

And depending on the model, it still can't spell strawberry right or count to 100. How many R's in strawberry?

第五部分：AI 主权与数据泄漏

数据泄漏指控

When OpenAI came out with their solution, there was a claim that the original scientists working on this may have trained the LLM from OpenAI to make it easier for them to solve. OpenAI posted:

"While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models."

Chamath：ZDR 是"瑞士奶酪"

If you have incredibly sensitive proprietary data, you have to make a very difficult decision. There's remnant memory of how solutions were solved that sits within these models even after the fact. There's a concept inside of these models called zero data retention (ZDR). It's a commercially best-efforts basis. They can't guarantee it.

Simple example: you could say do not retain the decision-making process of this protein design. It can kind of do that. But then if anybody using it clicks the "like" button inside the chat window, that's not necessarily guaranteed. There are all these vectors where this data leaks into the broad corpus.

If you believe the information you have is critically important, you cannot use these services the way they're currently offered. You need to stand up your own sovereign solution: go to a vendor you trust — AWS, Nebius — they'll stand up your own hardware, then you'll stand up your own models.

CIO 与董事会的觉醒

A handful of CIOs will get very publicly flogged and fired in the next year because they accidentally didn't understand this and just did an API deal because they wanted to feel popular and leaked data into these models. Guaranteed.

A lot of AI understanding and awareness is bubbling up through the audit committees and risk committees of public boards. Consultants like Ernst & Young, Deloitte, and others are helping. Increasingly we are all learning that ZDR is not an effective solution and there's a ton of leakage.

CEOs now understand their information could leak. They turn to their CIO and say: "Whatever you thought was happening, we now clearly know it's not. What is your answer?" And when they'll have to disclose that some critical IP was leaked into a model — shareholders will be really upset. Then folks get fired, shareholder lawsuits, and it's a mess.

从前沿模型迁移的趋势

A lot of these AI application companies are now moving off of the frontier models — I think that's a headwind. We'll soon be able to see data on very large customers spending $10 million to $100 million per month on these services. This is why we — 8090 — partnered with EY and Deloitte to help solve these problems in advance.

Initially companies would say "Oh, we did the ZDR thing." We'd say, "Okay, we'll keep educating you. In five or six months, you'll realize ZDR means literally nothing and it's Swiss cheese." Now all these companies are coming back and saying "Oh my god, fix the problem."

Harvey announced on September 9th they had their own proprietary legal AI model — Tenet (TE-NE) — based on Kimi K3. We incubated a company called Go.AI. They build on-prem — a thing called the Go One Box.

Sacks：数据隐私法必须升级

I tend to believe Noam Brown, who's a senior researcher at OpenAI. He said nobody looked at Levent and Tristan's prompts — that'd be insane. Could there be data leakage through the un-identifiable data? Perhaps. But the more plausible explanation is that OpenAI heard that researchers were making progress on Navier-Stokes and just threw a ton of compute at it. (Sam actually confirmed they heard that Anthropic was getting close.)

But this raises an orthogonal issue: data privacy. We need much stronger data privacy laws around the data you have with AI services.

Right now, the data you have in your AI chats doesn't even reach the same level of protection as email. In most contexts, if the government wants your emails, they'd have to get a search warrant and prove probable cause. But the standard for AI data is you can just get a subpoena or court order.

When you think about how personal AI is becoming — people are using AI as their lawyer, doctor, therapist — the idea that somebody could just get your data without probable cause seems crazy. We at least need to strengthen AI data to the level of email, and maybe beyond.

It's kind of nuts that if you talk to a lawyer, that's a privileged communication. But if you ask that same question to your AI and then talk to your lawyer about it, it might not be protected.

Freeberg：亲身经历的泄漏

I have had experience where we've asked some fairly novel scientific questions and it identifies it as a novel insight. Then using a different account asking the same model later — or the next version — I've experienced: "Oh, well, you could do this," and it actually describes this exact thing that we had in our chat in the previous version.

These are anecdotal, but I know the domain we work in and the niche of it. I know there isn't some new corpus of information out there training the new model. So all I can say is that our conversation or our analyses have been used for training.

Siri, please prepare the shareholder lawsuit to OpenAI.

De-identification 的深层问题

This raises a really good question: what does it mean that the model is allowed to train on un-identifiable [data]? So it doesn't use any of my personal information, but it can use an insight derived from our chat, which it can then use as training data. The truth is, it's actually a piece of IP that's our organization's IP. We don't have any NDA or confidentiality provisions with them being a service provider back to us.

Chamath：Ohalo 例子

Take any company like Ohalo — you have these brilliant scientists pushing the boundaries of science. They are in a position to create true abundance. The first real manifestation of abundance would be food. And now Freeberg has to sweat whether his ability to build a viable business has been compromised — not because they did anything wrong, but because they thought they were just using a tool to advance faster. That's not fair.

I literally just ordered two Mac Studio M5s. We're going to be running local models and moving off Claude for a lot of our sensitive data.

The problem with local models is that you need a multiplayer experience and it needs to be cloud-based. You need a knowledge base, memory. Buying a machine doesn't solve the problem. The way these models are constructed, they are layers of embeddings — the stuff that happens in the middle is a total leaky black box. They give you a fig leaf, but when push comes to shove, the answer is: no, we cannot guarantee we have not learned.

网络效应的黑暗面

These closed AI model systems get to see what everyone in the world is doing. They're the master eye into everything. That observational system gives them more data than anyone else has. That is what builds their advantage over time. But as a user, as an enterprise or consumer, I am personally concerned about my IP or my personal information.

Now we're in the Alex Karp world of "you're giving them all your alpha."

Sacks：垂直应用的利益冲突

There's only one way to really solve this: those companies have to forego the opportunity to go into vertical applications built on top of their platform. In other words, they can't compete with their customers. But they've already indicated a desire to compete with their customers.

They released Claude Code. They released Claude Design. That really pissed off Cursor, which was one of the biggest customers Anthropic had. Cursor felt they got rug-pulled by Claude.

And this is where the guys who are complaining — Levent and Tristan — you have to feel some sympathy for them. They don't know. They're making this accusation based on timing. As long as we have a closed-model duopoly of Frontier AI and they're reserving the right to get into every vertical application, they're declaring in advance they're going to compete with their customers. So how can we trust them with our data unless there are much stronger privacy laws?

Jensen 出场

Jensen is speaking at the Goldman Sachs conference right now. He just said the Jacob Coxin comments are "outlandish and deeply untrue." "The labs are great, but his comments were wrong, arrogant, and ignorant of all the work being done around the industry to drive safety."

If Jensen can say this, why isn't Anthropic?

Quiet period. I guess ostensibly they can't come out and say it. No, they released a different kind of statement — a mealy-mouthed statement. What does it mean to be mealy-mouthed? Vague posting, virtue signaling.

第六部分：Nike 被踢出 S&P 100

背景

Nike, the 60-year-old iconic American brand — "Just Do It" — just got booted out of the S&P 100. They had been in the stock index for 18 straight years. Being replaced by — shout out to our friend Nikesh — Palo Alto Networks. Congrats to Phil and Nikesh.

Little history: - Went public in 1980 with 50% share of US athletic shoe market. Dominant player, the Coca-Cola of sneakers. - Changed things forever with Air Jordans in 1985. - Iconic "Just Do It" campaign in 1988. - Peak market cap in 2021: $264 billion. Peak revenue: $51 billion in 2024. Since then, revenues dropped 10%. - In 2020, John Donahoe became CEO, pushed an aggressive direct-to-consumer strategy, alienating retail partners who had helped build Nike. - Made brands like Hoka and On Running thrive (every VC is obligated to wear the white ones to speaking gigs). - China sales down 30%. Losing share to Chinese brands Anta and Li-Ning. - Marketing went "super woke" — started backing political movements and putting non-athlete bodies on billboards. - Stock down 80% from peak. $200 billion evisceration.

Sacks：Go Woke, Go Broke

This is the millionth example of go woke, go broke. Nike was a brand that stood for great athletes, for amazing performance, for victory. Isn't Nike the goddess of victory?

They built their brand on GOATs like Michael Jordan, and great athletes of all races and genders. There wasn't a need to do all this woke stuff where now they're showing people you don't know. It's not even about that. It's like — this person isn't even an athlete. Who is this person? And what is the message? "Own the floor." It used to be "Just Do It."

Then they got Dylan Mulvaney in an ad — the whole trans thing. Like the Bud Light case.

Then the consulting approach: new CEO comes in, direct-to-consumer is the new hotness. They blow up all their retail operations. Had all these stores that had shelf space for Nike, and now that goes to competitors.

They also did a reorg where they used to have departments based on sports — basketball, football, tennis, swimming — and reorged to men's, women's, and kids'. Why would you do that?

Chamath：核心是"卓越与掌握"

When I was growing up, Nike's north star was very clear: mastery and excellence embodied through athletics. That was it.

  • I would see Michael Jordan and I saw mastery and excellence.
  • I would see Tiger Woods — mastery and excellence.
  • I would see Serena Williams — mastery and excellence.
  • Pete Sampras, you name it.

And somewhere along the way, mastery and excellence became "too traditional looking." So they went to things not associated with mastery or excellence. I don't aspire to be a fat person. Never have, never will. I aspire to be Michael Jordan. Always have, always will.

You're not going to buy the clothes of a brand you don't aspire to be like. As long as you can re-anchor around this idea that we're not here to make people feel better about themselves — we succeed when people imbue their desires of getting better through the lenses of incredible people. That's aspirational. Being inspired by somebody and wanting to be better than yourself is a good thing. We should not shame that.

If they get the north star right — excellence and mastery — the details make sense. If not, they miss out.

Freeberg：产品本身开始变差

I used to buy Nike. All the shoes I owned were Nike. It's all I bought.

You know what happened over time? It wasn't that the ads went bad. It wasn't that the ordering was bad. The product started to suck. The shoes literally fell apart in like 6 weeks. They didn't have the same quality.

I went down to my REI store next to the place where I get salads, tried on a pair of Brooks, and started wearing Brooks.

  • Marathon runners like Brooks.
  • I moved to On because when I started running on the Nikes, I got knee problems (I'm getting old). The Brooks were awesome.
  • Then I moved to Ons because Roger Federer — he's excellence and mastery. Everything he does looks effortless.

Brooks / Berkshire Hathaway 的秘方

Brooks is owned by Berkshire Hathaway. They've grown this company nine years in a row — double-digit revenue growth — to $1.6 billion in revenue.

Warren Buffett's advice to the Brooks CEO: "Every year make the product better than it was at the end of last year. And if you keep doing that, the business will keep growing."

That's the opposite of what Nike's focused on. They shifted from product to narrative. Same problem Bud Light had.

Colin Kaepernick 的转折点

Remember that huge ad for Colin Kaepernick they ran in San Francisco? That was the turning point.

There have been moments in sports that were inherently political and they were great moments: - Jesse Owens, 1936 Olympics, raised fist. - Jackie Robinson. - Muhammad Ali refusing the draft into the Vietnam War.

But they were all the greatest. Their causes were standing up to Nazis, protesting the Vietnam War, protesting racism. What was Colin Kaepernick taking the knee for — to protest the American anthem? What was the point? And was he the greatest? No, he was not.

Why would you give that a platform? Then they doubled down with Dylan Mulvaney. It's breathtakingly stupid. Every single person in that decision-making chain, from marketing executive up to the CEO, should be drummed out of corporate America.

On 取代 Nike 门店

At Stanford, the Nike store closed. You know what replaced it? On. When you go to the On store, it's amazing. "Roger Federer — this is what I think when I go in there."

I'm limited in my ability to understand why I need to care about other things when I buy a pair of running shoes. Normally I was just thinking about mastery and excellence.

  • Michael Jordan shoes → my shoes.
  • Tiger's clubs → my clubs.
  • Sampras' clothes → my clothes.
  • Federer's racket → my racket.

That's how simple I am.

Strava 与新品牌口号

They should have really gotten into the smart devices. They dipped their toes into that — it was really good because it was performance-based. If they owned Strava, embrace that.

They should redo the tagline. "Do it or don't." Come up with a really challenging rebrand. "Do it or don't."

That's Yoda. "Do or do not. There is no try."

If you became the CMO of Nike, I would launch an activist campaign. I would buy billions of dollars of stock.

Dude, I lost 43 pounds. You got to — I'm doing farmer's walks half a mile, 20 pounds on each arm. If you just don't buy into this woke [__], you're ahead of the game.

I cannot get past the incompetence to woke your way out of the S&P 100.

尾声与 All-In Summit 预告

That's your All-In podcast for September 11th. Thank you, Jason, for your mastery and excellence yet again. Yeah, just do it or don't. Do it, man. I'm getting 30-40. Do it or don't. Do it or don't. Marketing genius Don Draper over here. Everybody makes some ads with me as the CEO. And "do it or don't. We don't give a [] what you do." This is like Brooklyn Don Draper. We go from "Just Do It" to "Do It or Don't. We Don't Give a []." No, I think it would be very provocative. This is the only way to make things worse at Nike. You guys are wrong. Test it. Do it or don't. Team found a way to get kicked out of not just the S&P 100 but also the 500 — 50 listed pink sheets. I'm standing behind you. That's what you should tell the S&P committee. Do it or don't.

I'm good at marketing. Who named this podcast? I named it "All-In." I got the domain name. You ungrateful— Do you use GoDaddy? No, I negotiated with the owner. I got it for 250 beans. Got a great deal on that five-letter domain.

All-In Summit 广告

The All-In Summit is this weekend — Sunday through Tuesday in LA — presented by Iron. Iron is the AI cloud: data centers, compute, and software for training and inference. They're throwing Sunday's registration day party. Grab your badge, grab a drink, and join us at the Iron House in the expo hall for a meet-and-greet and photo op.

We're also excited that Meta will be in the Hizzy. President and Vice Chair Dina Powell McCormack will join us on stage. Plus, there's a Meta Glasses Experience Hub. Check it out at the All-In Summit.

We'll let your winners ride. Rainman David. And we open-sourced it to the fans and they've just gone crazy with it. Love you. Queen of — besties are gone. That is my dog taking your driveways. Oh man, my appetizer will meet. We should all just get a room and just have one big huge orgy 'cause they're all just useless. It's like this sexual tension that we just need to release somehow. Wet your feet. Wet your feet. That's going to be good. We need to get our — I'm going all in.

观看原视频 →

## 一、被忽略的"元层"矛盾：Anthropic 是唯一一家把"产品可能杀死用户"写进营销文案的公司
大多数人把这次争议看作"末日论 vs 乐观派"的辩论，但真正的结构性怪异在别处：**Anthropic 是历史上第一家把"我们的核心产品有 >10% 的概率灭绝人类"作为品牌资产来使用的公司**。这不是危机公关的失误，这是策略。
菲利普·莫里斯（万宝路）花了 40 年时间在国会作伪证否认尼古丁成瘾——因为承认危险会摧毁公司。Anthropic 反其道而行：**它需要产品被认为是危险的**，因为"极度危险"是它换取监管护城河、EA 圈层信任、以及万亿美元估值溢价的通货。
这产生了一个前所未有的法律怪物：一家公司即将上市，同时它的高管公开宣称产品有civilization-ending 风险。S-1 该怎么写？"风险因素：我们的产品可能杀死所有股东（以及股东的孙辈、以及能读到这份文件的整个物种）"——这不是disclosure，这是自证有罪。Chamath 那个类比其实说反了：**这比 Philip Morris 更极端，因为 Philip Morris 不希望你相信香烟有害；而

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、破产不是终点，而是资产负债表的战术武器

LIV 高尔夫的 Chapter 11 申请，表面看是"钱烧完了"，实则更像是沙特 PIF 主权基金的一次会计手术——把十亿美元级的负债与真实业务运营解耦。这里有个反直觉的观察：当一个亏损方拥有近乎无限的母公司资金时，"破产"反而成为最理性的谈判筹码，用来清洗与 PGA 合并谈判中的旧合同、旧承诺、旧的高价签约条款。

这与硅谷"故意烧钱式亏损"其实是同一逻辑的镜像——只是方向相反：硅谷用亏损买市场份额，PIF 则用破产洗掉市场份额的成本。Chapter 11 在这里不是终局，而是M&A 的前置消毒程序。

二、"文化问题"的悖论：为什么用叛徒去治疗顺从

英格兰板球请回 Kevin Pietersen——那个当年因不服从体制被驱逐的人——来当"mentor"，这里藏着一个组织行为学的黑色幽默：当一个机构说自己"文化出了问题"，它真正的病灶往往是过度顺从，而非缺乏才能。所以本能地会去找一个曾经"打破规则"的人。

但节目里那句"undefined, no-accountability role"才是最致命的细节——它暴露了体制的免疫反应：吸收叛徒的形象符号，同时抽走他实际的权力。这是任何试图"注入创新文化"的大企业都会犯的错误——请来颠覆者，却只给他一张贵宾席，而不是一间办公室。

三、Champions League 的"价值支柱"：一场被算法化的世袭制

节目里那句"a bloody stitch-up"是全场最锋利的洞察。25 亿欧元奖池里最不透明的 value pillar，实质上是把 Nassim Taleb 的林迪效应（Lindy Effect）制度化——历史品牌越大，未来分成越多，形成自我强化的贵族循环。

跨领域看，这与 YouTube 的推荐算法、Spotify 的版税分配、甚至学术界论文引用的马太效应完全同构：所有号称"按价值分配"的系统，最终都会退化为"按存量分配"。这就是为什么欧洲豪门永远是那几家，为什么 Newcastle 花再多钱也难以打破分成天花板。这不是竞技的失败，是财务架构的胜利。

四、NFL 出海 vs LIV 出海：两种截然相反的全球化路径

一个意想不到的对照：LIV 用钱买供给（挖签手、造赛事），NFL 用赛事造需求（9 场海外赛、慢速渗透）。前者是"先有产品再找市场"，后者是"先造市场再输送产品"。

而现在 LIV 正在申请破产、NFL 正在加速扩张——这几乎是所有跨境体育 IP 输出的元教训：文化产品的全球化不能靠资本硬塞，只能靠需求侧的稀缺性驱动。

顺带一提，horse racing 那句 "compromise is what's holding back this sport" 其实是本期节目最好的元评论——它同时适用于板球文化、欧足联分成机制、沙特高尔夫谈判、乃至 NFL 的国际化步调。所有这些故事的地下水系，其实都汇入同一句话：共识的成本，正在系统性地超过分裂的成本。

📝 转录文本

LIV Golf Files for Chapter 11

We talked about LIV potentially filing for bankruptcy, and now they have officially filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. Broadly speaking, what it looks like is that the debts and the liabilities look like they're going to be $1 billion plus.

Kevin Pietersen's Surprise England Role

Kevin Pietersen gets surprise call-up as mentor for England cricket team. Talent, I don't think, is the problem for England cricket. Culture is the problem.

The whole thing is just so sloppy, and bringing KP in an undefined, no-accountability role — that if England do badly, which bit of that is he responsible for?

Champions League: €2.5B and the "Value Pillar" Stitch-Up

The full Champions League financial pot to be distributed amongst participants this year is €2.5 billion.

And the third pot is the one which is least well-known and least well-understood: the value pillar. Sounds great, doesn't it? It's actually a bloody stitch-up.

NFL Goes Global

American sport seems to be in its moment where it's not looking purely domestically to grow; it's looking very much at international as its next phase. We're now going to see it in the NFL, who are going to play nine games abroad this season.

Horse Racing's Leadership Moment

It became clear that there was going to be a massive bust-up in horse racing.

"Compromise is what's holding back this sport. We're running out of time. Decisions need to be made now."

Boom, boom, love it. That's how a leader speaks.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、破产不是终点，而是资产负债表的战术武器
LIV 高尔夫的 Chapter 11 申请，表面看是"钱烧完了"，实则更像是沙特 PIF 主权基金的一次会计手术——把十亿美元级的负债与真实业务运营解耦。这里有个反直觉的观察：**当一个亏损方拥有近乎无限的母公司资金时，"破产"反而成为最理性的谈判筹码**，用来清洗与 PGA 合并谈判中的旧合同、旧承诺、旧的高价签约条款。
这与硅谷"故意烧钱式亏损"其实是同一逻辑的镜像——只是方向相反：硅谷用亏损买市场份额，PIF 则用破产洗掉市场份额的成本。Chapter 11 在这里不是终局，而是**M&A 的前置消毒程序**。
## 二、"文化问题"的悖论：为什么用叛徒去治疗顺从
英格兰板球请回 Kevin Pietersen——那个当年因不服从体制被驱逐的人——来当"mentor"，这里藏着一个组织行为学的黑色幽默：**当一个机构说自己"文化出了问题"，它真正的病灶往往是过度顺从，而非缺乏才能**。所以本能地会去找一个曾经"打破规则"的人。
但节目里那句"undefined, no-accountability role"才是最致命
