Part 2 — Reading: The Investment Canon and Beyond

Interviewer: On reading — do you think you've learned more from studying the books within your industry, the investment business ones other hedge fund managers have written, or from other domains? And how do you think about the competitive advantage that comes from reading more broadly?

Pasquet: Both.

Why you have to know the investment canon

First you have to know the investment canon, we call it. And there's a couple reasons for that:

  1. Common language. That's where you're going to pick up on the common language of your business.
  2. Reference examples. There are reference examples in those books that you have to know because those are often the reference examples that your PM (if you're an analyst) is going to use, other analysts are going to use, and other people are going to use. Even management teams are going to use them.
  3. Historical context. To be good at what you do in a space, you actually have to know the historical context of your industry. Because if you don't, you won't realize when things are changing.

And if I could add any value to your listeners is: you have to be change investors. Change is what creates volatility, contention, tension, apathy, hatred, narrative change, regime change, and all the things. And if you're not used to seeing when your industry is changing, you actually might not either make money or stop yourself from losing money.

The diminishing returns of the 30th investment book

There comes a point though where you don't need to read the 30th investment book that tells you that you have to buy things cheaply. Because in our business we lack terminology and vocabulary for really important things in investing. You actually have to figure out if other fields have developed things, processes, tools for those things.

Timing — the great vocabulary gap

For example, timing. The timing methodology in investing is largely non-existent. Fundamentally speaking, if you speak to most fund investors and you say "What do you use for timing?" — "We don't time." And they're almost proud about that.

If you speak to the traders and you say "What do you use for timing?" — "We use technical analysis." If you listen to Stan Druckenmiller — who is one of our heroes of course — somebody asked him in a book once what do you use for timing and he says "I use technical analysis and liquidity considerations." And for some reason the author of the book or the interviewer didn't go into with Stan and say "Hey, what the hell do you mean by liquidity considerations?" Or what actually happened is Stan did answer, but he edited that out for competitive reasons. When Stan probably had final cut, Stan's like "Yeah, don't put that in there." Or at least that's probably what I would have done.

So it happens that outside of investing, the timing literature is actually really profound — in sports it's profound, and in intelligence and the military. And does it help to actually read up about timing in those other fields and then apply that to investing? I would say that it does in a big way.

Portfolio managers wear many hats

There are things about leadership. Being a portfolio manager, you wear many hats: - You're a leader. - You're a coach. - You're a talent selector.

Show me the investment books that are about picking talent. How is that possible? I go to business schools often and I say "Hey, is there a class on hiring at this business school?" The answer is no. How is there not a class on hiring — one of the most important talents that you need? So reading outside of your field is very important.

Recommended reading

Within the field: - One Up on Wall Street by Peter Lynch - You Can Be a Stock Market Genius by Joel Greenblatt - The Letters of Warren Buffett, compiled by Cunningham - Any book by Hagstrom - All the books by Michael Mauboussin and his essays, including More Than You Know and Expectations Investing - Reminiscences of a Stock Operator - The Jack Schwager books - Steve Drobny's books - Other esoteric investors most people haven't heard of

Outside the field: - Psychology - Sales — one of the big analytical advantages you can have is looking at a company and saying "they're really good at sales." Most analysts look down on sales. Reading about sales and talking to a CEO about how he sets up a go-to-market strategy, lead generation, the first pitch — a lot of the business improvements that have come from Silicon Valley actually have to do with sales, and a lot of value investors don't know those business practices. - Sports, the military, intelligence — in many ways we are intelligence analysts. We're covering business things, and businesses have become very good at spying on their competition. Learning intelligence techniques and tactics is paramount.

Part 3 — Lessons from Inside a Top Quant Fund

Interviewer: So what you touched on there — when we're talking about reading — is really building sort of a qualitative decision engine in your head, right? To —

Pasquet: We call it analog training.

Interviewer: Analog training. I want to touch on the other side of that. Looking at how a fundamental hedge fund manager uses the quantitative side, especially given the fact that you had access to a top quant fund and you learned a lot from that process. What are some of the things you learned?

1. Their approach was behavioral

First we learned that their approach was behavioral — that their quant funds and quant tools and the way that they traded were designed to exploit the behavior of other market participants. That was the first place that I really understood that. Because my entire career, because of my background in backgammon and poker — it's not that I was a great technical backgammon or poker player. It was the psychological dynamics that I think I exploited over the backgammon board and over the poker table. And when I came to investing, that was what I was good at.

By the way, I actually didn't know I was good at that. But all my friends kept coming to me about it. So — oh, I guess they won't talk about it because that was the part that I was good at. One of the problems with early career is you actually you're unconsciously competent. You may not know what your strengths are. It's not until somebody shows them to you that you go and you turn that strength into 5x or 10x it.

We saw that the behavioral side wasn't only with small caps or midcaps — it could happen with massive companies and even more so with commodities, bonds, currencies even.

2. The importance of talent

This firm hired some of the most talented people that I'd ever seen, and it wasn't uncommon for me to feel intellectually inept when I was around them. They not only knew how to hire these people, but they knew how to motivate them and then incentivize them. And there's a lot of science. The founder of that firm, despite being — in a very complimentary way — brainiac on the nerd patrol, he was actually a very, very good businessman as well. Knowing how to motivate people and incentivizing them is not as easy as it sounds, especially for a quant fund.

3. Data — finding, acquiring, scrubbing

You actually had to know how to find a source of data and spend a fortune acquiring that data. That's actually a massive barrier to entry to doing a quant fund. Well, you need that access to that data. But then once you had access to the data, you actually needed to know how to scrub it. Why? Because often people entering the data are making mistakes. And if you're trying to use the data to pick up on market inefficiencies, your quant system might think that that blip is an inefficiency when that was just a mistake.

4. Transaction costs, leverage costs, and market impact

Lower your transaction costs and leverage costs — too high can eat into the profitability of the trade. And the importance of not having market impact. Very often if you trade a certain amount or at a certain speed you could actually make the market move in the direction that your algo says the inefficiency exists in — and you didn't want that to happen.

5. Temporal stops, not just financial stops

If you look at most trading systems they have a financial stop — if the position goes down 10% (arbitrary; probably not what they use, but 10%) they would get stopped out of the trade. But they said it was very important to have a temporal stop. If you're in the trade and you haven't made money in a certain period of time, you needed to get out. That's actually very valuable because sometimes even on a fundamental basis, we invest in something, and it's like 6 months later — what did we get wrong? Did we get the setup wrong? The timing wrong? The fundamental inflection point wrong? You need to have temporal points when you actually revisit the thesis.

A private lesson: go to the source material

There's one more, from me. I got a bit frustrated with this quant fund at some point because I had to look at them (one of my mentors had become president of the shop). At one point they would not tell me a lot about the models they used and I got a bit frustrated. So I made a list of where their employees mostly had gone to school, and I just showed up at the school and studied what the school's expertise was at when it came to the physical sciences and the other sciences out there.

And I think that's where we saw what were the scientific basis for a lot of the trades that they did. The lesson: go to the source material. Source materials matter — especially using a scientific principle that you then apply to capital markets. That's pretty cool and powerful.

Part 4 — Applying Quant Lessons to Fundamental Investing

Interviewer: What were the lessons you learned from the quant fund that specifically fundamental investors can apply within their own process, within the way they build their business, the way they make decisions?

Data integrity — even for fundamentalists

On the quantitative basis side — if data integrity matters, we have to remember as fundamental investors that the data given to us is mostly by management teams. Those management teams have an incentive for you to have a certain interpretation of that data, to be kind. So have a natural skepticism as to what data is out there, specifically by management teams that have lawyers and boards of directors and incentives to show data a certain way.

I was with a CEO once and he says: "You have really high conviction on your point of view right now based on data that I've given you or not given you." And he was right.

Direction, not accuracy

Quantitative techniques, specifically statistical techniques, are actually very important — knowing how to think statistically, probabilistically, in scenarios, and using quantitative models to be able to do so. We're not great at it but we use it. Our goal is not accuracy; our goal is direction. Whenever the quantitative models are pointing a certain way, that's good enough for us. Because we don't try to have any sort of accuracy that could actually be dangerous.

Don't compete for proprietary data

It's also one of the reasons why we're very skeptical of all data — all data that everybody else has. Some of the pods probably have proprietary data that no one else has access to. We're not going to try to compete there. Not only because it's very expensive to acquire that data, but again, you have to know how to scrub it, interpret it, invest based on it. Because most of our investing tends to be mid-term and long-term (and don't get me wrong, we take advantage of short-term opportunities as well), we try not to compete in that segment of the competitive landscape.

There tends to be even more so now a quantification fetish going on in the investment business currently that we think is very dangerous — because it tends to give you a sort of conviction that you should not have. The qualitative, specifically the qualitative stuff that machines have a hard time seeing — that's where the advantage is going to be.

Part 5 — Competing Against the Pods

Interviewer: How do smaller funds like yours compete against the pods? These guys have theoretically all the data. They've got so many advantages, even in how trades are routed — they can just cross them with PMs.

Play weaker players

The goal is — step back a second. A lot of game theory is very technical and mathematical, but it really can be reduced to one thing: play weaker players. Don't get into the ring with Mike Tyson. That's not what you want to do.

We don't try to compete with the pods. They are richer than we are, smarter than we are, move faster than we are, have more resources, in many cases are better looking. We don't do that. That's bad for our self-esteem and for our ego and also our wallet.

Don't compete on hiring, don't compete on horizon

We don't try to compete with them on who they hire. They're starting to interview sophomores and juniors in college now. I can't afford to pay an analyst $300,000 plus a bonus, including half a million dollars. These kids are great, and once they go through these places, the analytical turnover inside these shops is high enough that you get to hire them perhaps afterwards. It's very difficult to hire and compete with Ken Griffin or Dimitri or any of these guys. We have a lot of respect for them. We admire them greatly. We've studied them. We don't try to compete with them.

The type of ideas that we look at, the type of people that we look to hire — they're still good, but there's inefficiencies at both. And whereas pods have been lengthening the type of trades they do in terms of weekly, monthly, we tend to like dynamics that are 6 to 18 months length and even above that. There's names in our portfolio that we've owned forever, and there's names that sometimes we own for 18 months where the upside happens in weeks.

Don't compete on research dollars either

Another way that we don't compete is with research dollars. Some of the research costs that these larger hedge funds are paying the Wall Street banks to get one-on-one access to management teams at conferences — in many ways, some of these hedge funds pay more to get the first meeting so that they can then trade on that. We don't do that.

I'm writing my business plan again because we have to rewrite it to fit more the age of AI. And one of the sections is: we have no requirement in our process that says you have to meet management teams. No requirement that says you need all data. No requirement that says you need Wall Street research. No requirement to hire from certain schools. Strategy is about tradeoffs. Let them have that. We'll be right here. And there's a lot more advantage here than you would think.

Part 6 — Idea Generation

Interviewer: Talk to me a little bit about your process. Idea generation is the most important component of any investment process. What is your idea generation process for finding great stocks?

1. Other smart investors

There's an amazing book — it's part of the investment canon — Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits, and Phil Fisher says that he did a study of his idea generation and he noticed that close to 80% of his best ideas actually came from other investors. You'll find that to be consistent across the investment landscape.

There's so much information in the world that we find that the best filters of information are other smart people. We actually are not fans of quantification tools to filter out information. One of the reasons is we're evolving more and more into a world of private information and public information. A lot of stuff is going to happen on the private side that the public side will never see. I'm not talking about anything illegal, but there are sources of information out there that the big LLMs and the big models will never have access to.

Michael Dell talks a lot about on-premise information and on-premise algorithms — because if you're a government or an institution, do you want to give your information to some of the other models out there? No, you don't. So how are you going to get a semblance of what information is going on in business that can actually feed you ideas? In our opinion, it's other people.

Diversify your network — by style, age, country, geography

It starts with having a network of some of the smartest investors — but that is not just one style, because that's a mistake. If you're a tech guy, most of your network is actually going to be in tech. That's going to lead you to crowdedness and the same store investments. And crowdedness comes with its own risks. Better yet, most change, if you actually see it, tends to come from outside your field.

So it's very important to have a network of investors that are separated by strategy — long/short equity, long only, traders. One of my closest friends is a French trader that's one of the best traders I've ever met, and he's really good at trading US stocks, particularly midcaps. Having conversations with investors of different ages, different styles, different countries, and that live in different geographies. I speak to a lot of Texas-based hedge funds, California-based, Florida-based now, and even Boston-based.

If you're a rookie and you don't know these investors today, you can track them: 13Ds, 13Gs, 13Fs. A lot of them have public hedge fund letters that you should be reading. You can track them on Twitter, on LinkedIn. Hedge fund guys also tend to not speak enough to the real-money group — mutual funds, pension funds. There are some really, really smart people in those worlds.

2. The Top 100 CEOs list

Track what we call the top 100 list — a top 100 list of CEOs that you think are really, really good. And when they say something, study it. If the CEO of a very large social media company starts talking about certain aspects of semiconductors (that actually happened a couple years ago), maybe you should pay attention.

It helps if you have access to these CEOs, but are you listening to their conference calls? Reading their letters? Reading them on Twitter, LinkedIn? Today, if they're really good and they have a content strategy, odds are they're speaking on CNBC or on podcasts.

There's a very smart investor who says: "When you're looking for opportunities, opportunities just don't float around the sky. They're usually attached to people. So if you're looking for an opportunity, you're actually looking for a person." Our approach: smart money makers — track what they're doing.

3. Thematic work — and the collision of themes

You have to figure out preferably early what are the most powerful economic, geopolitical, regulatory, social, and demographic trends going on in the world and be able to understand how these forces are pushing a business forward or acting as a headwind.

Value investing taught you to look at things bottom up. And the reason why that happened wasn't because Mr. Graham or Warren were bad at understanding what was going on in an industry — it's because back then they didn't have access to the information that we have access to now. One of the reasons why value investing worked really well is you could buy something cheap that was very good and no one knew that it was good because there wasn't enough information on it. But today, there's so much information that if something is cheap, usually there's a really good reason why it's cheap and that reason is terrible.

You're not going to have a really good athlete that's great trade cheaply for a short period of time. People are going to know today if a company's a great company. Trust me, it hasn't escaped people that Visa or Mastercard — I often look at certain investors that are long only and quality-focused, I'm like: I bet you a hundred bucks to a hat pin that Visa or Mastercard is in that portfolio. And yes it is. The cat's out of the bag.

We know that high-quality businesses over a certain period of years are going to have a certain return. But guess what happened this year? Quality took a dive, and a really big one. And you have guys that are long only — it's going to take them a couple years, if not 5 years, to dig themselves out of that.

The insight there is: it's not that a theme is powerful — it's that when two themes collide, they're really powerful. That's where it creates businesses that could have what Charlie Munger called the lollapalooza effect, where this incredible emergence comes out of the business or the industry. One example: the aging of the population + robotics. We actually believe that some of the first good robotics products are going to be products that have solutions for the elderly globally.

4. Conferences — even if you have to crash them

There are 50 global conferences in the world today, and you don't have time to go to all of them, but you should be going to at least half a dozen to a dozen. When I was a kid and I couldn't get into these conferences, I'd crash them. I remember going to the conference every year — I would show up to where the name tag was and I would say "I don't see my name tag." And this really nice woman would call, "Oh yeah, of course, what's your name?" and she'd write my name down and I'd go into the conference. After 5 years of doing this, the CEO of this company who's running the conference — I'm having a drink with him — he's like, "By the way, we love you. We see you every year, but we still don't know who you are." And I'm like, "Well, I've been crashing this." He's like, "Why do you want to crash this?" I'm like, "I learn a lot from this." It's actually a private company. I used to learn a ton from them.

5. Test products — including "the female test"

Test products out. There's no greater joy for me than going to a conference or trying a product out, looking up to see how well known the product is, knowing how good it is, and then realizing this is going to be massive.

My female friends are amazing at finding new ideas. We call it the female test. You want to find out what's a great product, whether in retail, fashion, or others — ask your female friends.

Example: Lululemon. Very early on — I'm not into yoga, I've done yoga but I didn't know what yoga clothing was or athleisure. There was a girl I was going on a date with, and she's like, "Have you heard of this Lululemon?" It actually was a pretty good investment for us — not at the IPO, but later on.

There's a famous Canadian brand we first heard about from one of my female friends, and then one of the best money managers I know in Atlanta pitched it to me as a long. So I'm like, "Wait, first she's telling me this, then I'm hearing it from my buddy who's one of the best stock pickers I've ever met." I went down to the store in SoHo and took a look at it and it was: line out the door. OK — we have to do the work.

6. Analyze your own recurring charges — and travel

Whenever I'm with an intern, one of the things I have them do is: take out your credit card statement, or your parents', and highlight the recurring charges. Then look up to see if they're public companies. It's a very good way — because if you're a customer, you'll understand if the product can do well.

The last thing: travel. If you're a young analyst and you're not traveling at least 2-3 months a year, you're doing yourself a massive disservice. Not because you're going to get a massive edge doing it — I actually think you are — but also because you won't be able to do it when you're older and married. You won't be able to travel as much.

There's a way deeper game to idea generation than that, but started that way you've covered a lot of the bases.

Part 7 — People as Indicators & the Bull-Bear Debate

Interviewer: Another idea I hear you speak about a lot is using people as indicators. Can you talk a little bit to that?

Groups, not individuals

One of our tools is the bull-bear debate. Let's step back. There are analytical tools, informational tools, and behavioral tools. Most people, when they say they have a behavioral advantage — show me the behavioral tools that you use. For most of them, their behavioral advantage is: they have a behavioral finance list of things that they run their thinking through.

One of the problems of behavioral finance is that (1) it was come up with by academics, and (2) it was by testing individuals that they figured out these individuals were prone to doing these things. The problem with markets is that markets are not about individuals — they're about groups. So if you're going to have a behavioral advantage, it's about exploiting group behavior, not about exploiting individual behavior.

Don't get me wrong, sometimes you have one investor that's massively long, and as we saw recently, there were a bunch of people that exploited that levered dynamic. But most of the time it's going to be a group of people that are experiencing some sort of a group psychosis and then they're causing a supply/demand imbalance by either piling into a security or piling out of a security.

Debating your own side

One of the behavioral tools we use is a bull-bear debate. If we're short something, let's find a bull to debate. But sometimes we'll actually debate another short-seller by taking the bull side, even though we might be short. In those practices, doing five or six of them, you start realizing "wait a second, I'm wrong" — that in a debate I'm holding on too tight to this when this clearly doesn't matter economically, and what he's actually saying is what matters.

Often you realize the other person is wrong and they're holding on to their thesis not because of fundamental reasons but because of institutional reasons, cultural reasons, or something that happened to them in the past. If an analyst has lost money on a name and he's looking at it again, it's very hard for him to erase that loss from his judgment. And good luck if the PM has lost money in it, because the analyst is like: "I can't even pitch this to my PM because we lost money at this once."

Intellectual honesty and the Valeant postmortem

Having indicators in humans is very important. Be very upfront with people when we think — "here's what we think is going on" — and learn from it or not at your discretion. We're supposed to be in our business highly intellectually honest. But there's very few people that are actually intellectually honest in our business.

There's a very famous blowup — Valeant Pharmaceuticals. One of the estimates I saw was that hedge funds had lost a combined $40 billion in Valeant stock. That's how much they lost. Until now, we only know four postmortems on Valeant, meaning hedge funds that have done a postmortem that says "here's why we lost money in this and here's why we were wrong." Most people just move on.

Cross-referencing ideas — Rob Citrone

As a portfolio manager and investor, one of your tools is cross-referencing ideas. Even though I did that, I didn't have the term for it. I was listening to one of my favorite investors on a podcast — Rob Citrone at Discovery — where he says that one PM skill is cross-referencing an idea. When you cross-reference an idea and you get a sort of 360 review from the idea and you compile, you'll learn a lot from the individual conversations. When you compile the aggregate conversations, you're actually going to see what were the leading indicators and what were the lagging indicators.

So it's also going to give you a sense of timing. Some people, their point of view is the past. This is clearly changing. And other people, they're pitching you the future. Indicator work is very powerful.

Book recommendation: The Art of the Long View by Peter Schwartz. He gives you a whole bunch of processes and tools on how to do that in the book.

Part 8 — On Technical Analysis

Interviewer: You just mentioned the word timing, and I can't help but think back to the earlier part of our conversation where you touched on Druck and how he talks about timing — uses technical analysis and liquidity considerations. A lot of people say technical analysis is complete useless. What are your thoughts?

From skeptic to convert

I have to admit that I used to be one of these people as well. I used to think that it was hocus-pocus. There is no smart technicians, there's no rich technicians, all that stuff — until I met two people. One is my business partner who is an avowed technician. The other is a very private person, so I don't know if he would like to be named, but let's just say he's a partner at a major macro fund and has his own private investing gig on the side.

Both of them explained technical analysis to me in a behavioral lens — that it wasn't about picking stocks, but about helping you explain what was going on with the other market participants out there that were actually trading this thing.

Especially in a post-2022 market

It's very important to be a technician, especially in a post-2022 market. Because you know who uses technical analysis? The algorithms, the quant funds, the pods. If you're in a stock and it breaks a sort of technical level, you better have the staying power because it is going to crash and go down even more than you actually think.

Technical analysis is paramount in our opinion. And by the way, now there is no greater competitive pleasure than hearing really, really smart people say "I don't do technical analysis." So we love to hear that.

I would not use it for idea generation. Druck didn't say "I only use technical analysis." He says "I use technical analysis and liquidity considerations." But you bet your bottom dollar he also has a fundamental point of view as well. So you've got to use technical analysis, liquidity considerations, fundamental work, behavioral work — you've got to set up what's called in the industry a mosaic of advantages.

The moat–chart connection

Sometimes we have another mystical sense of technical analysis — not mystical in religious terms, but mystical in terms of moats. If a business has a moat and the moat is expanding, Mrs. Market feels that and that chart is going to be like [rising]. There's no such thing as a business having a moat for decades and the chart is like [flat/down].

So if a stock is like [rising] — and most value investors like to buy a stock that is flat, goes down, and they want to buy it there. Why? Because every reference example that they've studied 3,008 was always examples of something like that. American Express goes through the salad oil scandal, it crashes. Buffett is at the bar checking to see if people are still using American Express, puts 20% of his fund in it, makes a fortune. Today those reference examples don't matter anymore. If a business is down, usually it's down for a really really bad reason. Of course, there are reasons why it comes back, but until things change, it won't. So technical analysis is important because there's actually a connection with moats.

If a moat is expanding, we actually believe the chart should be strong. If you're showing me a chart that's come down like that, there's a competitive problem here. That's actually the first place that we start, and it's very common today. I would argue that when a stock is down and it has a moat problem, it's probably even better short than it was before.

CANSLIM and William O'Neil

There's an amazing book — it's come out of favor for some reason by most hedge fund guys because there's almost a negative perception to it, but it's total BS — How to Make Money in Stocks by William O'Neil, and he gives a methodology called the CANSLIM methodology. Most analysts today, specifically value guys that are really good analysts, should read that book. Because that methodology gives a lot of ways of thinking that can turn an analyst into a PM.

Step back a second. One of the inefficiencies that we take advantage of in the hedge fund business is that we don't train an analyst to be a better analyst. We train an analyst to be a future PM — whether he's going to be a PM or not one day. And by doing that, he's actually going to become a better analyst. He's still going through the analytical tools, but now he can think in terms of risk and reward, cross-referencing ideas, doing bull-bear debates, leadership, management, coaching. All the tools he's going to need to be able to run money one day. In fact, the analyst-to-PM transition model in the hedge fund business is broken, if not flawed.

O'Neil makes an amazing point: over decades, he's analyzed all these traders and only 2% of them were able to buy stocks when they were making new highs. Almost everybody is like, "Oh, the stock is too high right now, so I actually can't buy it here." Whereas if you really think about it, the best stocks that have ever been are always making new highs. But there's almost a disease in our business — "oh man, I can't buy that chart." Like, why not? "The stock's up too much." It's about where it's going to be, not about where it's been. I'd argue it's actually better in an environment (especially for our stock criteria) to buy at new highs. We're not afraid of that at all. On the contrary — if I see a stock that's down, something's wrong with it.

"Get bigger as things get better"

Druckenmiller has a principle we've adapted: get bigger as things get better. He didn't explain what "things" were when he said that at a conference, but for us it could be the fundamentals, the behavioral stuff, the thematic stuff, and the timeline of the idea.

We do use technical analysis. I've read maybe one book on it. There are definitely certain chart patterns that we prefer over others, but we do track volumes, moving averages, all these things — because they do give you a picture of what's going on with a certain group of investors.

Part 9 — The Future of the Analyst in the Age of AI

Interviewer: Where do you see the future of the analyst job? I ask that question with the context — I've had guests on this podcast who will say on this podcast that analysts are good, you still need judgment, all these things — and then off the record will tell me "I think the majority are screwed."

Structure precedes culture

We don't [think analysts are screwed], for a couple reasons.

First, let's start with structure–culture. Most people when they talk about culture often don't understand that the structure in which the culture resides matters a lot. Whenever you speak of culture, you should always have the person say "OK, that's fine, but how do you structure your investment team? Are they structured as generalists or specialists?" — because that structure is going to lead to totally different cultures. Are they structured in terms of your portfolio management structure — Jones model, market neutral, beta neutral, factor neutral — these are all things in which your culture resides.

One of the things that impacts culture is your tools. And one of the mistakes hedge funds are making today is adopting these AI tools and not understanding that it's impacting their culture. Because if one of your reactions is "I have to get rid of these juniors because they're not adding any value because I'm getting all the value from the AI tools" — well, you just fucked up.

Why? Because juniors ARE the culture

Because you know what a culture really needs? Juniors. They ask the naive question. They give you energy. They develop — in many ways, it's your legacy. The legacy of a hedge fund manager is not just that you made your partners a lot of money and yourself — it's that you made your team. And a lot of guys have left to start hedge funds. It is a godsend and a blessing that so many people left Julian Robertson and made fortunes, multi-billionaires. I could name 12 of them. That's a legacy.

So if you're not hiring juniors and not training them because you're getting cheaper AI tools, you have a cultural problem. In fact, you're probably going to have a problem where you realize it's not fun to go to the office anymore. You know what's fun? Having young people around you and taking down big scores together. Speaking to a whole bunch of old fogies that no longer want to short stocks, no longer want to go on the road and visit companies — I can't do that. So I'm with my wife Saturday, and the joke is "we're going to go Bed Bath and Beyond, maybe Target, we don't know." That, no. Let's go take down big scores together. Let's go get rich together. It's fun. Let's go visit companies together. Juniors want to do that. The established guys, they don't want to.

The bionic analyst — five analog skills

The future of the analytical community is a sort of bionic — somebody that knows how to use the analog tools and somebody that knows how to use digital tools. You know how to use the AIs to learn, dig deep into your thinking, find your weaknesses of thought, find and exploit inefficiencies. But you also know enough about the qualitative and the analog to be able to do what we call the analytical tools. There's five of them:

  1. Recall of past patterns, specifically competitive patterns. You need to know reference situations competitively — so that when you look at something, you're like: "You know, this reminds me of what Walmart did to the small regional guys at the beginning." Because those competitive patterns tend to repeat.
  2. Visualization skills. A CEO says something and your mind — because you know the industry structure, who he competes with, who his suppliers are, who his customers are — can actually visualize whether that's going to work or not.
  3. Reading between the lines. The CEO says this (live or in a transcript), and you're like: that's what he said, but based on his incentive structure, his culture, where he's based, who he knows — here's what he actually means.
  4. Leap of judgment. You look at a company's sales department and how they run sales, and there's a problem with it. Then you make a leap and you say "It's not a problem with the sales — it's actually a problem at the board level." Somebody: "How do you know it's at the board level?" Because if the board was good, they would have fixed this. They would have gone to management and said "What the fuck are you doing? You got to fix your sales." Generally a board level that's really good at sales is very important.
  5. Synthesis. You take recall, a little bit of visualization, a little bit of leap of judgment, a little bit of reading between the lines, and you synthesize it together in a thesis.

Those are the core analytical skills. Overuse of AI hurts these things, but doing them together — I think that's going to be the future of the business.

Why over-reliance on AI produces the worst PMs

I also believe — and I'm willing to be proven wrong — that over-reliance on AI tools is going to create the worst portfolio managers that we've ever seen a decade from now. Because to be a PM, you have to learn how to act: - Not only having those five analytical skills, - but you have to act within constraints, - you have to act without resources, - you have to act often without being able to see what somebody is pitching you (you don't know these companies; sometimes you're being pitched a company you don't even know), - and you have to learn the weaknesses in your analyst to be able to super-size them or under-size them.

It's actually a skill that most PMs have — when we talk amongst each other, it's like "Do you super-size this guy or do you under-size him?" PMs don't like to talk about it, but it happens. All these skills — AI over-reliance blunts. So my people are not going to have that problem. Competitively, I think it's the greatest period for long/short that we are entering — mostly because people are over-relying on these AI tools.

Part 10 — Building Both Analog and Digital Mastery

Interviewer: If you're a young person today and you want to have that combination of skills — the analog bug, reading, deep thinking without any tools whatsoever — and then also wanting to be at the forefront, how do you build those two in tandem? Because I don't know anyone…

Pasquet: There are trying to be a few — you know, people who are exceptional at these two.

A bionic protégé

There's one specifically. He was my intern and he's now at a holding company. He's actually my partner's little brother. He's built some tools that I'm so jealous of. It's unbelievable. In fact, we were looking at a major theme together, and I think in a weekend with these tools he found the crux company that we hadn't found after 6 months of looking at this thing. He did it in the weekend. It's literally the crux of the theme. It's actually a short theme, so we can't discuss it, but it's the thing that we track — when that thing goes, the entire sector is going to go.

But guess what? He also happens to be trained not only by me but by a really good investment bank, by a really good investor at the shop where he was at, and they've taken down major scores together. So he has the analog training and now he has the digital tools. Together — I don't know if people are going to adopt this term — but we call them the bionics. They have both human and machine in them.

There are a bunch. The way you get good at it is reps. It's the only way.

Know the weaknesses of your weapons

Some advice for posterity's sake. Know the strengths and weaknesses of these AI tools. You have to know them. You don't go into the battlefield without knowing the weakness of your weapon. You have to know the offensive advantages. You have to know the defensive advantages. You have to know when the weapon jams and what to do when it jams. If you're fighting a tank, you don't bring a handgun — you probably need something sturdier.

There's a lack of understanding as to what the weaknesses of these tools are. We think they're fantastic and only getting better. They have major blind spots, and you have to know what those blind spots are.

AI mistakes repeat across domains

One way to study this: if you look at artificial intelligence — whenever it's entered the field — when it entered intelligence, severe mistakes were made. When it entered the military, same. When it entered backgammon, same. Poker, same. Chess, same. Go, same. And those mistakes tend to repeat.

In fact, I would argue that outside of games, you have what's called wicked environments — environments that change in ways that are nonlinear and in many ways non-stationary. A lot of data that artificial intelligence uses is stationary. The world is nonlinear, prone to emergence, and non-stationary. So you have to be very careful using these tools out in a universe that frankly doesn't care if you're using these tools or not. It's like: "Oh, you think that you're right? Watch what happens." Boom. The world changes on you.

July 2025 — the AI-firms' comeuppance

I find it very funny that all the people that literally made their businesses into artificial intelligence were all down 10-15% in July because their tools didn't pick up on what was going on. They didn't realize there was a levered player out there blowing up. Very, very few market participants knew about it. By the way, we didn't know. Once it happened, we understood what to do, but we didn't know that was happening.

Read sci-fi

Funny enough, a lot of those strengths and weaknesses are in sci-fi books — where artificial intelligence goes wrong or goes right. You kind of need to learn what those are.

Elon Musk recommends reading the books of Iain Banks. I used to read those when I was a kid. The Culture series is about a universe where there's an artificial intelligence called the Culture that runs the universe, and the humans within it live and interact with each other. But every once in a while the Culture decides to become mischievous and create all sorts of trouble for the humans. Now the humans have to also battle other alien cultures that don't have AI, and the AI forces the human to battle these cultures. It's fascinating, but also hilarious to see the human stumble when he doesn't understand how to deal with the AI.

You have to read the Ender series by Orson Scott Card. Ender Wiggin has an AI in his ear that, as he's interacting with humans, is telling him what to say or asking questions and literally making fun of the humans as they're speaking. There's a scene where the AI thinks it's funny what happened to one of the humans, and the scene is designed so that you laugh with the AI, but you feel sad with the human. Ender gets upset at the AI and shuts her off, and the book goes into AI time. A machine in 1 second might be an eternity. Whereas for you, only 1 second passed, but for the machine it was an eternity. So the fact that you shut her off only for seconds was enough for her to be pissed off, and all the things that happened after with that.

You better know the strengths and the weaknesses of these tools if you're going to be using them. These kids don't understand it. PMs don't understand it. There's a lot of mistakes that are about to be made because of these tools — because now these artificial intelligence tools have not only become for analysis, but people are using them for portfolio management as well. The market is a complex adaptive system. It's complex, it's adaptive, and it's a system. It's going to adapt to you using your nice little AI tools. So be careful.

Part 11 — Building Personal Competitive Advantage

Interviewer: How should young people find and build out personal competitive advantages? The old systems of recruiting or learning under a mentor — fewer people can get access to that, or at least it's harder. What are the ways in which someone can figure out their own competitive advantage and scale that up into something defensible and profitable?

Start with what gives you energy

It helps to know what gives you energy first. A lot of my personal moat tends to reside around the fact that I'm an extrovert. What gives me energy is people. If I'm by myself too much, I actually get depressed. Because being by myself drains my energy. Knowing if you're an extrovert or introvert is very important.

As an aside — I find it a competitive pleasure to see that most people don't believe in personality typing. If you look at the reasons why they don't believe in it, they are nonsensical. Because they neither know the strengths nor the weaknesses of these tools, and they don't know the perspectives that these tools actually give you. They haven't studied it — they just say it's, as a friend of mine calls it, "astrology for nerds." That's what she calls Myers-Briggs. And yet there are definitely certain Myers-Briggs types that show up more often than others in the very wealthy or ultra-wealthy lists.

Design your workflow around your energy source

If the analytical work gives you energy, do the analytical work first. If talking to people gives you energy, do the talking-to-people work first. That's what I do. Very often, even before I've ever even studied a company, I'll go into the field and start talking to people about it. That gives me energy, and then I do the analytical work. But if you're an analyst and what gives you energy is being in your own internal world, do that — that's what's going to give you the analytical advantage.

If you're an analyst trying to get an analytical advantage, and you still need to do the field work and behavioral work by talking to people, and you're uncomfortable doing that — then your advantage is to find an extrovert and do that work with him. Feed him the analysis, he does the work, he reports back to you.

The power pair — leadership tension

Investing is a team sport. The power-pair concept is very important. If I'm an extrovert, I want an introverted dork with me doing the work together. If he's a slow decision maker, I'm a fast decision maker — that's really good. He slows me down, I speed him up. I'm good at the behavioral and the field work. He's good at the analytical work. We make a great team together — and 1+1 doesn't equal one. That's how you get the 10-baggers. That's how you create a sort of leadership tension.

Part of the job of a leader is knowing how to create tension in a team and knowing how to resolve the tension so that the tension alleviates. The way you do that is you take a big introvert and a big extrovert, have them work together. The introvert is exhausted by the extrovert — "I can't take it anymore. This guy wants to hug all the time. He wants to go out. I just want to read 10-Ks." And then the extrovert is like, "Dude, how do I get information out of this guy?" There's that tension, and your job as a leader is to manage that tension so that they find magic. Because tension leads to resolution, and the resolution we believe is alpha.

Analytical, informational, behavioral — on offense

By doing the things that give you energy, you then try to get an analytical edge, an informational edge, or a behavioral edge. Use those things analytically, informationally, and behaviorally on offense. So if you look at a company, there needs to be analytical elements you think you understand and other people do not. There need to be informational elements. There need to be behavioral elements.

The informational stuff — it's hard. There are people spending a fortune at getting better information. There are hedge funds that are hiring now Bain, Boston Consulting Group to do analytical reports to get a competitive advantage. So the information is tough to get. It still exists, but it's hard. And then you have the compliance factor — very often you have to get that information vetted to see if you don't have any MNPI.

Your network is your moat

One thing you'll realize is that your network is going to be your moat.

Step back a second. Most hedge funds are very fragile enterprises. There's no terminal value. Your assets go up and down elevators all the time. Your assets are contractually your assets for a short period of time. You tend to have chunky investors. You add the vagaries of the stock market. It's actually a pretty shitty business. When you get it right, the cash flows are amazing. But can I sell my business one day? No. Very few hedge funds have terminal value. I mean, Citadel, Balyasny, SAC — those guys have created terminal value, but most hedge funds fail. Most hedge funds have restaurant-level failure odds.

Interviewer: Higher, even.

Pasquet: Let's not go that far, but at least our economics are way better. But we fail. And by the way, if you study hedge fund fragility, the fragility has actually increased over time. And no one actually explains why or understands why. I wouldn't start a hedge fund until I understood — we've been around for what, a decade now. We're still fairly small and we're only learning how to grow. Right now. But I can tell you it took a while to get an edge. Took a really long time. There are people that just got lucky in the beginning, and then over time get a lot of assets, and their performance goes down, but the economics are good enough that they could have made some money. But this is a tough business.

One piece of advice — a lot of investors are really good at applying competitive strategy to their investments, but they're not good at applying competitive strategy to themselves. As an analyst — what are your barriers to entry? What is your moat? How can you deepen these barriers? How can you deepen and expand that moat? Very often it's going to revolve around your network.

Part 12 — Moats in People, Podcasts, and Life

Interviewer: Studying moats for me has been one of the most rewarding things I've ever done. Even with a podcast — network is huge. Being able to pull different references from different guests. That's right. Understanding social media algorithms and how to distribute content. Understanding how the sausage is made in terms of production. It's not something I ever thought about as a business — until it just turned out it was. And then I went, "Hold on a second — got to take it seriously, got to understand how the sausage is made." Viewing things from the frame of moats has transformed my understanding.

Pasquet: And then you start to see it not just in businesses, but in people. "OK, what is this guy's own moat? What's his own competitive advantage?" Hold on, I got to bet on this guy. Or, hold on, this guy should hire this guy. Because — oh my gosh, if he has this moat of a skill set, the business just explodes. You get moat expansion.

Interviewer: Precisely. What are some other ideas that you can take from the investing domain and apply to the human domain, the talent domain, and really understand the way people work — and by extension, the way systems and the world works?

Moats and barriers to entry — the Amazon test

There's so many. Even though we're not value investors, we use value concepts. The concept of moats and economic castles was first elaborated by Warren Buffett. Then Michael Porter took his competitive strategy framework and understood barriers to entry — he has five competitive forces, but really there's the first among equals, which is barriers to entry.

If you and I wanted this weekend to take Amazon's customers away from them, how would we do that? We'd quickly come up with a lot of barriers to entry. In fact, if somebody gave us a trillion dollars, could we go and take Jeff's customers away from him with the kind of returns on capital he has? I don't know. Good luck.

Margin of safety — in life, not just portfolios

The one concept I would apply in a really big way is margin of safety.

Margin of safety was coined by Benjamin Graham in The Intelligent Investor. And I actually do believe that he came up with it because Graham got wiped out in the Depression. One thing he realized is that if you needed to make an investment that was worth $100 and you were buying it for $50, you had a margin of safety of $50. Why is it a margin of safety? Because if you're partly wrong and it's only worth $75, you're still making that 25%.

But if you think about it, in many ways a margin of safety is actually a competitive advantage. If you're building a business and you're spending half of what your competitor is spending to build that business and earning the same returns, well, your returns are going to be higher. That's an advantage. Why? Because if things change, you have more money to use to take advantage of this change, whereas he doesn't.

Personal margin of safety

Thinking in terms of margin of safety in your personal life is an aspect of investing that I think is underrated. - Do you have a frugal lifestyle? - Have you put cash away as a margin of safety? - If there's change or you get fired, do you have enough cash to be able to pick your next role? - Do you have enough cash to have spousal support?

Because very often when things go wrong, it's not just you that you have to take care of — it's your family. I always say to guys: "Put at least three to five years away of personal cash, because markets are markets. You don't know what's going to happen."

What happens? You're an analyst. You make a lot of money. Your spending goes up. You do better — house in the Hamptons, kids in private schools. You're always working. The CEO of your personal overhead, by the way, is your spouse. She's spending money. But then guess what? The fund goes through problems. That bonus you think is coming is not coming. What happens? We've seen guys having to take their kids away from private schools, having to move to other neighborhoods, can't afford the house in the Hamptons anymore. It's deadly.

Coffins don't have drawers

It's very important to structure your personal life to have a margin of safety for your investment life. And there's going to be a lot of forces that tell you: spend more money, keep up with the Joneses, go to St. Barts — "Why aren't you in St. Barts for Christmas?" Be careful. Live below your means. Put cash away.

I didn't say be stupid either. There's a saying in Brazil that I love: "coffins don't have drawers." Live — but don't be stupid either.

Why high overhead blinds you

Most people don't understand why a very high personal overhead stops you from seeing threats and opportunities. A threat is coming or an opportunity is coming — but as opposed to focusing on it, what do you focus on? The fact that there's a leak in the basement of your house in the Hamptons. It's taking too much intellectual, emotional clutter — and financially. Instead of looking at threats or opportunities, you're in an art gallery, because you're buying art, because you met this really attractive girl at the art gallery that's selling you paintings.

Seriously, this stuff happens. And by the way, these art galleries have people that are designed to find guys like that. A friend of mine and I are like: "How come we've done so well and these art gallery girls haven't found us yet?" Because we don't have the kind of profligate lifestyles. Who are they going to go to? The guys that spend money or the guys that don't spend money?

The frugal billionaire

Very important to keep a frugal, balanced lifestyle. Every great investor I know tends to be highly frugal.

There's a reason why Warren is very frugal. A friend of mine was an analyst for probably the best long/short manager alive, and the long/short manager was very frugal to the point where he only travels everywhere on coach — doesn't have a private plane despite being a multi-billionaire, only flies coach.

My test for that: there's a yearly conference in Idaho, and he's often on the same plane that I'm on. And I'm shocked because I'll be sitting in business class and this guy's sitting in the back. The first time it happened, I'm like, "There's no way he's going to be in coach." No, he was in coach with his wife — multi-billionaire.

My buddy was an analyst for him. He was going to visit a company and he had gone out the night before. He's like, "I'm exhausted. I went out last night. I don't feel like sitting in coach. It's a 6-hour flight. Let me sit in business so I just sleep." So he gets into business class that he paid for himself. They were all going to a conference in LA. Another PM that knows him well is like, "You're sitting in business?" "Yeah, why?" "Your boss is here. He's going to be sitting in coach." So my buddy literally hides himself, and his boss walks in and goes to coach while he's sitting in business. He was mortified.

But that frugality — you know, we make fun of it because the person is cheap. But he doesn't have the clutter of wasted resources. When an opportunity comes, he can think about it. And more importantly, when change hits him, he can actually adapt. Because you know what stops you from adapting? Resource clutter. When you have to take the ship and veer it in another direction, if your boat is heavy, you're going to have a hard time doing that. You might get swallowed up by the time you do.

So I would say that that's the last thing — really learn how to use value investing principles, investment principles, in your personal life.

Close

Interviewer: Learn how to use value investing principles in your life and investing principles broadly, and you'll be able to take advantage of things when they come up. Thank you very much for coming on the podcast. This was a pleasure, man.

Pasquet: Thanks for having me. Thanks.

## 词汇的黑洞：投资界最深的秘密不是知识，而是缺失的语言
Pasquet 说了一件极具颠覆性的事——基本面投资者"不做择时"，几乎带着自豪。但真正的原因不是他们哲学上鄙视择时，而是**这个行业根本没有关于择时的词汇**。你无法练习一个你没有名字的东西。这暗合维特根斯坦的命题："我语言的界限就是我世界的界限"。所以他把军事、情报、体育的择时文献拿进来——不是为了跨界炫技，而是**去偷别人的名词**。更耐人寻味的是他讲 Stan Druckenmiller 那本书里"technical analysis and liquidity considerations"后面那段被访谈者删掉了——真正的 alpha 常常藏在"被剪掉的那一段沉默里"。这给出一个反直觉的搜索算法：**找到你所在领域里大家闭口不谈、或每次谈起就换话题的地方，那里就是竞争地图上最富集的矿脉**。
## AI 的自噬悖论：好工具正在系统性地生产坏 PM
这是全场最锋利的一刀，也是最容易被误读的一刀。Pasquet 断言"十年后我们将见证史上最糟糕的一批投资组合经理"——不是因为他们不够聪明，而是因为 AI 太好用。这

item.title: [Mercatus Center] Aishwarya Kekre on Land Fragmentation and Its Impact on Structural Transformation
item.dc:creator: Mercatus Center
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被误读的"小农优势"：一场统计幻觉的胜利

Aishwarya 论文中最耐人寻味的悖论在于——小农场每英亩利润更高这个看似"温情"的结论，可能根本不是"小的更美"，而是市场扭曲的统计残影。当她在模型中关闭"小农盈利优势"这一渠道时，整个福利结论符号翻转：土地碎片化变成了纯粹的净损失。

这暗示了一个令人不安的可能性：印度过去 70 年被歌颂为"社会正义"的土地再分配政策，其经济正当性可能建立在一个测量伪影之上。那些用来为小农辩护的"每英亩产出更高"的经验证据，或许只是投入品市场（信贷、劳动力监督、家庭劳动力的机会成本被系统性低估）扭曲的镜像。换言之，我们看到的不是小农的效率，而是大农被更严厉的税收和监管所惩罚的负片。

二、跨领域连接：土地碎片化 = 印度版的"专利丛林"（Patent Thicket）

这是最出人意料的类比。Aradhya Sood 提到 Tata Nano 项目需要与 12,000 名地主谈判 4,000 英亩土地——这在结构上等同于生物科技公司为开发一款药物需要绕开数百项重叠专利的"反公地悲剧"（Tragedy of the Anticommons），Michael Heller 在 1998 年正式命名了这一现象。

有趣的是： - 专利丛林中每个专利持有人都是理性的钉子户，集体阻止创新 - 土地丛林中每个小地主都是理性的持有者，集体阻止工业化 - 两者都源自"过度产权私有化"——不是市场失灵，而是产权颗粒度过细导致的市场无法组装

这个连接的启示是颠覆性的：印度问题的根源不是"资本主义不够"，也不是"社会主义不彻底"，而是产权的粒度（granularity）出了错。土地被切得比可交易的最小经济单位还要碎。这跟频谱管理、水权分配、甚至太空轨道分配面临的问题在数学结构上是同构的。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：印度可能不是"农业过剩"，而是"土地负债"

传统叙事说印度有过多劳动力被困在低生产率农业。但 Aishwarya 的模型揭示了一个更深层的机制：土地本身成了一种"负债性资产"——它锁住了劳动力（作为家庭劳动力的机会成本沉没），却又无法被抵押、无法被交易、无法被转换用途。

这里有一个让人后背发凉的推论：当一份资产的持有成本（社会地位、家族关系、法律纠纷风险）大于其变现价值时，它在会计意义上是资产，在经济意义上是负债。印度 2.8 英亩的平均农场，本质上是世代相传的负债性文化资产，就像日本泡沫破灭后那些"负价值"的老宅一样。

跨领域联想：这与经济学家 Hernando de Soto 在《资本的秘密》中描述的秘鲁棚户区惊人相似——那里的居民拥有"资产"却无法转化为"资本"。但印度的情况更荒诞：不是缺乏产权登记，而是产权太清晰、太多方、太固化，反而制造了同样的"死资本"。

四、意外观察：福利结果的 50/50 分裂说明什么？

论文中一个容易被忽略的数字是：50% 的地区福利上升，50% 下降。这不是噪音，这是一个信号——说明印度已经处于结构性转型的临界带（bifurcation zone）。半个印度的经济动力学与另外半个正在朝相反方向演化。这几乎注定了未来十年印度的地区不平等会以历史罕见的速度扩大，也解释了为什么"一个印度"越来越成为一个政治想象，而非经济现实。

工资下降 1.92%、地租上涨 5%——这个约 7 个百分点的裂口，就是印度民粹主义、种姓政治、以及"农民抗议"三年不歇的隐藏能源方程式。

📝 转录文本

开场与介绍

Shruti： Hi, Aishwarya, welcome to the show. It's a pleasure to have you here.

Aishwarya： Hi Shruti. I am very excited to be here. Thank you for having me on the Job Market Series. And like, this is my first time ever on a podcast, so it's also exciting and a little nervous.

Shruti： Well, it's all downhill from my podcast, you know, after this. No, I wanted to kick off my Job Market Series with you because—I mean, the paper is on land and land fragmentation and structural transformation. These are two themes that have preoccupied my imagination and my work for a long time. So when I saw this I was like, okay, this has to be a good start with this paper. And I am really excited.

论文核心发现概述

Shruti： So what you do in your job market paper is you look at the impact of land fragmentation, specifically on India's structural transformation. And because of a combination, you know, of land redistribution laws and land ceiling laws and India's inheritance laws and customs, average operational land holding size is sort of half in India since the 70s—you know, down from 5.6 acres to 2.8 acres. And you find that this greater fragmentation actually reallocates labor away from manufacturing to agriculture, thereby reducing manufacturing activity—which is exactly the opposite of what the policy goals and the development goals are in India. And this, of course, what you find is more acute in the case of land-intensive industries.

More specifically, in terms of the results, you find that on average, district-level farm size fell by 12.45% between 2001 and 2011, implying a 3.2 percentage point increase in agricultural employment share and a 2.2 percentage point decline in manufacturing employment share. That's the first big result, and again, exactly the opposite of what the policy goals and intentions are.

The second major finding is that between 2005 and 2013, the average decline in farm size implies a 30% decline in manufacturing employment, a 20% decline in the number of firms, and a 15% decline in the average firm size. These are very large effects, and I didn't expect—you know, when I started reading the paper I did not expect the effects to be this large.

And then again, you know, the negative effects are larger in more land-intensive industries. One surprising element, at least you know it was surprising to me, what you find is that while this is the news when it comes to manufacturing, smaller farms may offer endings being more profitable per acre—you know, and there are various reasons for that. You talk about how they mostly rely on family labor, there is, you know, less supervision, and so on. But that is a slightly counterintuitive result.

So everything is not going in one direction. There is sort of this tension, you know, in your land fragmentation story. And you know, this small farm profitability increase may be partially offset by some of the other costs, because it hinders structural transformation, especially, you know, industrial land assembly and so on. But then there is the broader question of, you know, overall is this good? Does it leave farm workers and manufacturing workers better off or worse off? And then eventually you create sort of a general equilibrium model to walk us through those effects.

So, is this a good summary of your paper and have I largely got this right?

全球背景：分化的农场规模趋势

Aishwarya： This is absolutely a very good summary of my paper. And what I would just like to add to it is that, you know, as you said, what basically steered me towards this question was this divergent observation on farm sizes.

So what we see is that since 1970 onwards, you would see this pattern that in low- and middle-income countries, the average farm size has been just declining over time. And this is completely opposite to the experience of high-income countries, where farm sizes have increased along the process of development. And if you look at this along with the fact that what we know in developing countries, the largest share of their employment is still in agriculture, which also happens to be the sector with lower labor productivity—it made me, you know, connect the dots that, does this phenomenon of declining farm size have any role to play in explaining why such a large share of employment still remains in agriculture in developing markets?

So that's where the whole question started. And then because of my familiarity with India, and as you very rightly discussed, for several reasons India is a good setting to study this question. We have the problem of declining farm size—it's almost halved in the last 50 years. And we do see a stagnation in the manufacturing sector, and still agriculture remaining like the largest employing sector. So it was a very good setting to actually study this question.

研究方法与关键机制

Aishwarya： Basically, what I do in this paper is I started by doing something empirical investigation. First I just wanted to see in the data what is really happening—like, is land fragmentation actually affecting structural transformation? And for that, I look at Indian districts and I look at the period from 2001 to 2011. And as you rightly said, what I find is that declining farm size actually hinders structural transformation. And I find that people are actually moving out of manufacturing and into agriculture during this period.

And one of the mechanisms that I document in the paper is through this manufacturing side friction that as land sizes decrease, manufacturing activity also goes down in terms of number of firms and employment and average firm size.

So given this finding, the goal with the model then was that I wanted to quantify what are really the underlying mechanisms operating in, and then how do we really interpret this finding in terms of welfare. So then comes the model. And as you mentioned, one of the key and surprising findings, even for me, was that although land fragmentation hinders structural transformation, but if I look at district's welfare which is the district's real income, it actually improves with land fragmentation. There is a negative relationship between the two things.

So that was a very surprising finding. Then, what really is driving this welfare effect? And so I decomposed this to actually see who is taking away all these gains and who is losing from land fragmentation. And that's where the model, as we will discuss this further as well, reveals that it is the workers that actually bear the entire cost of land fragmentation—like the real wages in districts go down. And all of these gains essentially are just coming from increases in the rents that landlords can make—land-owning individuals can make from land fragmentation. So basically we are looking at this very big distributional gap and we should be careful about how we interpret this welfare gains in the model.

什么是土地碎片化？

Shruti： Yeah. So, you know, before we get into the precise mechanism and then the welfare effects, I want to actually start with: what is land fragmentation, for those who are not land nerds like you and me? Right? This is not a phrase we hear often. I think most people are aware of the fact that land ends up being quite a roadblock. It's very difficult to buy and sell land in India, very difficult to convert land use, it's very difficult to assemble parcels for industrial projects. So those are sort of the themes that get picked up in the headlines.

But can you first just set up for those who are unfamiliar: what is land fragmentation? How does one think about it? And how does one go about measuring land fragmentation in the Indian context?

历史根源

Aishwarya： So, what is land fragmentation? I'll just speak through the lens of India now. So broadly, very simply, what I am trying to measure by land fragmentation is the decline in farm sizes, right? But where does this all come from, where does this start?

So there are several factors in India that have contributed to this decline in average farm size, and it goes all the way back to the policies that were implemented right after independence from the British rule. So after 1947, one of the policies that was implemented by the government was the Abolition of Intermediaries Act. And what that Act did was that it transferred land from large landowners to landless tenant farmers. And in doing so, it actually created almost 20 million new land-owning small farmers. So what it did was that it immediately set us up with smaller farm sizes to begin with.

人口增长与继承法

And then over time, there has been a combination of factors that have just led to this small farm size even further decline with time. For example, in India, as most people must be aware, inheritance laws do essentially lead to a parcel of land being split among all heirs of an individual. So now if you look at that law and then you think about the growth rate of population in India, what I see in the data—and there is this figure in my paper which shows that the number of farms has almost increased at the same rate of rural population growth. So with the fixed supply of land, these inheritance policies and population growth have imposed that on average, farm size has continued to decline over time.

社会规范与监管障碍

And then there are also a lot of other things that have over time prevented the consolidation of land. For example, in India there is a lot of social norms regarding land ownership. People attach a lot of like higher status in the society with respect to land ownership, which makes people reluctant to part away with even a small piece of land regardless of how viable it is for production. And then even if people are willing, then as you said, there are so many regulatory hurdles, there are poor property rights, and then there are these multiple processes that you need to navigate in order to either sell your land within agriculture, even to like just convert to non-agricultural uses, that make the process of consolidation even harder. So all of this factors together have basically led to this farm sizes just keep on declining over time.

测量方法

And in terms of measurement, as you said, what I do is that there is the Agricultural Census of India which is done almost every five years. And what this Agricultural Census does is that it records the number and area of operational holdings in India at the district level, which is what I use, by different size classes.

And what do we really mean by an operational holding here is that it is a piece of land that is operated by either one person individually or jointly with somebody else. So it is not really land ownership, but it is at the level of who is really operating a land parcel. Right, so it gives me a sense of how many operating land parcels are there in India over time.

Now ideally what I would like—for my context, we go further, might become more clear—is that I would like to study land fragmentation based on land ownership. So it might be a case that I am the owner of the land but I lease it out to multiple small farmers. So which means that I would see in the data that there are a lot of small land holdings available here, but the reality is that I'm just leasing it out to others. So ownership and operational holdings in that sense might be different indeed.

But what I find is through the Indian Human Development Survey, it revealed that there are very few farming households that are actually engaged in leasing—it's roughly 11% of the entire sample. So which kind of gives me some reassurance that I can still use these operational holdings as a proxy for actual land ownership because most of the people do not engage in land leasing.

So essentially, what then I do with this data is I treat this as my proxy for land owning. And using the 10 different size classes that are available in Agricultural Census, I use the number of farms in each size category as a weight and take the midpoint of every size bin as a representative size to create a weighted average farm size of a district. And I am able to track that from 2000 until 2015 over four rounds of Agricultural Census.

租赁市场的扭曲

Shruti： And we have such terrible land laws when it also comes to leasing that it completely disincentivizes leasing, right? So I completely understand why, you know, survey results—along with other surveys also—suggest that actually leasing is a very small number overall, right? Like, there are states like Kerala which like explicitly make it very very hard, longest land, which is prohibited effectively.

So, but you know, here there another interesting question. The way you set up the paper is that it's very hard to consolidate land for manufacturing. But what I find is it also very hard to consolidate land for agriculture, right? So, we managed to kill both ends. Like, I mean, if someone managed to have a really large farm, then they could just get the change of land use certificate and, you know, they can manage to sell it. But we don't allow farmers to sell land to non-farmers because of urban land ceiling laws or caps on what individuals and households can own. So you are prevented from selling to a richer farmer, right?

So I know part of the story is social norms and people like to hold on to ancestral property and things like that. But I think people at the end of the day are rational. When it is so hard to actually transact in land and sell it to a farmer, and the prices get so depressed because we have kind of distorted the agricultural land market, that it functionally becomes impossible. And then of course we say, oh, however, it is attached to our property or something like that. But what it really comes down to—for everything else we somehow managed to sell, we also managed to offer, you know, close positions and industrial property as collateral, but somehow we can't manage to sell it. So I am always a little bit—I'm not so sure about the social norm story. But I mean, for your paper that hardly matters.

如何测量宏观影响？

Shruti： So, now that we know that the operational size, which is a good proxy for, you know, overall land holding size by ownership, tends to be extremely small. What is a good way for us to think about the impact, right? Because this could have so many different kinds of impact—like, you know, on agricultural productivity, on your ability to transform to manufacturing, agricultural wage labor, you know, agricultural labor and their wages, industrial labor and their wages.

So, can you walk us through—when you study a big picture question like structural transformation, how do you go about measuring the impact of something like land, which kind of touches everything?

机制一：农业渠道

Aishwarya： I think, you know, what basically—there are some bits and parts of this in the literature which kind of got me interested in this question. So for example, I can think about two separate channels through which this land fragmentation phenomenon actually affects structural change. And these two separate phenomena operate through the two separate sectors. So one operates through the agriculture sector, one operates through the manufacturing sector.

So let's just like start with the agriculture sector. So there's this vast literature that basically says that the yields or the output per unit of land on a farm are related to the farm size. So basically, what it is saying is that with fragmentation, as farm sizes change, it can alter my returns from cultivation, it can alter how much I can produce on my land, and how much profits can come—I can make from that land. And that can change my incentives of remaining in agriculture versus leaving agriculture. And when I say leaving, I'm talking to the less of land, like keeping my land under agriculture or removing it from agriculture.

反向的农场规模-生产率关系

So in terms of incentives, that is one channel that exists in the literature. And there are various arguments for it. So, it doesn't necessarily go in one way or the other. So for example, if you think about smaller farms, there is this whole literature on inverse farm size productivity which essentially says that the yields are larger on smaller farms. And often it is attributed to things like smaller farms use family labor more intensively, and family labor requires less supervision. It can also be like, you know, if you think about the principal-agent problem, they will shirk less. So because of these factors, using more family labor on smaller farms, you can raise the yields on smaller farms.

But then there is the other side of the literature as well which says that mechanization is important, and there are economies of scale in mechanization which can prevent smaller farms from adopting these technologies that improve your productivity, enhance your productivity. Right? So by fragmentation, as farms decline, farms can on the other hand also suffer from a lack of mechanization which can reduce their yields. So overall, we don't know in which direction fragmentation can affect your returns from cultivation and therefore your intentions to remain in agriculture.

So that's the agriculture side of the story which is there in the literature.

关于机械化门槛的讨论

Shruti： So just to clarify one part—do we not know which direction it will go in, and do we not know what are the thresholds? Like, economies of scale and mechanization, I mean, it's pretty obvious, right, what direction will it go in? It's odd to think that land would be an exception to this. So, is this just a question of thresholds—that up to a certain threshold where mechanization is pretty much impossible and unfeasible, a slightly smaller holding with family labor ends up doing a little bit better than a slightly larger holding with outside wage labor, but past a certain threshold, of course, mechanization and economies of scale are gonna eat that, right?

Aishwarya： That's right. That's 100% right. And that's where the seminal paper of Foster and Rosenzweig from 2022 comes in—that in the Indian context with a more representative data, they are able to observe both small farms and large farms at the same data set, and that's where they show that this is a U-shaped relationship, that there is a farm threshold below which the returns from using family labor are higher, and above which as the component of family labor, the cost of that—the share of that keeps on falling, then there are greater returns from mechanizing.
