机制二：制造业渠道

Shruti： You said this is one mechanism, right, which is through agriculture. What is the other mechanism?

Aishwarya： Right, so I think I found that second mechanism to be super interesting because objectively when you think about it, it's not very obvious that farm size declining can directly affect manufacturing. Because why is it not happening in the manufacturing sector?

But there is this very interesting finding by Deichmann et al. and Ejaz Ghani and coauthors which shows that in the context of developing countries—and I think these papers look at Indonesia and India—they show that manufacturing activity is actually moving stately towards peri-urban rural areas in developing countries. And these are the areas where agriculture is the predominant land use.

So what this automatically does is that it sets manufacturing at competition with agriculture for this limited resource which is land. And then for manufacturing activity to expand at all, agricultural land actually needs to move from out of agriculture and into manufacturing.

And this is where then this problem of declining farm size becomes salient. Because if you think about a firm which is trying to aggregate to a given size of land, in the presence of fragmentation, it will have to negotiate with multiple landowners, coordinate, bargain, everything with multiple landowners. And as we know that this process of converting land in India from agriculture and non-agriculture is costly, it's tedious, it has multiple stages. So now that I have to do it with one vs. five farmers, it is naturally going to raise my land acquisition cost as a firm. Yeah.

And that can basically dampen the expansion of manufacturing activity, it can dampen the removal of land from agriculture to manufacturing, and that can have implications for structural transformation as well in terms of some of the pull forces.

2005 年印度教继承法修正案作为工具变量

And that's another reason why I like India as a setting, because we have this inheritance law that was passed in 2005 which kind of gives me some variation in how land fragmentation changes across districts.

So to just give all the listeners like a background on that—inheritance in India is governed differently for different religious groups. But for the Hindus, the Sikhs, the Buddhists, and the Jains—and I will just together call them the Hindu Plus community, which comprises more than 80% of India's population—it is governed by the Hindu Succession Act of 1956. Now prior to 1956, ancestral property of an individual in a family would just go down the male lineage. But after 2005, this law was nationally amended, and what it did was that it granted inheritance rights over ancestral property to women as well. So, women also became equal coparceners when it comes to ancestral property.

And what it does for my setting is that by increasing the number of potential legal claims to a land parcel, it actually induces land fragmentation.

暴露度测量

And so that is the source of variation that I'm using. And because my analysis is at the district level and this reform was passed nationally at the same time, the way I capture this—I use this as an instrument by measuring the exposure of a district to this reform. And the exposure is measured by the share of rural Hindu women, a Hindu Plus women, in a district population before the reform. So in 2001, what is the share of rural Hindu Plus women in a district's total population?

So the districts with this higher share are more exposed to the reform. They are likely to undergo more land splitting and therefore larger declines in farm size. So this instrumental variable strategy somehow helps me get some variation from the land fragmentation side that I can then use to study how it impacts structural transformation.

一般均衡模型

Shruti： And so in some sense, the reason comes from—do you tell us exactly how this is happening?

模型框架

Aishwarya： Right. So, I tried to get to the welfare results using this two-sector general equilibrium model. And I omit services from my model because I don't find significant effects there. And then I try to see—this model is essentially based on models by Farrokhi and Pellegrina in the trade literature and also by Hibbich and Redding. So these people recently, like they have these papers in the trade literature which looks at structural change, and their models are based on land allocation. So that's where I got my idea because I'm probably trying to study this, this might be a good framework to begin with.

模型运作机制

So what is happening in this model is that within every district, there is a fixed supply of land, and this land is held by some N number of landowners in fixed parcel sizes. And specification in the model do not account for any transactions of land between landholders because, VC that is not very prevalent in India, that's not very easy for landowners to transact between among each other. So I can treat this parcel of land that's an endowment to a landlord as an exogenous endowment.

Yeah. And what I do with this is that essentially, the whole point of structural transformation in this model comes from the land allocation decision of the landlords. So each landlord has this land parcel which has a distinct suitability for agriculture. So you can think about it as differences in soil quality, fertility, which makes some parcels better suited for agriculture as compared to others. But each plot is equally productive in manufacturing.

So from a landlord's perspective, the landlord first observes the suitability of their land plot, and then they decide what they want to do—put it to agriculture, or they want to lease their land plot to a manufacturing firm. Because I model there this one representative manufacturing firm in each district which wants to take land from landlords for manufacturing production. So basically there is this land allocation decision that landlords need to navigate.

模型的简化设置

In the model, it's a very simplified framework because I wanted to get to its larger implications for structural transformation. So it is—I just have two factors of production in this model, it's just land and labor for now. And in this model, I essentially don't treat separately agricultural versus manufacturing wages, but it's more of like—land, the labor in this model is willing to supply its labor inelastically to whichever sector has demand. Right? There is going to set one common wage in the district in their equilibrium.

碎片化如何进入模型

And so this is how land fragmentation enters the model—there is a fixed stock of supply. So you think about any hobbies and even like the general process of land fragmentation, what it is going to do is that it is going to increase the number of landlords. And given the fixed supply of land, it just basically changes the land endowment of each landlord. So on average, the land fragmentation shock just decreases the size of the land owned by a landlord.

And then it alters the land allocation decision through precisely the two channels that we have been discussing so far—that in the agriculture sector, as that land size becomes smaller, it changes the per acre profits from that particular land plot. So it alters the rents or the profits that a landlord can get from putting his own land into cultivation.

In the manufacturing sector, because of small farm sizes, this land acquisition costs are going to increase, which are going to reduce firm profits, as a result of which the rents that landlords can receive from firms are going to decline. So this friction comes basically model like this—reduced form wedge on the rental rate that firms can offer to landlords. And this wedge is modeled as a function of the district farm size, such that when the average farm size declines, this wedge increases and it reduces the rent that landlords can get from the manufacturing sector.

So in a very reduced form way, I'm trying to capture this entire story into the land allocation decision. So as the shock hits, what it does is—through both these sectors, it basically alters the relative rent a landlord can get from putting the land in manufacturing versus agriculture. And that shapes and that drives the land allocation process, and consequently it shapes the labor allocation as well. Depending on which sector expands, there is more labor in that sector, and that drives structural transformation as well in the model. So, that's like a big picture overview of just how the model is working in the set.

弹性估计

And so, one of the central exercises in this paper was essentially to estimate the elasticity with which as farm sizes change, how these two frictions in the manufacturing and agriculture sector shape.

So, what I did in this paper was that for the manufacturing sector, I actually used like firm-level data from the Annual Survey of Industries. And what's good about this data is that it actually reports what is the value of new land purchase made by a firm. Using that data, I am able to estimate the elasticity with which the land acquisition cost change as district farm sizes change. And what I find is that between 2001 and 2011, on average, this land assembly friction that is there in my model increases by about 35%. So it is a very large increase.

And similarly, than using micro data from farms from IHDS, which reports in detail the output and input expenditure at the farm level, using the panel structure of that data, I am able to estimate that within the sample of households by land size changes due to inheritance—so it's like more of an exogenous change in the farm size—in this sub-sample, I find that the profits per acre increase as farm size are smaller. But this profitability advantage in my sample is—it's roughly like on average, it increases by 1.1%, this is what I find.

令人震惊的福利结果

Aishwarya： So then when I took these are like elasticities, I use them to actually quantify the model. And what I still find is that so when it comes to welfare, all master, the model does a good job of replicating the structural transformation results that I find in the empirics, which was really assuring—that it is very closely able to match the empirical estimates. So, it does show that structural transformation is hindered.

But then when you look at welfare, which is the total real income in a district which is the income of workers and landlords together, that actually goes up. And there is substantial variation—there are some districts that even lose. In fact, 50% of the districts in my sample experience welfare loss, but 50% also gain. So the variation is from -0.8% to about 1.85%. So it's a huge variation. But overall, the relationship is negative—that districts that experience more fragmentation are experiencing overall welfare gains.

分配效应的分解

So, I was overall a bit puzzled to like basically, like, think about okay, what's going on here. And so, I basically then look at the distributional implications. And what I find is that the two components that make up welfare is wages and land rents.

And what I find is that real wages are actually falling by about 1.92% on average, and all of these gains are coming from land rents increasing, which increase by almost 5%.

So even whatever we're seeing as a positive effect is actually not overall should be concluded as a good thing, because we are creating a very large distributional gap. The workers who are in the models are landless are essentially the ones who are bearing the cost of this land fragmentation, because manufacturing frictions prevent the expansion of manufacturing activity. And it's a fact that manufacturing is related to be more labor-intensive than agriculture. So when the more labor-intensive sectors shrink, it reduces the aggregate labor demand, it reduces the wages in the model. So that was like the key takeaway for me from this model—that yes, we do find some positive effects, but there are these like very sharp distributional implications that we should be careful about.

小农盈利优势的警示性解读

Aishwarya： Right, exactly. And like another thing that I wanted to pinpoint is that there is this discussion on what really the small farm profitability advantage means. So basically what this exercise shows is that this profitability advantage is an important counter-weighing force against this very large manufacturing section. So to the extent to which this profitability advantage is a real resource gain and is it just reflective of some distortions in the input markets, we again need to be conscious about promoting small things in a lifetime policy.

So, although my paper is not taking a stand on decomposing this and whether this is a resource gain or whether these are distortions, but something that should be interpreted with caution is definitely something I would.

结语：破除小农浪漫化神话

Shruti： And also interpreted with common sense, wouldn't you say? Now there is the story across the world that things get more productive as fewer people work in agriculture, and there is more mechanization and there is larger holding size. I see no reason to think of India as some kind of, like, you know, sort of unique outlier in this story. Like I have literally no reason to believe that. It may be true for very specific things, you know, particular kind of organic farms that produce a particular kind of mango or something like that. But largely when we are talking about like regular agriculture, scale effects are everything. Ambedkar was saying this 120 years ago, people are still saying this now. But we do have a very romantic notion attached to the small farmer and this small sort of land holding, a sort of family farm. And I think some of this comes from the colonial experience and otherwise. But I'm pretty glad that you're helping us, you know, overall dispel these crazy myths.

Thank you so much for doing this. This is truly a pleasure. The paper is fantastic. It's really really rigorous and very important, because we just see what a big barrier land has become to India's structural transformation—which is really the only ladder we have towards greater economic growth and development in India. So, thank you so much for doing this.

Aishwarya： And a very long ladder too, but yes.

Shruti： Yeah, for a very large number of people, right. So, thank you so much. It was really fun engaging with you on the job market paper.

Aishwarya： And even I learned a lot from this conversation.

Aishwarya 论文中最耐人寻味的悖论在于——**小农场每英亩利润更高**这个看似"温情"的结论，可能根本不是"小的更美"，而是市场扭曲的统计残影。当她在模型中关闭"小农盈利优势"这一渠道时，整个福利结论**符号翻转**：土地碎片化变成了纯粹的净损失。
这暗示了一个令人不安的可能性：**印度过去 70 年被歌颂为"社会正义"的土地再分配政策，其经济正当性可能建立在一个测量伪影之上**。那些用来为小农辩护的"每英亩产出更高"的经验证据，或许只是投入品市场（信贷、劳动力监督、家庭劳动力的机会成本被系统性低估）扭曲的镜像。换言之，我们看到的不是小农的效率，而是大农被更严厉的税收和监管所惩罚的负片。

item.title: [Lex Clips] DHH on drama with Theo | Lex Fridman Podcast Clips
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

声音的贝叶斯先验：为什么播客能拆解仇恨

DHH 观察到"人们在听到我的论点之前，已经在脑海里为我预装了某种声音"——这其实是预测性大脑（predictive brain）的教科书案例。神经科学告诉我们，感知从来不是被动接收，而是先验假设与感官证据的持续博弈。当先验足够强（"这人是法西斯"），文字这种低带宽介质根本产生不了足够的"预测误差"去更新它。播客的独特之处不仅在于"更长"，而在于更高维——语调、犹豫、笑声、沉默、口误，每一个都在向大脑投递贝叶斯更新信号，绕过意识层的敌意过滤器。

这里有一个反直觉的推论：互联网仇恨的根源不是"信息太多"，而是"信息维度太低"。文字之所以易被武器化，恰恰因为它留下太多空缺，让读者用最坏的假设去填补。

跨界连接：DHH 无意中重演了 Axelrod 的博弈论实验

DHH 说了一件小事：他仍然认为 Theo 当年在 TypeScript 事件上"a bozo move"，但决定 follow back。这不是软弱，这是在囚徒困境的迭代博弈中重启合作。1980 年代政治学家 Robert Axelrod 通过计算机竞赛证明：长期最优策略是 tit-for-tat 加上 forgiveness——即使对方叛变过，也要偶尔给出信任信号，否则合作会进入死亡螺旋。DHH 那句"我不必在所有事上同意你"几乎是这一博弈论原则的口语版：在拒绝报复的同时保留判断。

出人意料的观察是：DHH 这样一个以火药味著称、以在 Twitter 上正面开撕闻名的工程师，其实在实践一种极具东方色彩的智慧——"憎其行而不憎其人"。这几乎是禅宗语言，却出自 Rails 创始人之口。这个矛盾本身值得琢磨：也许真正好斗的人才有资格谈原谅，因为他清楚情绪能量的代价。

被轻描淡写掩埋的最锋利洞见：宽容不是美德，是信息熵

对话末尾有一句被 DHH 顺口带过、几乎无人注意的话，可能是整段最锋利的思想：

"My feed is more interesting when there's people talk about things that I care about."

他没有把跟随异见者包装成道德义务，而是包装成自利的信息策略。这暗合复杂系统理论的一个基本事实：同质化系统的信息熵低，学习价值也低。一个只关注"自己人"的 feed，本质上是在给自己喂"预测已知答案"的低营养内容——你以为在获取信息，其实在消耗算力去确认自己已经知道的东西。

真正让人意外的是：社交媒体算法与"多元对话"其实并非天然对立。推荐系统只是放大用户的短期偏好。问题不在算法，问题在我们默认把"舒适"当成了"想要"。DHH follow back Theo 的那一下，是用户对算法的一次微小但有力的逆向训练——他在告诉系统："我的效用函数比你以为的复杂。"

一个更深的隐藏结构

值得注意的是：让 DHH 和 Theo 结怨的（Twitter 争吵）、让 DHH 决定重新关注 Theo 的（follow back）、让 DHH 觉得 feed 变有趣的（异见发言），都是同一个平台的同一个功能。这是社交媒体最少被讨论的悖论——它自带解药，只是我们习惯只吃毒药那一份。桥梁与深渊，用的是同一根钢材。

📝 转录文本

On why podcasts humanize disagreement

DHH: This is one of the reasons why I actually really enjoy podcasts, because I have found that even in long-form writing, when I make long-form arguments, people hear it in whatever voice they have in their head for me. And that often gets pre-programmed in advance of the arguments — just like, "well, this guy is a whatever, fascist." Um, and then they hear the words and they read the words in those… when they see or hear the actual tone of how I'm presenting the arguments, they may not agree with those arguments. I mean, many of them, of course, obviously don't. But it's much harder to just dismiss or hate someone like that.

Lex: Mhm.

DHH: At least that's what I've found. And that's the response that I've gotten — that people like, "well, I had a certain opinion, and then I heard you on Lex."

Start from "they're a good person"

Lex: That actually sounded much more reasonable. But even more than that, I would love it if people just exercise this kind of approach to other people — of like, assuming they're a good person.

DHH: Yes.

Lex: And then, if they have an opinion you disagree with, they're a good person who has an opinion. You can maybe think they're stupid, fine. Just think they're lost, but think of them as a good person. I think if you… there's one of the things that gets engagement is kind of on other people.

DHH: Right.

Lex: And if you just approach other people as — you're looking for bad, you will always find bad in them. There's something annoying about them. And if you look at people in that way, you're not going to learn from it, and you're going to fill your heart with hate. It's just a bad way to live and to interact with the world. And that is one of the things that the internet kind of encourages.

So it'd be nice if you just approach even people who you really disagree with — it's like, "oh, I might learn something from this person." The Black Panther person, William Buckley — you might hate… it's just a microcosm of this.

The Theo story — following back

DHH: There's a guy, Theo. I don't know if you follow him. Um, we had a bit of a thing over the fact that we stopped using TypeScript for a project, and he didn't like that, and had opinions about that and other actions. And after that I thought, like, "what a bozo."

Lex: [snorts]

DHH: And — and you know what? I still think that was a bozo move. And then I can also think like, "well, the dude's really into AI, he's trying out all these models, and we can share some excitement about that." So I just started following him yesterday. Awesome.

I don't have to agree with you on everything. I don't even have to like some of the things that you did or said or whatever. I can follow you anyway. So if I can follow back Theo, then I think there's room for world peace here.

Lex: [laughter] Yeah, he's actually a really good example. He's really opinionated, and changes his mind quite a bit, can get snarky, but I think he's a good person underneath.

DHH: And either way, I just — you know what? My feed is more interesting when there's the people talk about things that I care about. And, uh, yeah — I don't have to agree with you on everything. I just don't.

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] Coinbase’s Everything Exchange: Agentic Finance, Stablecoins & Tokenization with CEO Brian Armstrong
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"暗经济"：76% 低于 30 美分的意义远比看起来更颠覆

Brian 随口给出的这个数字，其实揭示了一个支付层面的物理不可能性——不是效率不够，而是数学上无解：当交易本身价值 1 美分而固定费用是 30 美分时，传统金融轨道在物理上无法感知这个市场的存在。

这产生了一个非常反直觉的推论：Agentic 经济不是一个"更大"的经济，而是一个用传统仪器观察不到的"暗经济"——就像宇宙学中的暗物质，构成了大部分质量却对旧仪器不可见；或者像深海热泉的化能合成细菌，它们在生物圈里活跃了数十亿年，直到 1977 年才被人类发现。当 Brian 说"agentic 经济将比人类经济更大"时，他其实是在说：未来经济活动的大多数将发生在一个我们目前用 GDP、支付通道、CPI 这些"望远镜"根本探测不到的频段里。这可能意味着未来 10 年最大的宏观经济误判，不是通胀预测错，而是整个衡量框架系统性地漏掉了主要经济活动。

二、跨领域的隐藏同构：Coinbase 的 "Brain" ≡ New Limit 的表观遗传重编程

这是这次访谈最让人拍案的地方——Brian 同时经营两家表面上毫无关联的公司，但它们解决的是同一个抽象问题：

  • Coinbase 的 "brain"：不改代码库本身（DNA），而是把团队/服务/个人累积的上下文（事故历史、AB 测试、PR 审阅记录）作为可注入的"表达模式"，让新 agent 表现得像资深员工。
  • New Limit 的 epigenetic reprogramming：不改 DNA，只是通过转录因子恢复老细胞失去的表达模式，让它重新表现得像年轻细胞。

两者都是"表观（epi-）"层面的干预，都是在抗击信息/功能的熵损失。这解释了为什么 Brian 能在两个截然不同的领域产生高质量直觉——他不是在做两件事，他是在两种介质（软件、生物）中攻击同一个根本问题：如何让系统在时间维度上不失忆、不失能。顺便一提，这个同构还能扩展到他对"freedom cities"的兴趣——特殊经济区本质上就是一种"社会性的表观遗传重编程"：不重写国家层面的法律基因，而是在局部制造一个新的表达环境。三个项目，同一个思想模式。

三、市场对 Coinbase 自己的"表观遗传滞后"

一个几乎被采访轻描淡写略过、但非常尖锐的事实：Coinbase 88% 的收入已经不来自比特币交易，但股价仍然与比特币价格高度相关。

这是市场自身的表观遗传现象——底层"基因组"（业务组合）已经根本性改变，但市场对它的"表达模式"（估值心智模型）还停留在旧的表观状态。有意思的是，Brian 没有借机大力兜售这一点——因为他隐隐知道，这种重编程只能通过时间和累积证据实现，喊话是没用的。这是投资者可能捕捉到的一个非对称套利窗口，也是"信念的惯性"如何真金白银地体现在资产定价上的活体案例。

四、预测市场的隐藏杀器：知识本身被证券化

Brian 提到把预测市场扩展到"大生活问题"——上帝是否存在、我们是被设计还是被进化——这段话看起来像散漫的畅想，但它其实指向一个远更颠覆性的方向：没有 resolution date 的预测市场 = 信念的股票市场。

你从来不会从 Nvidia 那里收到"最终真相分红"，你只是押注价格走势。同理，一个关于"意识的困难问题是否真实"的市场不需要终局判定——它只需要在新论文、新实验、新事件冲击下重新定价。这暗示着一个奇怪的未来：知识和信念本身会流动性化、被套期保值、被证券化。你博士论文的核心假设在一个流动市场里被定价 43 美分——你的激励结构会怎么变？学术圈的"发表-同行评审"机制在这样的世界里几乎会被彻底重排。Brian 可能没意识到，他随口谈的这个东西，是对学术激励系统最激进的替代方案之一。

五、意外的品味标签：Brian 反直觉地看重"给孩子加地板"而非"加天花板"

关于胚胎编辑和认知增强，Brian 拒绝了一个常见的科幻悲剧叙事（"所有人都会被推进同一个套餐、多样性消失"），并给出了相反的论断：编辑不是压平，而是抬地板——去掉精神分裂症、抑郁、罕见遗传病，剩下的孩子还是他自己。这个视角悄悄地把"增强"重新定义为去除损失，而不是追求上限。放在他的整个投资和创业组合里看，这几乎是一个隐藏的元哲学：Coinbase 让穷国也能持有美元资产（抬地板），New Limit 让老细胞恢复年轻功能（抬地板），认知增强让孩子摆脱先天疾病（抬地板）。Brian 表面上是个追求上限的技术乐观主义者，实际上他所有的赌注都在做同一件事：系统性地把地板抬起来。这可能是他和其他"硬科技"CEO 最本质的区别——他不是在造尖，他是在做基座。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open: Why Traditional Rails Don't Fit the Agentic Economy

The minimum fee typically on a debit or credit card transaction is about 30 cent fee flat plus the additional percentage. Arguably, it doesn't really work well for anything under a dollar. Certainly, it doesn't make sense to pay 30 cents to send a 1 cent payment. And I believe the stats we last saw on this are that about like 76% of the Agentic Commerce transactions we're seeing are under 30 cents.

We don't want the AIs to be unbanked, you know. We want to bank the AIs. They deserve financial services as well. The AI agents themselves are going to have to have their own accounts. And so we've made some simple tools where with a single command, you just prompt, you paste it into your AI agent, it can now have its own financial account.

So it'll be interesting to see how the agentic economy evolves. There'll be more agents than humans in the not too distant future. It kind of stands to reason that the agentic economy will be bigger than the human economy at some point in the not too distant future as well.

Introduction

Today on No Priors, we are joined by Brian Armstrong, the co-founder and CEO of Coinbase, one of the world's most important and earliest crypto companies that has also been quite aggressive at adopting AI.

Brian is also the co-founder of New Limit, which is an anti-aging and longevity company doing really interesting things in biology, including certain types of high throughput screening to understand aging, different uses of AI, etc.

Brian is one of the most forward-thinking people I know on different aspects of science, technology, art, the world, etc. So, it's very exciting to have this conversation with them, and we'll be talking about everything from what's happening in the crypto world to what's happening in AI to what's happening in biology to how different individuals can have an impact over time. So, it's a very fun conversation.

— Brian, thank you so much for joining us today. It's a pleasure to see you.

Yeah, good to see you a lot.

— So, I was hoping we could talk about a few different topics. I think there's a bunch of stuff relevant to Coinbase and crypto and, you know, Agentic Finance and things like that, but also you started a company called New Limit which is focused on longevity and aging and biotechnology. So I think it'd be great to sort of cover both as part of this conversation.

Yeah.

The Everything Exchange

— And maybe we start with Coinbase. So Coinbase has been making some really big moves. You've been floating this concept of the everything exchange as you've been building out what I think is a new global payments layer. Can you tell us, you know, at a high level, what are some of the directions of the company and some of the areas you're most excited about right now?

Yeah, so we're at a really exciting time in Coinbase's history because on the one hand, every asset class is coming on chain. It's now possible to trade everything in one place with good liquidity and good cross margin. And so for markets and trading — that out there is stocks and commodities and crypto and derivatives, perpetual futures — like it's all coming to one place where traders can do everything in one spot, including prediction markets too. And they can do that in more countries now given the regulatory clarity that's emerging, which we can talk about if you want. So the everything exchange is kind of our bread and butter, our core business.

Stablecoin Payments

Uh, the next big area that's emerging is stablecoin payments, which have just been growing like crazy. Even when Bitcoin prices are down, stablecoin payments just keep growing. And so we're helping companies all over the world integrate stablecoin payments, which are fast and cheap and global. You can send money at the speed of information, right? It's kind of like under 1 second, under one cent US, to move money anywhere in the world.

Agentic Finance / AIFI

And then the third big one is something I know you talk a lot about on this podcast, which is how is AI changing — because AI is changing everything and so it's obviously going to change financial services too. And so we call this Agentic Finance or AIFI. And we're building this into Coinbase in a number of different ways.

AI advisers for humans. The first way is that people who have their existing financial account, they're going to want to have an AI adviser. Kind of like how wealthy people are able to get access to these investment advisors. But everybody should have access to them now. And they can help teach you about, you know, building the right portfolio and dollar cost averaging, tax loss harvesting, and all these kind of things. And you know, if the market dips 5 or 10 or 15%, leg into this kind of portfolio over time and try to save money on fees and earn yield while it's sitting in cash. And you can just talk to it like a human and it'll do all these things for you. At least that's the vision and it's getting better and better. So we've launched an adviser in the Coinbase product.

Banking the AIs. Uh, the next thing is that the AI agents themselves are going to have to have their own accounts. And so we're on a mission to kind of like go out there — we don't want the AIs to be unbanked. We want to bank the AIs. They deserve financial services as well. And so we've made some simple tools where with a single command, you just prompt, you paste it into your AI agent, it can now have its own financial account and it's using a self-custodial wallet and crypto rails. So there's not like a KYC process. Our AI agents don't have a government ID. They can't walk into a bank branch, at least not yet, without their humanoid robots companion. And so now any AI agent can have its own financial account to do payments, to pay for goods.

— And is that tied to an account of somebody who's already on Coinbase? In other words, is this sort of like a subsidiary account? Is it an entirely new thing? Like how do you think about the hierarchy of that?

Yeah, so we're doing it both ways actually, just because I think there's going to be demand for both use cases. So it's going to be possible to create a separate agentic account with segregated funds on Coinbase in the near future, and you can give your agent access to just that to do trading and payments on your behalf. That's kind of linked to your identity as a human. We're also going to provide self-custodial wallets to any AI agent out there that wants to hold a balance in stablecoin — or even it could actually raise money. It could, you know, issue a token.

The Under-30-Cent Agentic Economy

And so what's fascinating is that today we often talk to these agents and, you know, it's sort of like one person to one agent and they go get some work done, but they often get stuck. There's like, "Oh, here's a paywall. Can you put in your credit card? I need to spin up these AWS resources," or "You wanted me to book this hotel for you, but here's the web page — can you go put in your credit card?" That kind of thing.

And in the future, I think you're going to want to have these agents have their own spend accounts, kind of like having a personal assistant or an employee who has their own spend account. AI Inside Coinbase: The "Brain" System

— What, I mean, the other thing you folks have really been focused on is the use of AI within Coinbase itself. Can you talk about, I know there's obviously coding and other things, but what do you think are some of the more interesting projects you all have done internally?

Yeah. So like a lot of companies, we started off with the basics. We got some coding tools. We got it hooked up into our various data repositories. And then the things that we've started to do recently where we're sort of pushing the boundaries — I think one of them is that, you know, we basically want to get as close as we can and actually achieve recursive self-improvement, right? And what does that mean in various ways?

So it means that you have a brain for the company. That can be a whole bunch of subsets, by the way — you can have a brain for each team, you can have a brain for each service, like repository within the company, you can have a brain for each individual — which, by the way, I believe they should be able to take with them when they leave Coinbase. So we're creating some good policies on that.

What Is the "Brain"?

So let's say you have a service, like a GitHub repository or some backend service that's running. And today we have engineers spinning up agents to make changes to that. What we're just now launching and seeing recently is like, every time the agent comes in to make a change to that service, it's actually ingesting the brain for the team working on it and for that repository.

And so what is that brain? It's basically a history of all the incidents that have ever happened with that service, all of the financial controls that have to be enforced with that, every AB test that we've ever run on that, of course the full GitHub history of pull requests that were accepted or rejected. And so the people running that team at any time can go in there and look at it. Today it's just markdown files, right? It sounds kind of simple at the end of the day. But the getting of this all hooked up —

The Recursive Self-Improvement Loop

So okay, so let's say you ask the agent, "Hey, I want to make a change to this service." It ingests the brain, it makes that change, and then as a human you go to review it and you're like, "Ah, it missed something." Okay, now the simple thing someone might do in that moment is, okay, go make a manual edit to fix it and then ship it. But the key step that we're trying to really enforce now in our software factory or software development life cycle is when you go to make that change and edit the agent's thinking, that context has to go back into the brain — so that you not only fix it in this case, but in all future cases going forward. And then what you start to see is like the accept rate for one-shotted PRs or that kind of thing, it just starts to tick up over time, and you've now got like a recursive self-improvement system.

Toshi and Agent Orchestration

So that's one of the big ideas we've been working on recently — and just getting our own internal agent harness, which we call Toshi, integrated with all these tools. Like, it can now make calls out to external vendors and pay using the agentic finance economy over these X42 protocols. If you want to edit the brain as you're making a change to that PR, and it goes back into the brain, putting that into the harness. Asking it to sort of like, okay —

The Platform: AI-Guided Pooled Screens

And so, anyway, long story short, the science progressed faster than I thought. We've got a lab now in South San Francisco, about 50 or 60 people, running these large-scale — it starts with AI, as with all things these days. You can test millions of hypotheses about what sets of transcription factors — which are these proteins that could reprogram different cell types. It's a massive search space, so we're using AI for that. We've built the leading frontier model for epigenetic reprogramming that recommends the next set of experiments that we should run in our lab, which are these large pooled screens. And we run those at as big a scale as we can, but it's like moving atoms and liquids in a lab, not just software.

And so we do these large pooled screens to see if we can get phenotypic hits for compounds that might be possible to reprogram these cells. The best ones of those we then run through functional assays, which are typically animal models, and those are a little more expensive, a little slower. And the best ones of those we run through human trials.

Milestones

And so the exciting thing is we've now demonstrated successful reprogramming of at least one human cell type in these humanized mouse models. We're now testing that in non-human primates. And then the first phase one clinical trial will be launching next year. So there'll be — I don't know, three to 10 other drug candidates coming off this platform in the coming years.

New Limit's Roadmap: Liver, Vascular, Immune, Then More

— Has New Limit announced where it's starting, or what indication areas it's starting with in terms of what it's hoping to impact biologically or from a patient-centric perspective?

Yeah, it has. It's actually — on the website, there's newlimit.com — you can check out therapeutics. So we've published the roadmap there.

The first three cell types that we've started running our platform against: - First: liver cells, or hepatocytes. - Second: vascular cells. - Third: immunological cells — for your immune system, T-cells most specifically.

You know, we're following a pattern that's kind of similar to the GLP-1s, like Ozempic and all these things — which is, initially in drug design or drug search, you're going after an indication which has a high unmet medical need. It's typically sometimes a smaller market, and that's just how drugs are developed. Because you go after things where people have no better options.

First Indication: Alcoholic Liver Disease

So, for instance, with our liver program, the initial phase one clinical trial will be in people with alcoholic liver disease. And today they don't really have any other options other than a liver transplant, and most of them don't have that in time. So I think the survivability of it within 12 months, once you're diagnosed, is very low.

So we'll do a phase one in that, and that alone would be a pretty large market. Sadly, there are a lot of people in that situation. I think we estimated that if that drug alone works in ALD, it might be worth $20 billion or something.

The Bigger Vision: Healthy People, Aging Reversal

But the goal here is not just to make a liver drug for alcohol damage. It's ultimately to make a drug that healthy people — if you're 40 and you want to have a liver that's like your 20-year-old liver, or your immune system, or your vascular system, or eventually, you know, your brain, your muscles, all these different cell types, your skin. That's a big one, right? That's probably a trillion-dollar market right there if you can get your skin rejuvenated.

But the idea is that over time, you'd be able to take a cocktail of these therapies, and they would target probably different cell types with slightly different payloads, but they would all have the same theme: reprogramming your cells to restore function they had when they were younger.

And most of the diseases that take us out are all correlated with age. Like, when you're in your 20s and you get some errant cancerous cell or a little bit of damage to your liver — whatever — your body recovers from it. And then as you age, they lose this function. And so most of the diseases that take us out, they're all highly correlated with age. And so instead of going after each disease, like the symptoms of it, we're sort of trying to go for the meta-problem of: well, how do we just restore the function your cells had when you were younger? And maybe that would be a way to take a bite out of a lot of these major diseases and attack the root cause of it.

— This goes back to the Yamanaka factors that you mentioned, where they were able to change the imprint for both age as well as cell type, and you're saying just focus on the age component of it. So you're reversing the potency of the cell to something that has more regenerative capabilities. You know, like younger cells or tissues generally are able to rejuvenate or regenerate better than older tissues, right? You see that with wound healing or injuries or other things like that. Somebody's in an accident when they're old versus young, right? They get better much faster. So it's really fascinating stuff.

Looking Ahead: The Next Five Years

— So I think you're this really unique and wonderful mix of somebody who's really grounded and pragmatic, but who also thinks big and goes after these giant shifts or trends. What are you most excited about over the next five years — either for Coinbase or New Limit, or in general, like in the world?

Yeah. Well, I'm always thinking about this. You know, on my free time and my weekends, I'm always thinking about: what are the most important trends? What is technology making available now that wasn't available before? What do I want the future to look like? How can I help shape that, create that, for civilizational progress?

An Aside: Be a Builder

And so, I think it's good for more people to do that. Just as an aside — it's not exactly what you asked, but I think that everybody should try to contribute in some way to civilizational progress and think about what they could build. Because it's easy to be a critic. It's easy to poke holes at what other people are doing, or to be an activist or whatever. It's kind of a common thing amongst a certain generation. I think it's better to try to be a builder. And you're going to fall flat on your face, and you'll get an appreciation for how hard it is to contribute sometimes. Maybe more empathy. But it's actually much more fulfilling if you helped build something in the world that benefited a lot of people.

Direct Focus: Agentic Finance + Stablecoins + New Limit

So anyway, to answer your question directly — I mean, my main focus is going to be on Agentic Finance, right? That's what's happening at Coinbase. And then stablecoin payments, the everything exchange. Like, crypto is really only powering about half of 1% of global GDP right now. There's maybe about 700 million people in the world who have used crypto or hold crypto, but not all of them use it every month, which might be more like in the 50 to 100 million people range. And so we need to get that to a billion or more. Like, that's how we're going to truly update the financial system. We can do that with humans, we can do it with agents. That's going to be a big focus. And then of course, New Limit.

Frontier Idea: Cognitive Enhancement

But I think if you want to talk about frontier ideas that I've sort of been contemplating — I mean, one idea I've been contemplating a little bit is around cognitive enhancement. And there, you know, there's been these things people have realized — like, in development of children, if you give them enough folic acid and certain nutrients like that in certain countries, it actually raises IQ. Like, they just develop better.

And it might be interesting — I might host a dinner on this at some point of just, you know, what are the various ways someone could target therapies, whether in adults, children, embryos, whatever — to try to just level the playing field a little bit of the baseline cognition and IQ that people are born with, or could be born with. I think that's another one of these big meta-problems. I haven't found a great thesis about how to exactly tackle that, but if somebody has one, let me know.

— That's super interesting. It's basically: how do you increase the collective intelligence of humanity?

Yeah, there's the biological form of that, and then there's like the digital or AI form of that.

— Exactly.

I really — we're in a race right now. Like, AI is getting smarter and smarter. I think humans need to at some point take control of our evolution and get smarter and smarter. And then of course, there's the hybrid of the two with brain machine interfaces, where some people will choose to merge, some people will not.

But even if — you know, I believe that, like you do, there's going to be probably more AI agents than humans in the not too distant future — humans still need to advance and progress. Like, that's important. I think there's a lot that we can do with these AI tools to actually benefit humanity. And, you know, healthier outcomes, live longer if you want, have more energy, have less back pain, wake up not tired in the morning, and, yeah, increase our cognition. And just have healthier offspring, have children that are free of diseases.

Embryo Editing and the Overton Window

Like, um, there's a company I invested in called Preventive that's doing embryo editing, which is a controversial topic. You know, people have seen these movies like Gattaca and things like that. But actually — like, 80% — if you look at the pure research, 80% of Americans support embryo editing for disease prevention. Nobody wants these rare genetic diseases for their children. Everybody wants healthier, better lives for their children. I think that's one of those topics that seems controversial today. I think it'll be more normal over time, and at some point it'll be abnormal to have children without doing this kind of screening and editing. Because it'd be like — this is so risky, like, why would you do that? You know, it's like driving without a seat belt, or something like that.

— I always wondered, by the way, on that one — whether or not, if you imagine in a future where gene editing is reasonably common, there may be like packages that you buy, right? There's the intelligence package and there's the health package.

Yeah.

— I sometimes wonder whether, if you think about different ways to be intelligent — there's processing speed, there's recall. You know, there's like five or six different ways you can imagine different forms of intelligence. And I sometimes wonder whether these packages will effectively diminish the neurodiversity of humanity, because it'll push everybody down the same package. It's almost like you're buying, you know, the Ford Model T of intelligence for everyone or something. So, I've always been curious about what are the implications of active editing relative to just human diversity and capability set. And, you know, will parents default opt in to the basic package, or whatever, which will always be the same thing. So it's kind of a random aside, but there's all these weird downstream implications of some of these things.

Yeah, so I've heard that argument before, and I actually think it's the opposite. I actually think it could increase diversity. The reason is that there's just unlimited diversity of human preferences, right?

I think if it was this simple — and it may not be this simple — parents would say, "You know, okay, do you want to have a great artist, a great general, a great engineer, a great politician?" You know, it's like every parent is going to have some different favorite thing. And by the way, that sort of assumes that they're mutually exclusive. A lot of this might just be like raising the floor, and then the kid is still who they are and what they were going to be — just, they don't have schizophrenia or depression or something, right?

So anyway, I think I actually don't think it'll decrease diversity. I think you actually could — I mean, in the limit case, you could actually get diversity that's really out there. Like you could have kids born with gills — they can breathe underwater — or, like, you know, have wings and fly or something. Like, who knows how far it could go if you really can take control of your evolution.

Special Economic Zones and Freedom Cities

— So one thing that's long been discussed in crypto circles and libertarian circles and other things are basically different forms of special economic zones. And obviously those have been implemented at scale in some cases, like Shenzhen in China — I think in part exists as a large-scale manufacturing region in China because it became a special economic zone, one form. There's others that have been discussed in the Philippines relative to certain US interests. You know, so there's really interesting things right now there. How do you think about that, or how's your thinking evolved over time, especially since crypto's played a prominent role in some of the underpinnings and philosophies behind some of these things?

Yeah. So I'm super interested in special economic zones because, again, I'm interested in meta-problems that unlock progress across a whole category of things.

And I think if you look at what slows down progress in many parts of the world, it is overregulation, right? Like, Europe certainly could be an example of this. You know, the US has its own version of it that is not perfect. And there has been interest at various points in different solutions to this. You know, there's seasteading, and Mars, and going up — brain upload into cyberspace and all these kinds of things.

Próspera

There's one called Próspera, which is in Honduras. And Coinbase actually made an investment in that just to learn more about it and see what was going on. And they've had, I'd say, a mixed — with the local government there, but they're getting closer to a resolution, is my understanding — that will, you know, I think they're going to make it. I think they're going to do a good job.

The US Substrate and Freedom Cities

There was, I'd say, a little bit more interest in this before the most recent Trump admin, just because the deregulatory environment has created a lot of opportunities here in the US, and that's a great substrate market to build on.

There was actually an idea that was discussed at one point, I think, in the campaign, about something called Freedom Cities. If people Google it, they can kind of see that idea. And the idea was to try to create some federal land in the US. You know, the federal government owns lots of different pockets of land. And if we say, all right, we want to — we think it's important strategically for America to get really good at nuclear power, or drug discovery, or having a crypto, or drone delivery, or whatever it is — you could take a piece of land somewhere. The US has a ton of land, right?

You could take a piece of this federal land, 10 or 100 square miles, and say, "You know what? In this area, you don't need to go through all the normal red tape on EPA and all these things, and, you know, local community. You can just build data centers there. You can build nuclear power plants there. You can do unlimited drone delivery there. You don't have to get approval from the FAA." Because we want to create these zones where experimentation can happen in a safe, contained way to see what works and what doesn't. And if something works via experimentation, then you can go through the normal process in the rest of the US to see if it's ready to be brought to that location.

Why Sandboxes Matter

The problem right now is, in many cases, there is no sandbox to go try this innovation, and that is just incredibly stifling. You can't really solve a problem as an entrepreneur unless you can iterate on it, right?

And so anyway, I think it'd be really fun to get some of these Freedom Cities or special economic zones in the US. Yeah, as you mentioned, like Shenzhen, Singapore, Dubai — these have been very successful in many other parts of the world and driven a ton of economic growth. And in some ways, the US is 50 special economic zones because of federalism and the state system. So that level of competition has, I think, allowed the US to be the leader globally in this. But we could go even further and do even more.

Closing

— Yeah, very exciting. Brian, thank you so much for joining me today.

Of course. Thanks for having me.

— Find us on Twitter at @NoPriorsPod. Subscribe to our YouTube channel if you want to see our faces. Follow the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. That way you get a new episode every week. And sign up for emails or find transcripts for every episode at no-priors.com.

item.description:
## 一、被忽视的"暗经济"：76% 低于 30 美分的意义远比看起来更颠覆
Brian 随口给出的这个数字，其实揭示了一个**支付层面的物理不可能性**——不是效率不够，而是数学上无解：当交易本身价值 1 美分而固定费用是 30 美分时，传统金融轨道**在物理上无法感知这个市场的存在**。
这产生了一个非常反直觉的推论：**Agentic 经济不是一个"更大"的经济，而是一个用传统仪器观察不到的"暗经济"**——就像宇宙学中的暗物质，构成了大部分质量却对旧仪器不可见；或者像深海热泉的化能合成细菌，它们在生物圈里活跃了数十亿年，直到 1977 年才被人类发现。当 Brian 说"agentic 经济将比人类经济更大"时，他其实是在说：**未来经济活动的大多数将发生在一个我们目前用 GDP、支付通道、CPI 这些"望远镜"根本探测不到的频段里**。这可能意味着未来 10 年最大的宏观经济误判，不是通胀预测错，而是**整个衡量框架系统性地漏掉了主要经济活动**。
## 二、跨领域的隐藏同构：Coinbase 的 "Brain" ≡ New Limit 的表观遗传重编程
这是这次访谈

item.title: [Lex Clips] DHH on danger of over-optimizing life | Lex Fridman Podcast Clips
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

优化悖论：治疗本身成了疾病

DHH 无意间揭示了一个令人不安的系统性真相：现代健康优化文化正在制造它声称要治愈的病。戒酒潮的宏观数据看似胜利——酒类销量暴跌、年轻人清醒率飙升——但同期孤独症、抑郁症、婚配率崩塌也在同步创下历史新高。这不是巧合，而是因果。当你把一个持续了 13000 年的社会润滑剂突然抽走，你不只是移除了它的"危害"，你还移除了它承载的所有隐性功能：陌生人之间的破冰、周五夜晚的松弛、求偶仪式的容错空间。这正是 Chesterton 之篱的教科书案例——在拆除一堵你不理解为何存在的墙之前，先弄清它挡住了什么。

跨领域连接：Oura 环、量子力学与"清晰性诅咒"

DHH 摘掉 Oura 环的那个瞬间，其实是一次微型的海森堡时刻——测量行为本身改变了被测量的对象。他睡得不好不是因为身体，而是因为一个屏幕告诉他"你睡得不好"，于是产生了元焦虑（对焦虑的焦虑）。这个模式跟人类学家 James C. Scott 在《国家的视角》里描绘的现象惊人相似：现代国家为了"看清"社会而强制推行的标准化度量（地籍、姓氏、公制），最终摧毁了地方性的实践智慧（metis）。你的可穿戴设备正在对你的身体做同样的事——把只有"睡得挺好"和"睡得糟糕"两种感觉的模糊连续体，切成 47 个量化指标，然后每一个都变成了一个可失败的 KPI。Goodhart 定律的私人版本：一旦深睡时长成为你的目标，它就不再是好睡眠的指标。

让你意外的观察：DHH 是在用工程师的语言讲一个非常古老的宗教教义

作为一个以极简主义著称的程序员，DHH 表面在谈健康，实质在谈"有意的低效"作为一种系统性美德。这与生态学中的冗余原则（redundancy）、Taleb 的反脆弱理论、甚至禅宗的"侘寂"美学都指向同一个洞见：一个被完全优化过的系统是脆弱的、无灵魂的、也常常是不快乐的。更出人意料的是，硅谷那些最激进的效率信徒（从 Bryan Johnson 到 biohacking 亚文化）与传统宗教的苦行僧共享同一套心智架构——把身体当作待驯服的敌人，把每一次纵欲都视为道德失败。DHH 实际上是在提议一种世俗版的"安息日"哲学：不是因为神命令你，而是因为一个不能容忍一杯红酒的人生，其实是一个已经输了的人生。他没说出口但呼之欲出的结论是：过度优化本身，就是最深的失败模式——因为它把"活着"重新定义成了"不死"。

📝 转录文本

触发点：Diary of a CEO 的那杯红酒

Just recently we've been talking about this over optimizers. I saw Chris Williams and Modern Wisdom had a bit where it was like, "Yeah, okay, maybe we did go a little overboard." And the triggering thing was the Diary of a CEO where the host was saying something to the effect of, "I had a glass of wine and the next 3 days were ruined."

Okay. And that to me, I mean, in his circumstance, I'm sure that's true. Like if you have not drank any alcohol for a very long time and you have just a little, I could see how it can have effect. But also there's something in that that just triggered a visceral reaction, I think, for a lot of people and myself included where I was like, "Fuck, man, I should have a glass of wine just right now even though I don't usually drink."

Yeah.

酒精作为社会润滑剂：一个被忽视的宏观代价

And in effect, I think the alcohol question is a good microcosm to zoom in on. So, we've all stopped drinking, apparently. Like alcohol sales are way down.

Mhm.

Certainly amongst young people. And then on the one hand, on the pure health metrics, whatever, we can go like, "Oh, wow, isn't that great?"

Mhm.

And then I go like, "Yeah, I'm not so sure it is." Like the social lubricant that alcohol can provide maybe missed.

Is missed.

I mean, we are in an absolute epidemic of loneliness and misery and depression and and whatever and a fair amount of it just probably comes because you're not interacting enough with other people. Now, that's before we even talk about coupling, right? Like way down. People having a very hard time meeting a spouse and a lot of that has moved over to apps that have all sorts of negative outcomes and consequences, right?

Like maybe we will look back or maybe we are we are looking back and thinking like, "Do you know what? Maybe I'm wasted every once in a while was not the worst thing in the world." And whether wasted or not, maybe just having a couple of drinks every Friday or Saturday when you're out and about was part of what helped society get to where it is, maybe the fact that humans have literally been drinking for whatever it is like a 13,000 years fermenting things had a social purpose. And we pull out Chesterton's fence of our own chagrin, right?

跨文化印证：在中国乡村的破例

As you mentioned, in the spirit of that, so when I traveled across rural China, I did smoke a little bit in my early 20s, but I picked up just for that trip.

A social connector right?

And I drank humongous amounts, even though I don't really drink these days because of the social thing. It's the way they show love. And I also ate shitload of carbs, which I'm usually low carb, but I just like meat. So, just because it's the way they show love. And actually, even in that society, cigarettes, but in most societies, liquor is a thing to do together.

Yes.

And it's a bond. It doesn't the the benefits that that entails can in many situations outweigh the negative consequences like long-term for whatever however you measure them.

现代性的近视：把生活压缩成单一指标

And this is the myopia modernity. That we reduce things down to like, well, one glass on this long-run study meant that you had a 0.1% greater risk of some heart defect. Yes, but if you didn't live at all, what's the point?

And again, it's also easy to flip over the other side. Like, the only way to live is to get drunk every weekend and eat a bunch of crap and smoke 40 cigarettes a day. No, it's not. Like, it doesn't have to be the either or.

摘掉 Oura 环：为什么不再需要知道自己睡得不好

This is one of the reasons I stopped wearing my Oura ring. So, I wore the Oura sleep ring for many years, 4 years. And one day I was just like, I don't need to know that I had a bad night of sleep. Like, I know. This added I don't know what to call it anxiety. I don't have a lot of anxiety, but this added just like reminder that I had a bad night of sleep. What purpose is it actually playing here? Why do I need to have all these stats?

Why do I need to optimize everything to the point where again after that single anecdote from Diary of a CEO, I was like [ __ ] I kind of want the opposite. Like

Yeah.

I don't barely drink at all. I drink a glass of wine once a month, maybe. Like, you know what? I should start just on the weekends, get a glass, maybe two.

Yeah.

插曲：不要叫 40 岁的女人"wonderful woman"

And also, I mean, I've never been the person to fret about my diet. Um This is just one of the great privileges of being married to and I'll do a quick aside here. Don't ever call a woman in her in her 40s a wonderful woman. My wife was so pissed that not only last year that I come on her birthday, that was bad enough, but that I called her a wonderful woman on the show because that sounded like her name was Nancy and she was 65 in the suburb of Rochester. So, I'm like I was trying to play the the 50-year-old like, "No, I don't know. I'm Danish. How how would I know?" But that didn't go over well. So, I'm going to say awesome woman instead.

[snorts]

If you

[laughter]

传统分工与"不走极端"的中道

marry an awesome woman who also not only knows how to cook, but enjoys it, um do you know what? There's a very traditional division of labor here that has been quite stable through several tens of thousands of years in human societies that perhaps also wasn't the worst idea in the world. And I also know there are plenty of men who like to cook and there are women who don't, but as stereotypes go uh that certainly helped me. Like I I don't think I would have been able to just be as relaxed about food if I didn't eat relatively healthy on a on a regular basis.

But the overall point being just getting out of that optimization game without turning in to the opposite. You don't have to be a fat slob on the couch either. You you can move around.

item.title: [Lex Clips] DHH on William F Buckley interview with a Black Panther leader | Lex Fridman Podcast Clips
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的核心悖论：他们正在做他们批判的事

最反讽的观察是——两位对谈者花了大半段时间在讨论"如今无法自由讨论政治"，而这场对谈本身就是一次流畅、克制、彼此让步的政治讨论。这不是失败，而是隐藏的证据：他们所哀悼的Buckley时代并没有消失，它只是迁移了栖息地——从公共电视演播室搬进了播客的长时长语境里。真正死去的不是"理性对话"，而是"在短时序媒介里进行理性对话"的可能性。Twitter的280字符不是言论平台，而是一台部落分拣机。

二、跨领域连接：政治光谱正在变成"高维物体在低维投影"的经典问题

这里藏着一个来自数学与信息论的意外类比。Lex描述的现象——"无论你说什么，都会被塞进蓝箱或红箱"——本质上是降维塌缩（dimensionality collapse）。一个人的世界观可能是30维的向量（对乌克兰、税收、教育、AI、家庭结构各有独立判断），但社交媒体的算法激励结构强行把它投影到1维的红蓝轴上。就像把一个球体压成一条线，绝大多数信息必然丢失，而丢失的正是"人味儿"本身。

更妙的是：DHH无意间提到"在科技圈现在可以持有非2020共识的观点了"——这暗示降维压力是有场域梯度的。学术界维度更低（≈1维），科技界维度稍高（≈3-5维），私人友谊维度最高。这解释了为什么"逃向播客"和"逃向私人晚餐"成了这个时代知识分子共同的迁徙路径。

三、令人意外的观察：Buckley神话其实是一种"技术奢侈品"

大多数人把Buckley-黑豹党那场对谈浪漫化为"人格高尚"或"文化优越"的产物。但真相可能更冷酷：那是一种媒介稀缺性的副产品。1970年代只有三个电视频道，上电视本身就极度稀缺，所以嘉宾没有"表演给追随者看"的激励——他没有追随者，只有观众。而今天每个发言者背后都拖着一个算法化的观众剧场，每句话都在同时对两个受众说话：对面的人，和场外的粉丝。

这就引出一个不安的推论：礼貌不是美德，礼貌是激励结构的输出。想恢复Buckley式对话，靠"呼吁人们更宽容"是徒劳的——这等于要求人违背激励行事。真正的杠杆点不是道德，而是重新设计让"表演给部落看"变得昂贵、让"探索性思考"变得便宜的媒介结构。长播客碰巧做到了这一点：它太长，剪辑党没耐心；它太慢，愤怒挖不出爆点。这或许才是"播客文艺复兴"背后真正的机制原因。

四、隐藏的系统性真相

Lex说"如果你不上网，你根本不会知道自己的观点是左还是右"——这句话的分量远超他自己意识到的。它意味着红蓝身份不是从我们内心生长出来的，而是从网络反馈回路里被安装进去的。你不是先有立场再上网站队，而是上网这个动作本身在塑造你的立场，就像磁场对准无序的铁屑。这与神经科学里"预测编码"的模型惊人相似：大脑不断根据反馈调整自己的模型。社交媒体只是把这个过程从个体尺度扩展到了社会尺度——我们不再拥有观点，观点通过我们发生。

📝 转录文本

一、Buckley 与黑豹党成员的对谈：一个失落时代的样本

One of the great illustrations of that for me was when I watched a clip from William F. Buckley's show — I think it was called Firing Line or something like that. And he had a member of the Black Panthers on his panel.

It was quite obvious that those two gentlemen did not share a lot of politics. They were able to carry a conversation for — I think I watched 25 minutes. And Buckley's just asking, like, "So, what do you think about this? What do you think about this?" And the Black Panther would reply as you would expect a Black Panther to reply in the '70s. Like, there was not a lot of conciliatory tones.

And I just thought, like, "Wow. That is so rare." If you had seen that show today, it would have been a shouting match. It would have been just accusations being hurled back and forth. The fact that Buckley was able to just have these conversations with people he vehemently disagreed with — and still explore all the intellectual facets of their standpoints and letting them speak to those facets — talks of a lost era that I'd very much like to get back to.

I mean, I always actually love talking politics with friends that I trusted could talk about these topics in a way where it didn't have to be existential.

二、当代的困境：从"对话"到"贴标签"

Well, but there's something about the current era where that's harder and harder to come by. And so, what you just articulated is important to say regularly — to remind people of an ideal we should all strive for: to be able to have differences and talk about them.

Because politics is fun. I've gotten used to saying I hate politics at this point, but what I really mean is: whatever the system that's currently happening — where there's certain topics, I just know, we know all the phrases you can say that somehow put you in a bin of blue or red, and that creates drama versus a conversation.

I could think of a lot of harmless — if I wasn't paying attention to the internet — I could think of a bunch of harmless statements I can make analyzing the situation in the world that would trigger everybody to say, "Oh, that guy's a leftist piece of shit," or, "You know, right-wing fascist."

And then objectively, if I wasn't paying attention to the internet, I would be shocked — and I have been shocked, because having been paying attention to the internet deeply, but reading and preparing a lot, for example for the war in Ukraine — I have been shocked how certain statements from me can come off as one way or the other, and I get viciously attacked for it.

三、系统的惩罚机制：站队 vs. 自由思考

But what that attack is doing is, it's saying:

"Hey, you [ __ ] who thinks he could just move about and think freely — pick a bin and sit in that [ __ ] bin. Put on that blue shirt or red shirt."

And then actually what I've realized is: things calm down. The system doesn't pick on you if you just say, "I'm a blue person," or, "I'm a red person."

Right.

But if you're just curiously exploring the world and reasoning about the world, the system punishes you. And I hate that — because I want to get back to the Buckley and the Black Panther discussion.

Yes.

四、务实的妥协：选择性开口

And you were just saying opinions. But then, looking pragmatically at the situation, I have realized not to mention politics unless I really care about an issue — because I realized there's a cost. They'll put you in a blue bin or red bin. So you have to be more deliberate about choosing. I have been trying to be more conscious of that, too. And then when I do choose to speak up about it, it's usually because I have deliberated and I think, "You know what? This is worth it."

Yeah.

Now, I say that, and then I also catch myself thinking the opposite all the time — that I follow some person or another for whatever their technical work, and then I learn their political standpoint, and I often do think, "I wish I didn't know that." So, I mean, it's hypocritical then to think that of other people and then go, like, "Well, occasionally I will —"

Yeah.

"— chime in on a debate that's controversial." And then you have to accept that there's a price to that. And I do think you should — and more people should — be somewhat conscious about that.

五、自我矛盾中的希望：也许只是一个时刻

And again, we're both contradicting ourselves here by saying, like: wouldn't it be nice if we could talk about politics in a more free and open forum, and just intellectually turn ideas around? Yes, it would. Is that currently possible in the climate of social media and so forth? It's quite difficult.

Now, some of it could simply also be a moment — and we could get past that moment. Maybe there is a way to get back to Buckley's conversation with the Black Panthers, even on social media, in a way where those discussions don't lead to the sort of just vicious mob cancellation nonsense drives that we've had, right?

六、结论：2025 vs. 2020，一个渐进的缓和

I actually think we're closer there now than we were 5 years ago. Like, the tribalism — and the sanctions those tribes were able to exact on heretics in 2020 — way greater than it was in 2025. Certainly within tech.

Now, I know if you're in academia — I mean, try going into the sociology department at, uh, I don't know, Harvard, and mention some right-wing ideas. I don't think it's going to go over very well. And I don't think you're going to recover from it quickly.

But in tech, and in many other business domains at least, it is now possible to have an opinion that does not square with what the consensus was in 2020. That's for sure.

最反讽的观察是——两位对谈者花了大半段时间在讨论"如今无法自由讨论政治"，而这场对谈本身就是一次流畅、克制、彼此让步的政治讨论。**这不是失败，而是隐藏的证据**：他们所哀悼的Buckley时代并没有消失，它只是**迁移了栖息地**——从公共电视演播室搬进了播客的长时长语境里。真正死去的不是"理性对话"，而是**"在短时序媒介里进行理性对话"的可能性**。Twitter的280字符不是言论平台，而是一台部落分拣机。
## 二、跨领域连接：政治光谱正在变成"高维物体在低维投影"的经典问题
这里藏着一个来自数学与信息论的意外类比。Lex描述的现象——"无论你说什么，都会被塞进蓝箱或红箱"——本质上是**降维塌缩（dimensionality collapse）**。一个人的世界观可能是30维的向量（对乌克兰、税收、教育、AI、家庭结构各有独立判断），但社交媒体的算法激励结构强行把它投影到1维的红蓝轴上。就像把一个球体压成一条线，绝大多数信息必然丢失，而**丢失的正是"人味儿"本身**。
