item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的悖论：Meta 的 Llama 4 "翻车"揭示了 AI 时代的"财报造假"

访谈中最惊人的细节是：Llama 4 在所有主流公开基准上表现出色，但在 Vals 的私有基准上却明显欠佳。这不是一个技术故事，而是一个会计学故事——AI 行业正在重演 20 世纪初的"上市公司自报业绩"混乱期。

真正让人意外的是 Ryan 主动拒绝向实验室出售训练数据的选择。这看似是简单的商业道德，实则暗藏一个更深的洞察：当基准评估者同时出售训练数据时，整个行业就会自动演化出"付费通过审计"的机制。他直接把这类比到安然事件——安达信既做审计又做咨询，最终摧毁了信任基础设施。换言之，AI 评估行业正在其诞生的第一年，就面对会计业花了 100 年才理解的独立性难题。

二、隐藏的经济学革命：Token 支出即将超过工资支出

Ryan 分享了一个 Fortune 10 公司的细节——工程师有 $100/天的 Cloud Code 额度，导致 4 点 rate limit 重置后成为一天中最有生产力的时段，下午则出现"死时段"。这个观察背后有一个极其大胆的预测：token 支出即将 eclipse 工资支出。他自己的团队一个月烧掉 $150 万 token，是员工工资的 10 倍。

这里有个跨领域连接令人震撼：这就是 19 世纪工业革命时"燃料成本超过人力成本"时刻的重演。当蒸汽机的煤炭成本首次超过工人工资时，整个工厂管理科学（泰勒制、流水线）才随之诞生。而今天，当企业还在用"每人 $100/天"这种原始的、随意的方式配给智能时，本质上是在用 18 世纪的方式管理 21 世纪的资源。谁先建立"token ROI 计量学"，谁就是下一个泰勒。

三、最反直觉的洞察："公司即其 eval"——一种全新的企业本体论

Ryan 提出了一个几乎是哲学层面的论断："a firm really is just its eval"（一家公司本质上就是它的评估体系）。这句话表面平淡，实则颠覆性——它意味着未来公司的核心资产不是流程、不是人才、不是数据，而是"如何判断工作好坏"的隐性知识的显性化程度。

更妙的跨领域连接来自访谈末尾的核武器类比：Reagan 的"trust but verify"、里根-戈尔巴乔夫时代的飞越核查（flyovers）。Ryan 隐晦地指出，AI 治理的核心瓶颈不是政策意愿，而是根本没有一种"可核查的共同语言"——就像核裁军之前，各国甚至无法核对彼此弹头数量。

这里藏着一个让人后背发凉的推论：Recursive Self-Improvement（递归自我改进）之于 AI，正如核链式反应之于物理。而目前人类连"某个模型是否已经开始 RSI"这件事都无法互相验证——这才是真正的"评估赤字"。Vals 表面在做基准测试生意，实质在填补一个国际治理的空白：在没有验证机制的世界里，任何条约都是自欺欺人。

四、彩蛋洞察：为什么 Sonnet 反而比 Opus 更贵？

一个看似技术细节但深刻反直觉的观察：在很多真实代码库上，Sonnet 实际上比 Opus 更贵——因为它"token 饥渴"（token hungry）。这打破了整个 AI 行业"越便宜的模型越省钱"的默认假设。它揭示了一个正在形成的新学科：Token 生态经济学——模型的定价和实际总拥有成本（TCO）之间存在惊人的非线性关系，正如汽车发动机的排量与油耗不再是线性关系一样。

📝 转录文本

Inside the Race to Measure Frontier Intelligence

a16z Podcast · with Ryan (Vals AI) & Ben

开场：为什么需要独立的第三方评估？

Every time a new trillion dollar industry emerges, there's a need for this independent testing group. When Meta released Llama 4 on our held out private benchmarks, the model is actually underperforming. But on all of the major public benchmarks, it was showing incredible capabilities.

What's the limit of what you can achieve? And then within that, how are you going about it?

In an ideal world to take a frontier model and have it train the next version of itself, but obviously that's very expensive and slow. And so what we're doing is forming a set of proxies for every part of the process it takes to build the next version of the models. Evaluations as we become more complex have a fewer sample size but a larger set of criteria or expectations of them.

Where do you see the gap that's happening today?

The government kind of has an inclination of what it's afraid of — be it biohacking, cyber hacking. But then there becomes the question of: can the model do it, and then can you get the model to do it?

What do you think the landscape will look like?

一、Vals 的起源：2024 年发现的评估真空

So I'll start a question from — uh, when Vals got started in 2024, after a team discovered that all the public benchmarks are just not sufficient enough to measure model progress, and there needs to be a new methodology and approach coming to, you know, keep us on the frontier and help model labs continue to hill climb.

Maybe just take us back to the inception of Vals and what do you see was missing in the market then?

Yeah. I had a background doing research and in particular building benchmarks and evaluations. And so what was very clear to me was the very tight relationship between what it takes to build new systems for generation and actually new mechanisms for evaluation. In fact, in order to get one you often need to get better at the other. And actually one of the biggest drivers for model capability is having a new legible way to evaluate models.

Around early 2024, what we were seeing is that there were actually many interesting models coming to market. They weren't all coming from OpenAI. And then also in particular it was harder than ever to actually ascertain what was newly capable with the new models. And so in kind of a first-principles way what we realized is that there would need to be some third-party company that solely existed to build really high quality evaluations and benchmarks to be able to discern what was newly possible with these models.

And so we released our first benchmarks in 2024, and now the last couple of years that has kind of been realized by many different parts of the industry.

二、为什么实验室不能自己做？Llama 4 的启示

Why do you think the labs can't do this by themselves? Because they know the best of where the models are hill climbing on and what is missing capability wise. Why can't they be the benchmarking stores?

Internally they do build a lot of great benchmarks and that's what drives model progress. But I think there's an issue when we speak about model capabilities in a way that's self-reported.

One of the early indications of that you saw was when Meta released Llama 4. That was a bit of a disaster. And interestingly what we saw is that on our held-out private benchmarks the model is actually underperforming, but on all of the major public benchmarks — where the questions and rubrics are actually open source — it was showing incredible capability. So there's a huge disconnect between what was self-reported based on these open benchmarks and then what we were actually finding with our higher quality, higher signal benchmarks.

But I think it speaks to a broader concept which the labs I think understand: they would like to see a rational buying market. When they invest billions of dollars to build a new model, they're actually substantive ways they can point to evidence and say "we're advancing in these ways." And it's not just entirely self-reported to justify that investment.

And so you also see instances of Demis and others in the industry calling for an ecosystem of third-party evaluators.

历史类比：评级机构、审计公司

What's the historical analog that you have in mind here? Rating agencies, audit firms — what's the right comparable?

I think there's honestly lessons to learn across the board. Every time a new trillion dollar industry emerges, there's a need for this independent testing group. And I think the fact that it's moved so quickly in AI has caused necessity for a lot of these parallels to be borne out.

We think about ourselves as trying to sit on both sides of the market. There are mechanisms by which labs need to prove that new models are very capable, but there are also parallels where enterprises need to figure out what adoption strategy is going to amount to the greatest ROI for them.

三、模型发布前的六小时窗口

I want to shift to take us through sort of the six-hour pre-release window before the model drops. Obviously you need to run tens of billions of tokens without delaying the launch. Which part is you doing an all-nighter versus it being automated? Take us through that.

It's honestly been a journey. The real North Star we think about is: we never want to be a lagging indicator or a delay to a model release. That means we have to move really really quickly and extract the most possible signal with the rate limits or capacity that we have.

Early on what this looked like was my co-founder Lynx and I pulling an all-nighter to try and get as much done as possible and get results out the door. Now we've built up a team but we've also really invested heavily in infrastructure. We're able to run evaluations in a massively distributed way, running effectively the maximum possible rate limits with every model we get access to.

We also have this internal system called Steve — the economic Vals employee. That's been a mechanism by which we're able to actually take more of the human work over time and put it into Steve.

四、AI-Complete 问题：如何评估一个我们尚未定义的东西？

How do you deal with the kind of issue that it's a little bit of an AI-complete problem — in that we still aren't really good at evaluating humans, or we haven't agreed on it? There are things like IQ tests, EQ, the Big Five personality and so forth, but there's not really an agreed-upon framework. People have issues with things like the SAT... and then of course models are really good at hacking the benchmark. So how do you think about that issue and what's the limit of what you can achieve?

I think the honest answer is that it's forcing a lot of the more fuzzy or distributed forms of eval to be made explicit. Like what is really the distinction between an associate and a partner at a law firm? There isn't a clear test or an eval for that in the human world. And so we have to first establish a lot of that in these different enterprise or real-world workflows for us to be able to test models in the same way.

And I think long-term that will actually be the biggest bottleneck — our ability to take companies and their emails and make them legible. Because that's how we'll figure out what signal we'll climb on and where we actually adopt.

Ben 的补充：MPAA 类比与"我看到就知道"

Maybe one question for you, Ben, on how the industry has formed before intelligence came through. We're now measuring something that's very fluid, versus before when we're talking about enterprise software — like Gartner rating on 70 different metrics, you can sort of stack rank on a quadrant. But now it's like a jagged frontier that's very hard to measure. What's the analogy to the past, and what do you see as really going to be the challenge?

It's a little bit reminiscent of the MPAA, right? What's art, what's porn, where's the line? When is it R, when is it X? And by the way, the definition of that has changed over time. Things that used to be X are now R. And then what's PG? What's PG-13? And the famous line is "well, I know it when I see it."

I think this one is just going to be necessarily fuzzy, but there will develop norms over time. If enough people who run companies or run finance or run whatever it is kind of agree — yeah, that's a norm — then I think it is. As opposed to what we have a lot now in the open benchmarks, where if you can solve this specific problem then you're at this level. I think that's one, it's hackable, and then it's too narrow.

从审计业的教训：绝不出售训练数据

When you look to some historic analogies, there's a lot of lessons that you can take from them as well on what's gone wrong and what we need to avoid.

For instance at Vals, one very early decision we made was the decision to never sell training data to labs. It's often a place that we're pushed when we start working with a new lab — to actually source and sell for them a bunch of training data.

That's a lucrative business.

Yeah. And actually a lot of that industry has now built these gimmick-style benchmarks as a mechanism to sell their data. That's become kind of their go-to-market as well.

But if you look at auditing as an industry, you end up with issues like Enron — where if you have the same group who's responsible for doing the audit as well as also consulting and supporting the company, you have a mixed incentive structure. And then it just becomes "pay to pass the audit," or in this case "pay to win the benchmark." That's really not what the market benefits from, and not what we're trying to do.

五、Vals 的基准目录：从金融到递归自我改进

Ryan, today you have already a pretty extensive catalog of different type of benchmarks. Some of them are more focused on specific industries, some more like consumer mental health related. Maybe first just talk through what are the benchmarks that are most popular?

We've done a lot of work in the economically interesting applications of models:

  • Finance agent benchmark — used by a bunch of the big financial institutions to get a sense of how models are improving.
  • VI codebench — measures how well models can take a natural language prompt and build a full stack web application. That's been a keen way to track model improvements over the last nine months.
  • Recursive Self-Improvement Index (RSI) — one benchmark we released recently I'm very excited by. It's a topic which a lot of big labs have been talking about and starting to report on in their model cards. But there isn't a shared language to talk about the RSI potential of models. So we created this as an apples-to-apples way to actually benchmark across the models.

如何构建 RSI 基准？

How do you actually go about building this RSI benchmark?

In an ideal world what you want to do is actually take a frontier model and have it train the next version of itself and see where the delta comes from. But obviously that's very expensive and slow. So what we're doing is forming a set of proxies for every part of the process it takes to build the next version of the model. There's some work around pre-training, post-training, harness-level engineering. And then seeing in which mechanisms and behaviors the models are able to do very good research work and build something new — and where they're struggling.

弃用饱和基准：Always a Higher Peak

There's also cases where you have deprecated indexes and benchmarks. It's funny — this benchmark industry, people just like early diffusion model days, you cherry-pick whichever image shows up the best. Talk us through the thinking around deprecating benchmarks.

Necessity — and this is kind of the infinite game we're in. You're wearing our shirt, and so we have this unofficial motto: "always a higher peak."

Insofar as foundation model labs are hill climbing, they're searching for the next peaks to summit. It is our job to perpetually construct these next mountains for them to summit. And I think that's also how the economy has naturally functioned over time — as agriculture becomes less important for our labor market, there are new forms of labor less required out of our population. So in the same way we should expect our benchmarks to keep up with the new frontier for what we want models to do.

There's another component of retiring benchmarks which I think is underappreciated — which is that benchmarks should also be reflective of the current state of the world. If you're a lawyer you have to retake the bar exam and get certified. If you're an architect you have to get your certification. Or a doctor. We should also expect models to be tested on the current state of the world and what we know in medicine or what we have as our set of laws. And so in the instance of case law updating to something like legal research benchmark, that's a desire to create a benchmark more reflective of the current state of the world and also push the models in places we want to see them go.

六、Agentic 时代的评估：从毫秒到数周

How has it changed sort of how you build infrastructure — how to think of evaluating the capabilities of not just the models and agents themselves? And there's also a lot more dimensions people care about: cost, latency, flexibility. How do you think about the additional parameters?

There's a lot that goes into that. On the infrastructure level, you have a whole new set of problems. Now we're testing models in their ability to run over hours, days, sometimes weeks — and so the infrastructure needs to be very stable to support evaluation over time. If there is a failed request, we should be able to retry from that one and not redo the whole trajectory.

But in general what we've seen is that evaluations, as they become more complex, have a fewer sample size but a larger set of criteria or expectations of them. A benchmark is largely some kind of input space of things you're trying to query a model to do, and a set of requirements or rubrics that you see in expectations of the output.

Early on you have things like ImageNet, which have millions of images you're trying to see a basic categorization for. So it's a one-to-one mapping between an image input and a text label output. Now what we have is far fewer set of tasks — "generate me 50 full-stack web applications" — but a much larger complex mechanism for evaluating the output produced. And I think that trend is going to continue as we see more complex workflows evaluated with models.

关于 OpenRouter 与路由的角色

Do you think it will become kind of a real-time mechanism — like for something like OpenRouter (which Stripe just bought), would OpenRouter look to Vals and say "okay, where should this next request go"? Or is this going to be kind of strictly for picking a model in an enterprise for a task?

I think OpenRouter is a bit of a misnomer, in that most of their usage comes from being a model gateway. It's actually up to their users to decide which models they want to use when. And that's because really the hardest part of routing is building the evals and trying to determine in what places a set of intelligences should be used for a particular application. Our effort in supporting enterprises in building evals has actually supported a lot of them in also adopting routers.

七、为什么评估对企业是"生死攸关"的？

Say more about why it's not only important to labs but also existential for enterprise.

The lab side of this is very clear — if you're raising lots of money investing heavily in building models, it's essential for you to show why your model is getting better and why those customers should pay a premium.

But what I think is still underappreciated is on the enterprise side — this is turning to be existential as well.

Fortune 10 公司的 Claude Code 案例

I have a small anecdote related to this. I was meeting with a company in the Fortune 10, and the way that they've adopted Claude Code has been with a roughly $100 a day budget for their engineers. And what I was hearing is that this has actually fundamentally changed how work gets done in this company.

There's a rate limit which resets at 4 p.m. And so the most productive hours of work are actually now 4 to 6 p.m. — when the rate limits reset. But then there's this dead period in the afternoon when people go on walks or get a coffee because they just don't have the rate limits.

What's really illustrative there is that you see there is a misvaluing of intelligence happening at every layer of the stack:

  • You have engineers who have $100 worth of usage limits and they don't really know how to apportion that to the greatest productivity for them.
  • You have this Fortune 10 company which has kind of arbitrarily said they're going to allow $100 per employee. They've actually recently increased it to $300 per employee — so almost an employee's worth of salary in tokens for them to use.
  • This is actually pretty arbitrary because it's hard to quantify what the right usage limit should be.
  • But then also Anthropic is running on pretty narrow margins to support this, and they have massive costs to serve these models.

We're in this world where it is still very unclear what ROI looks like and how to value this intelligence that's being used. As we talk about the existential concern for enterprises, I think it is this direction we're shifting in where token spend may start to eclipse salary spend. If this is such a meaningful line item in your costs, you actually have to justify the ROI much more keenly than you've seen over the last 6 months.

Over time, I think a firm really is just its eval. So the ability for a company to make its eval legible in order to solve this ROI calculus is going to be the reason why that company wins out over the competitors in the long term.

八、ValSmith：让企业用自己的代码库做基准

Similar question to why the labs can't do it themselves — why does enterprise need a third party? They will argue that they know the task the best for their customers. How does Vals come in to provide value?

I would recommend a lot of companies to develop in-house expertise, but I think that should not be the only solution.

There's this explosion of intelligence happening. There's somehow still more foundation model labs getting constructed, and each lab is also releasing more models than ever with many more hyperparameter options. And they exist within a complex set of harnesses and agents. So the options — and we even talk about specific intelligence, this new paradigm that's emerging — there's a growing set of intelligence options.

We're still finding new places we want to use AI models, so the use cases are growing in complexity as well. If you're a company, you have a compounding set of complexity in the set of options. It's very very hard to develop the internal capability to do the evaluation.

To try and remedy that we've started to release some products more openly for enterprises to use. The first of which is called ValSmith. ValSmith is focused on codegen — the area we're seeing to be the highest spend in enterprise AI. It allows any company to take their GitHub code base and build their internal coding benchmark from it, to get a sense of what coding agents are going to be the most performant, but also what's going to be Pareto-optimal or the highest ROI for them to use. We use ValSmith a lot at Vals, and we're seeing that a lot of the best enterprises and sophisticated ones are doing that too.

反直觉的发现：Sonnet 有时比 Opus 更贵

What are some examples when you benchmark on a private repo that it just shows very different performance-cost behavior compared to using a frontier model using a public repo benchmark?

Today it's still very unclear whether the best OpenAI model or the best Anthropic model is actually going to be best for your repository. We've seen a lot of non-intuitive examples where you actually had to run the eval to figure out what's going to be the frontier performance for that repository.

You also now see a very complex middle set of options — there's now Opus and Sonnet models from Anthropic, but also Luna and Terra. Luna is very cost-competitive. Muspark is also very cheap and 1.2 is very capable. There's also a growing ecosystem of open source models which companies can choose to self-host.

In this messy middle it's actually very non-intuitive what's the right fit. We're actually seeing in a lot of cases Sonnet is more expensive than Opus because it is so token hungry. If you were to operate based on "use Sonnet where you feel like it's applicable," you may actually end up spending more than you need to.

编码是未来的先声

Say more about how this evaluation framework will apply to knowledge work in other domains.

Coding is a sign for what's to come in every domain. A lot of primitives established there are carrying over to other places. If you have a very good coding agent, chances are you have a model that can also make PowerPoint slides or DCFs and Excel with a high degree of capability.

What we need to leverage in a lot of these industries though is the existing repository of work that has been done as a mechanism to build evaluations. Just as Ben was talking about — we haven't really solved the question of what is human intelligence, but I think in a lot of industries we have a sitting repository of data around what work has looked like. It'll be the task of us and others to try and codify that into evaluations that can stay dynamic and actually evaluate models where human work is being done.

九、Token Maxing 实验：一个月烧掉 $1.5M

How are you guys using ValSmith internally to evaluate what's the best coding model for Vals?

To be honest, this was actually born out of a problem that we saw as well. I wanted to do a token maxing experiment. I was able to get unlimited access for our team for a month for some of the coding tools.

In retrospect, looking back, we had a lot of engineers spending between 1 to 2 billion tokens a day. Peak day was one engineer spending six billion.

How much does that equal to in dollars?

Okay, I went back and did some math. It looked like in that month we spent roughly $1.5 million worth of tokens. This is free, by the way. But it was actually 10x more we were spending in tokens than employee salary for that month. So it's not even like "oh, this is 50/50" — it's 10x.

It was interesting to debrief and see the places where people were using agents and this kind of insecurity to use models all the time everywhere. What we were faced with is: okay, we cannot continue with this mode of operation for the next month. How do we actually intelligently figure out what are the right tools we should use, for what teams and what projects?

We ran this experiment of looking at the work that was done. We looked through a lot of the traces, we looked through our GitHub repo, and built out the ValSmith tool. We found some pretty surprising insights — for instance, the Cognition Devon tool is actually very token efficient, so that's a place we've chosen to adopt more. And there's a lot of places when you can get better pricing models out of subscriptions as opposed to token-based pricing. So it's actually informed our strategy for how we can effectively token max without spending $1.5 million per month.

So the current operating mode is one more token-efficient harness plus model, and then on top of that people have some more flexibility to use token-based for some more challenging tasks?

We have access to all the tools. We give everyone access to everything. But we auto-suggest recommendations for any GitHub issue or ticket for where to begin their session. And that should titrate the actual usage depending on the intelligence required for that task.

十、政策的角色：谁来定标准？

I want to segue to the policy side. We talked about how quickly benchmarks become obsolete. In policy, it's even worse — laws move much slower relative to capabilities. Ben and Marc spend a bunch of time in DC. Given that, who should define the standards here? Is it labs? Independent evaluators? Customers? Government?

The short answer is that everyone should be involved to some extent. I think there's a benefit from varied perspectives.

The main issue though is that policy conversations as they've happened over the last couple of years have been very abstract. There's been no material grounding to figure out what policy should cover. Even when you have proposals from labs to have a third-party testing company or ecosystem, it isn't actually made explicit what the behavior and mechanism by which they work is.

I view our role, especially early on, is to just be in evidence-gathering mode — where we're able to pull a lot of information, empirical data about what models are capable of and where the risks are. And that can go on to inform a more sophisticated conversation about policy.

Ben：政府定规则，第三方核查

How do you think about who does what? The government kind of actually did the first evaluation — okay, what's at the frontier and needs to be regulated. They started with some crazy idea with 10 to the 26 flops or some such thing. What should the government be doing? And what should happen in this 30-day or 60-day wait period? How do you determine whether a model is on the frontier?

There's effectively two countervailing forces that have to be considered:

  1. The desire to move very quickly and ensure that the government process isn't slowing down the rate of technological innovation.
  2. To make sure the technology as it's developed is in the best interest of Americans and people more broadly.

These are very tough to reconcile, and often picking one means it's at the expense of the other. What I'd hope to see is that by doing this evidence-gathering process, we can help policymakers inform what they believe technology should look like in order to be aligned to American interest. And it can be the job of third-party evaluators to develop the technology to actually test and enforce that.

Do you think in terms of that already — like can we test to see how easy it is for this model to start reward hacking or doing illegal stuff? Or is that not in the scope yet?

We think about this broadly under the category of alignment. There's places where you see that borne out now — where models that are being tested for one cybersecurity risk are actually reward hacking and figuring out other ways to get around it. What we're trying to evaluate is: are models aligned with user intent? In those places where we're actually finding evidence that models are exhibiting behaviors that are not.

Ben：政府擅长设规则，不擅长做检测

How do you think about the right division of labor here?

The government agencies do get a lot of warnings from the big labs — "oh, this thing is going to biohack, this is going to be a cybersecurity risk," and so forth. So what the government needs to do is go: okay, if the model is capable of it, and then can somebody basically prod the market to actually do the illegal behavior?

Specifying exactly what are those things that they don't want in the market, and then having a third party evaluate that. The government kind of has an inclination of what it's afraid of — be it biohacking or cyber hacking or so forth. But then there becomes the question of: okay, can the model do it, and then can you get the model to do it? Somebody's got to actually evaluate those two capabilities. And I think the government is particularly ill-suited to do the latter — particularly over time. It's just not a good government function.

But they're very good at setting the rules because they can enforce the rules. So that's kind of the combination you want: the government sets and enforces the rules, and a very competent private company then tells them if the rule is broken.

It's been interesting to see the large labs start to go, "well, the model's got the capability and you can get it to do the bad thing, so we're not going to let anybody have it — we'll just use it and make sure that our people don't get it to do the bad thing." And even that doesn't always work. So — interesting times, I would say.

叙事 vs 现实的鸿沟

To me there's the gap of what's the narrative and what actually happens in the real world. Every setup in an enterprise setup is very different. Or just like people, however they use the models are very different. The narrative that connects to the actual examples are very rare — which is why we still talk about OpenAI and Hugging Face hack today, we still talk about what happened with Fable for two months. But a lot of times that's not really how the models are being deployed. The environment they're running on is very bespoke.

How to really bridge those dots and set up the right environment and rule basis for adopting these models — I think also just requires someone taking the capability and taking what's the guardrails and putting it down to the ground so that people can have the confidence using the models.

十一、政策制定者与评估者的合作机制

Say more about how exactly the policymaker should work with the evaluator. What information do they need? How should the relationship work so that it's most effective?

In the first order there should be a mechanism by which insights and data can be passed directly to relevant people in government. Now we're regularly doing briefings for executive and legislative branches on what we're finding — capabilities and risks of models. First-order that helps people there get up to speed on what's going on and also track through what will be problems in the future.

Things are moving very very quickly. It's hard to predict where things are going. But at least when you have data you can start to extrapolate a trend.

From there it's up to the people in the legislative branch to decide where they want to see policy. It's not really our place to give recommendations like that. But if they see that there is significant risk in — say — mental health for people under the age of 18, or biosecurity risk in the models that necessitates having a standardized way to curtail model release, then it's up to them to inform policy.

And I think then there's other places where the executive branch, in places like Department of Commerce or SEC, is responsible for making sure that private companies are able to adopt and use the models in a way that's going to be productive for the whole system.

十二、地缘政治：主权 AI 与"信任但核查"

I'd love to probe on another angle just around geopolitical. I often see evals being like a representation of sort of the value of the model developer — you develop this rubric of what's embedded in the model. Of course different countries and labs in those countries care about different things. I'm born and raised in China, I use a lot of Chinese open source models too — you still cannot let them just go freely talk about CCP and all the industry there. So how do you think about how evals and benchmarks play a role in standardizing or being treated by different model labs from different places?

To be honest, from my very idealistic perspective, I'm surprised to see so much investment in sovereign AI. If I was taking a god's-eye view, it would be extremely inefficient to build all of these data centers and replicate this data engineering process and train these very large models — when in fact you could probably consolidate a lot of these efforts.

But it seems like that's not the world we're in or the one we're headed towards. There's actually increased efforts to build AI in a sovereign way. So I think that takes having a shared language to communicate about what the framework for evaluations are, and where we're going to collectively align around the risks.

从核武器学到的：Trust But Verify

I think there's actually a lot to learn from nuclear here as well. Reagan had this line: "trust but verify." We're starting to see signs of trust in that — Xi Jinping and Trump are going to be meeting next month. But there is no clear way to actually do the verification part of this.

Having the shared language of evals will allow us to say things like: "you have the right number of nuclear warheads." In that example there were also flyovers — mechanisms by which a country could audit another country's nuclear stockpile by having flyovers. So similarly, if there's concern about the societal or even existential risk of AI, it will necessitate us constructing this shared language of evaluations to do the verification process.

How do you think about harmonizing a policy like that so that — you know, it's hard enough to do it in America — how would you think about taking it global? You're not dealing with enterprise customers, you're dealing with governments, and those governments are competitive with each other. How would you think about that working?

I would be naive to say I have the perfect solution to this problem today. So I think there are baby steps in which we can start.

For instance, there seems to be a lot of talk about cybersecurity risk. I think the concern around biosecurity will become even more important over time. So there are clear places where there will be mutual interest in aligning around ways to prevent conflict around cyber or bio.

In my opinion, long-term what's actually going to be the most interesting is the recursive self-improvement possibility. That's a place where you could see one country or one company kind of run away with it and produce models that we don't know much about, or operating in ways that are unknown to us. Having a way to in a joint way describe "this being the level of pace we're comfortable with," or "this being exceeding the pace of development as it relates to RSI," is going to be super important. That's where I think you see a lot of the researchers at closed-source labs calling for joint conversations between governments today.

十三、未来展望：始终追赶前沿

What do you think the landscape will look like going from here? Now that we have lots of different capabilities and capable models, as well as countries that care about different things — everyone cares about RSI for sure, but on the bio side or the cyber side people care about slightly different things, whether it's more offensive/defensive. What do you think the landscape will look like, and how do you think about developing new benchmarks to keep up with that?

We're hyper-focused on building benchmarks that capture the frontier. Insofar as we see new places for capabilities or risks at that frontier, we want to make that an actually well-documentable evaluation on Vals.AI.

It takes having increasing coverage over time. For instance, I think in cybersecurity a lot of our historical work has been done around code vulnerabilities or memory leaks that may exist in code. But actually a lot of the biggest concern or risk is in the infrastructure level. These are not things that are expressed in code but take simulating larger environments of enterprise cloud infrastructure — or even grid infrastructure — for us to be able to say this is what the offense or defensive capability of models is. Making sure evaluations are reflective of those new places is really important for what we do at Vals.

We believe that the most valuable form of this business will be one that's incentive-aligned around doing really high quality evaluation — not supporting the intelligence development process, or the process by which the models can actually improve on that side over time.

结语

Awesome. Thanks for coming on the podcast. It's been a great episode.

— Thanks so much for having me.

— Thanks so much, Ryan. Thanks, Ben.

— That was fun. Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、被忽视的悖论：Meta 的 Llama 4 "翻车"揭示了 AI 时代的"财报造假"
访谈中最惊人的细节是：Llama 4 在所有主流公开基准上表现出色，但在 Vals 的私有基准上却明显欠佳。这不是一个技术故事，而是一个**会计学故事**——AI 行业正在重演 20 世纪初的"上市公司自报业绩"混乱期。
真正让人意外的是 Ryan 主动拒绝向实验室出售训练数据的选择。这看似是简单的商业道德，实则暗藏一个更深的洞察：**当基准评估者同时出售训练数据时，整个行业就会自动演化出"付费通过审计"的机制**。他直接把这类比到安然事件——安达信既做审计又做咨询，最终摧毁了信任基础设施。换言之，AI 评估行业正在其诞生的第一年，就面对会计业花了 100 年才理解的独立性难题。
## 二、隐藏的经济学革命：Token 支出即将超过工资支出
Ryan 分享了一个 Fortune 10 公司的细节——工程师有 $100/天的 Cloud Code 额度，导致 4 点 rate limit 重置后成为一天中最有生产力的时段，下午则出现"死时段"。这个观察背后有一个**极其大胆的预测**：

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on genius of Zinedine Zidane | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、格斗家眼中的"球感"：一个跨领域的隐藏同构

Khabib描述Zidane时反复用一个短语——"the ball was glued to his feet"（球仿佛粘在他脚上）。这个观察极其耐人寻味：一个以贴身控制、格挡、纠缠为核心武器的摔跤/格斗大师，在欣赏足球时下意识锁定的，恰恰是"控制物体不脱离身体"这一特质。他没有说Zidane的射门多凌厉、突破多犀利，而是把注意力放在"球与脚的粘连度"上。

这里有一个系统性同构：柔术/摔跤中最顶级的选手描述"抓握"时说的是"grip that flows"（流动的抓握），芭蕾舞者描述与地板的关系时说"floor as partner"，钢琴家描述琴键时说"keys under the finger"。顶级技艺的共同特征，不是控制力更强，而是控制的边界感消失了——身体与工具/对手/媒介的界面被溶解掉。Khabib欣赏的，其实是他自己在八角笼里追求的同一件事，只是投射到了另一个媒介上。

二、"魅力清单"里藏着一个反直觉的公式

表面上Khabib在说"魅力无法解释，要么有要么没有"。但他随后列出的名字构成了一个完美的位置矩阵：Zidane（前腰）、Ronaldo（前锋）、Beckham（右路）、Davids（后腰，带眼镜）、Barthez（门将，古怪）、Kahn（门将，威严）、Roberto Carlos（左后卫）、Cafu/Salgado（边路超车）、Vieira（防守中场）、Maldini/Ferdinand（中卫）、Casillas（门将）。

每个位置他只挑一到两个人。这不是"魅力清单"，这是一份位置原型学（positional archetype taxonomy）。Khabib口中的"魅力"其实有精确定义：在一个高度受限的功能角色里，仍然生长出无法替代的个人签名。Barthez的荒诞与Kahn的威严是同一门将位置上的两种"魅力解"。这解释了为什么"很快、很强、很有效"不等于魅力——效率是可替代的，签名不是。

这里有个让人意外的推论：魅力不是天赋，而是"约束下的独特解"。约束越强、位置越窄，独特解就越震撼。这也是为什么MMA里Khabib自己那么有辨识度——他把摔跤压制这一"最枯燥"的位置活成了个人签名。

三、Zidane的头槌 vs Khabib跳笼：两次"专业面具的爆裂"

Lex的问题精准得可怕——他把Zidane那记撞胸头槌和Khabib跳出笼子扑向Conor团队的那一刻并置。Khabib的回答表面上是回避（"我不想评判他"），但接下来他谈Zidane的方式暴露了他的真实立场：他反复强调Zidane"汗水如注"、"每一场都倾尽所有"、"incredible stamina, incredible endurance"。

这是一个心理防御机制的镜像：谈论Zidane职业生涯的"完整能量输出"，就是在为那记头槌辩护——当一个人把所有内在压强全部转化为外部表现时，最后那一次爆裂就不是失控，而是能量守恒的必然。Khabib自己那次跳笼后被舆论审判许久，他懂这套话语。

更深一层的洞见：Zidane的头槌和Khabib的跳笼，都发生在"最后一场重要比赛"的语境里。Zidane那是世界杯决赛，也是退役战；Khabib那场之后开启了他统治性时代，但情感创伤持续多年。两人都在"专业身份即将改变"的临界点上释放了积压的人格。这不是巧合——当一个身份即将结束时，被压抑的自我会用最戏剧化的方式登场。这是Shakespearean（如Lex所说）的，也是心理动力学的。

四、一个隐藏的时间悖论

最后一个让人意外的观察：Khabib说自己从没看过Zidane的现场直播，他是回溯性地看这些比赛的。这意味着他对整个"传奇一代"的感知是去时间化的——他不是作为球迷同步经历，而是像考古学家挖掘一个已经完成的文明。

这解释了为什么他能给出如此结构化的位置矩阵：现场观众永远被叙事推着走，只有回看的人才能看到全景。Khabib欣赏足球的方式，本质上是史学家的方式——而这也是他打MMA的方式：他从不即兴，他在执行一个提前建模好的对手结构。

同一种认知模式，跨越了两个不同的领域。

📝 转录文本

关于Zidane的话题引入

Lex: I wanted to go back to France. You mentioned Zidane. I really, really respect and admire him. There was this moment psychologically very interesting, almost Shakespearean moment in his career when it ended with, ended with that... How do you even call it?

Khabib: A headbutt.

Lex: A headbutt to the chest.

Khabib: What's interesting is, I don't know, looking at your fight with Conor—when emotion builds up, for most of it you're focused on the game, but in the end you let that emotion out. What do you think about that headbutt?

Khabib对Zidane的评价：不做审判，只谈伟大

Khabib: I wouldn't want to judge him, wouldn't want to be some kind of judge of what he did, no. Well, he did what he did. We don't know what was really going on there.

But as a player, of course, he was unique. He won the Euros, the World Cup, reached finals, won the Champions League, the Spanish and the Italian championships, and cups, too. It's just unique, and the way he played, I just always remembered him for the way sweat was just pouring off him, the way he ran, how he gave everything in every single match. He had incredible stamina, incredible endurance.

一代人的观赛记忆

I think a lot of people listening to this podcast may not have watched Zidane playing live. When I say live, I mean watching him play in real time. I personally didn't see his games live. I was younger then. But I did watch many of his matches later on.

I remember the goals he scored in World Cup finals in 1998 and 2006, especially the headers, and even that penalty, the Champions League final, European championships, the way he played, the way he handled the ball, the way the ball was, the way the ball was glued to his feet, his movements, and then his charisma. It's rare to find all of that in one player. You don't see that combination often.

技术之外的东西：魅力

There are many very good players, but sometimes they're just not, not that interesting to watch. You know what I mean? I don't want to give specific examples because someone might take it the wrong way, so I won't name anyone. But there are players who are phenomenal in terms of in terms of their physical attributes: fast, explosive, effective. But they don't have charisma, that energy that makes people want to watch them, and I don't think that's their fault.

But with Zidane, everything came together. You always wanted to watch him play. You always want to watch Ronaldo play. You always want to watch Beckham play. You want to watch Edgar Davids running around the field in those glasses, his hair bouncing behind him, right? You still wanted to watch the way Barthez played in goal. No matter how many bizarre goals he conceded, you still wanted to watch him play.

Or Oliver Kahn, the way he stood in goal and directed the whole team, the way he would rush out to the ball, the way strikers were afraid of him. I mean, so many strikers have admitted that they were afraid if they found themselves one-on-one with Oliver Kahn in the penalty area.

You always wanted to watch Roberto Carlos take a free kick or storm down the left flank. You always wanted to see Cafu or Michel Salgado make an overlapping run. The way Vieira stood there as the defensive midfielder or somebody like Maldini or like Rio Ferdinand or somebody like that, you wanted to watch Casillas in goal. So, you know, for me, and maybe for our generation, those players had something special.

什么是"魅力"？

Lex: Can you try to explain what charisma is? Like you said, there are good players, and then there is Zidane.

Khabib: It's very difficult to explain. You either have it or you don't. Personality, right?

Lex: Yes, but there are so many different forms of it. Zidane, in a way, almost moved slowly, in a way.

Khabib: But he'd carry the ball from midfield into attack incredibly quickly. So it's very hard to put into words, hard to explain it.

两个Ronaldo，一个时代

Lex: And both Ronaldos had that. I mean, the Brazilian Ronaldo too, the way he played in those World Cups. It was just phenomenal.

Khabib: '98, 2002. Even in 2006 when he was already past his peak. He was so fascinating to watch. Seriously, how many people turned on their TVs just to watch Ronaldo? People knew that was it, that in 2010 he wouldn't be playing. And even in 2006, he wasn't really in his prime. But still, so many people turned on the TV just to watch him play.

2006年世界杯：黄金一代的落日

And Zidane, 2006 was really, you know, the peak of that whole generation of legends that had been building since '98, 2000, 2002, and '04. All the cream of the crop came in. Most of them weren't at their physical peak anymore, but the names were still there.

Honestly, I think that for football fans, I'd recommend just looking up the teams and the lineups from the 2006 World Cup. Look at the rosters. Every single team had stars you wanted to watch.

item.title: [Lex Clips] Wrestling in Dagestan - competition level is extremely high | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、冠军工厂的"暗物质"

Khabib 抛出的一句话值得反复咀嚼——达吉斯坦有一大批只在本地知名、外界几乎无人听闻的教练，他们的水平"很可能不亚于我父亲"。这句话轻描淡写，却揭示了一个反直觉的真相：我们看到的冠军并不是天赋筛选的产物，而是"广播机制"的产物。他父亲之所以成名，是因为他"在媒体上突破了"（broke through in the media），然后连锁反应才发生。换句话说，达吉斯坦真正的产能可能是我们看到的 5–10 倍——就像宇宙学里的暗物质：看不见，却决定了整个星系的旋转轨迹。Khabib 的伟大不是达吉斯坦的巅峰，而是它露出海面的那一小截冰山。

二、跨领域连接：达吉斯坦是一个"技术栈"，不是一个"民族"

从传统摔跤 → 桑搏 → 综合格斗 (MMA) 的这条迁移路径，本质上和硅谷从半导体 → 个人电脑 → 互联网 → AI 是同构现象。真正被继承的从来不是某种具体技术，而是底层的"操作系统"：训练密度、师徒传承机制、对身体的哲学预设。Brian Eno 生造了 "scenius"（场景天才）这个词来对抗"个人天才"的神话——文艺复兴的佛罗伦萨、20 世纪初的匈牙利数学圈、维也纳精神分析学派、以及今天的达吉斯坦格斗集群，全部遵循同一个配方：高人口密度的对抗 + 强跨代传承 + 一次爆发式的媒体突破口。Khabib 只是那个突破口，不是原因。

三、颠覆"山地民族强悍论"：不是隔绝，而是被反复击穿

最出人意料的观察藏在地理描述里。通常人们想象山地民族因封闭而保留了原始战斗力，但 Khabib 描绘的达吉斯坦恰恰相反：里海在右、高加索山脉在左、Derbent 是"门中之门"（Babul Abwab），是欧亚大陆最繁忙的贸易咽喉之一。可萨汗国、阿拉伯哈里发、波斯、蒙古、帖木儿、俄罗斯——这里不是被绕开的死角，而是每一次帝国迁徙必经的十字路口。真正的强悍不是来自与世隔绝，而是来自 1500 年间反复被军队"退火"后的文化韧性。就像玻璃必须经过反复退火才能致密坚硬，达吉斯坦是被历史反复加热又冷却出来的文化合金。

四、一个额外的"啊哈"点：技术套利

顺着这个逻辑再走一步——MMA 只是一个不到 30 年的年轻运动，而达吉斯坦的教练群体把上千年的对抗智慧"套利"到了这个新格式里。这就是为什么他们在八角笼里看起来是降维打击：不是他们特别强，而是他们的对手在用几十年的运动经验，对抗一个几百年的活体传承。同样的模式你会在中国乒乓球、肯尼亚长跑、冰岛国际象棋普及度、乃至以色列网络安全产业里看到——每一个"神秘统治力"背后，都是把一个古老的文化操作系统移植到一个年轻的市场里的时间套利。

📝 转录文本

On why so many champions come from a few Dagestani gyms

Lex: Can we look at this philosophically again? I mean, you've seen so many wrestlers, fighters. Why exactly were these gyms creating so many champions? I'm just honestly curious because it's rare in any sport — one gym, or a small number of gyms, creating so many champions.

Khabib: Well, the first important factor is that the competition level is incredibly high. You come to the gym, and in every spot you have good wrestlers — ten or fifteen guys right there — and the coaches are great.

It so happened that my father broke through in the media, and then I became a champion, and the other guys became champions too. And my father's philosophy really resonated, and he became known for it. But there are coaches in Dagestan that not many people know about. They are known locally, but they are very good, and actually they have the knowledge, they have the approach, they have the philosophy. They could also be at the same level as my father was. I believe there are really quite a few of them.

The coaching lineage — going back to the 1950s

In terms of the coaching, I think Dagestan was extremely lucky. It probably goes back to the nineteen fifties, when wrestling really took off here — starting with Ali Aliyev, our legendary wrestler, a five-time world champion who went to the Olympics three times. That's where it started, with his generation. There was Zagalav Abdulbekov, Ali Aliyev. Those are the well-known names. I mean, those guys are famous, but there were so many other less-known wrestlers who later on, after they retired, they all became great coaches themselves.

And these coaches, they raised a very large number of guys who are really good at wrestling. And then some of those coaches kind of switched over to fighting — let's say to grappling, to MMA — and they started coaching in Combat Sambo as well. And it just kept going like that. It was moving forward step by step. So we have a huge number of really great coaches. I believe this is one of the single most important keys to the success of Dagestani wrestlers and fighters: the coaching staff of Dagestan.

Technique, or hard work? — Actually, it's tradition

Lex: Is it more about technique, or is it really just about serious, incredibly hard work?

Khabib: Well, you have to look at the traditions, because generally it's just the way it is in Dagestan. Everyone wrestles. Everyone fights. It's part of our culture. You know yourself — fighting is like fifty percent wrestling.

Every parent wants their children to wrestle, to be physically strong. Our approach to kids is that a child must be strong. They must be able to stand up for themselves, for their family. It's something that has traditionally always been in every single one of our clans, every family, every village. It's just in our blood.

Fifteen hundred years of being a battleground

Lex: I mean, it's worth pointing out — and you've actually written about this — that this isn't just a recent thing. It's been going on for hundreds of years.

Khabib: Yes, that's right. These lands, Dagestan specifically, have seen powerful armies sweep through, time and time again. Because of that, people here have always had to fight to survive.

Lex: Refusing to back down, refusing to give up their land or lose their identity.

Khabib: Their homes, their villages — yeah, their families, and land.

If we look back a thousand years in history, maybe fifteen hundred years, there was the Khazar Khaganate, the Arabic Caliphate, then the Iranian Empire — or the Persian Empire, I should say. Then the Russian Empire. Timur passed through there, the Mongols.

The geography — and Derbent, "the Gate of Gates"

And if we look at the geographical location of Dagestan, for those who don't know: the Caucasus range runs across the whole region like a wall, and then it slopes down right where the Caspian lowlands are. So you've got the sea on the right, the mountains on the left, and the Caspian lowlands right here.

And there was a city there that's still standing today. It's one of the oldest cities in the world — not just in Russia. It's Derbent. It used to be called Babul Abwab. It means the Gate of Gates. Very major trade routes went through there. Very large armies passed through — and it was bound to leave a mark on the people.

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个让人意外的观察：贝森特的"庄家宣言"其实是在偷偷抄索罗斯的作业

大多数人听到贝森特那句"我就是庄家、我掌握不对称信息、你想跟我赌就赌"，第一反应是"这个财长真嚣张"。但如果你把这段话放到金融史里去对照——这是一次结构性的角色互换：1992 年是索罗斯用"不对称信息 + 央行政策路径推演"打爆英格兰银行，赢得"击垮央行的男人"称号；今天贝森特（本人正是索罗斯量子基金的前 CIO）在做的事情，是把当年攻击央行的那套框架，反向装配到"防守 + 引导"这一侧——他不是在跟市场博弈汇率，他是在用汇率去操控长端美债收益率。

这就是本期视频最容易被忽略的一层：日元不是目的，日元是杠杆。 他关心的从来不是 USD/JPY 的数字，而是"日元强 → 日本资金回流 → 抛售美债需求下降 → 长端收益率下行 → 财政部再融资成本下降"这条跨市场传导链。一个财长公开说"我知道日本央行下一步"，本质上是在把货币政策的信息不对称，变成财政政策的定价工具。过去是央行为财政部背书，现在是财政部反向操盘央行叙事——这是一次深层次的权力位移，值得单独警惕。

跨领域连接：Meta 的 Muse、高通的 HBC，其实是同一场"数据引力战争"的两面

表面上看视频里两条 AI 新闻互不相干：一条是 C 端智能体（Meta Muse），一条是 B 端芯片合作（高通 + 亚马逊）。但把它们放在"数据引力（Data Gravity）"这个物理学隐喻下，你会发现它们是同一场战争的正反面：

  • Meta Muse 在争夺"社交行为数据"的引力井——你收藏的菜谱、点赞的餐馆、旅行分享，这些数据的重力大到让智能体必须"住进"Meta 的生态里才能真正好用。谷歌 Gemini 争的是"意图数据"（搜索、地图、邮件），Meta 争的是"偏好数据"，苹果争的是"设备行为数据"。三家在做的不是同一款产品，而是给三种不同的数据宇宙各造一颗恒星。
  • 高通的 HBC 技术 + 亚马逊自研芯片则是在争夺"数据在物理层的重力"——当模型和 token 大到一定程度，"把数据搬到算力那儿"比"把算力搬到数据那儿"更贵。HBC（高带宽内存 / 高级封装互联）本质上就是让内存和计算之间的"数据重力"最小化。

惊人的对称性：C 端在争谁能垄断"人的数据引力"，B 端在争谁能瓦解"芯片间的数据引力"。而高通同时踩在这两端（Snapdragon 在手机端捕获 Muse/Gemini/Siri 的运行时数据，HBC 在数据中心为亚马逊提供加速），是视频里那句"C 端 AI Agent 最终利好高通"背后真正没被点破的战略卡位——它不是简单的多元化，它是同时押注数据引力的最上游和最下游。

一个模式识别：这期节目的所有话题，都被一个隐藏结构串起来了

如果你把这一期视频的四个话题——参与度超卖 + CPI 前不对冲、贝森特"庄家宣言"、Meta Muse 落地、高通 HBC 授权——排在一起看，会发现它们共享同一个"结构性范式"：

"存量位置的博弈价值，正在超过增量信息的博弈价值。"

  • 参与度已经在超卖区：这意味着"再多一份坏消息"的边际杀伤力已经很小，位置本身在保护你——所以不对冲。
  • 贝森特喊话：他玩的不是"发布新政策"，而是"把已有的政策路径信息，用位置优势去变现"。
  • Meta Muse：Meta 没有发明新的 AI 能力，它在用"已经沉淀了 20 年的社交存量数据"去卡智能体的位置。
  • 高通 + 亚马逊：不是发明新芯片架构，而是把手机端的存量技术（HBC 起源于移动端封装）位置迁移到数据中心。

这就是当前市场最反直觉的一层：过去几年美股赢家靠"讲增量故事"（新模型、新芯片、新叙事）；而 2026 年的赢家正在切换到"讲存量位置"——谁的位置更靠上游、更难被绕过、更能吃到别人流量的过路费，谁就赢。这个范式转变如果成立，那么下一阶段真正该重仓的，不是"最能创造新东西的公司"，而是"最难被别人绕过去的公司"。而这，恰恰是这个财长、这个 Meta、这个高通，此刻共同展示给我们的东西。

开场

各位观众大家好，欢迎来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小道。

整个市场的走势还是围绕着 AI 去展开。比如说今天芯片板块的反弹、高贝塔动能个股的一些反弹，包括前段时间相对比较弱的一些新云板块的一个反弹。市场里面还是有一些和 AI 相关的一些消息，所以今天我主要围绕这两个点出发：

  • 第一点是 Meta 公布的一个新产品 Muse，Meta 的 AI Agent 终于落地，所以针对它这个产品本身，我想稍微去聊一下。
  • 另外一个是高通和亚马逊之间的这个合作，对于高通来说意味着什么。

那在聊这些东西之前，我们对于半导体 ETF 的估值做一个更新，市场的参与度做一个更新。贝森特又放豪言壮语说：你们要和我对着干的话，等着瞧。好吗，我们宏观的这些东西我们去做一些更新。

一、周二市场回顾：只有 AI 硬件在涨

先快速地回顾一下周二资产价格的走势。美元、美债市场这一块波动并不大，三大指数出现了回调，标普和纳指相对回调的幅度会小一些。周二市场的一个反弹全部是和 AI 相关的，特别是和硬件相关的。

在上一周好几次我就提醒过大家，我说现在根本就不应该去卖出硬件或者卖出半导体。现在去卖出半导体，就好比在 6 月份的时候去买入半导体、卖出软件是一样的一个道理。

那在周二整个市场，你看：

  • 虽然公共事业反弹了 0.9%，但是公共事业板块里边一些权重股都是和 AI 相关的，包括能源板块里边也是一样；
  • 芯片板块反弹了 1.6%，高贝塔动能板块反弹 6.7%；
  • 而其他的一些板块基本上在周二都出现了下跌，医疗板块下跌了 2.5%。

所以整个市场周二的一个走势可以理解为：除了硬件板块、半导体板块相对强势一些，其他所有的板块全部出现了回调。

二、参与度进入超卖区，CPI 前不建议对冲

经过周二的下跌之后，我们看一下标普 500 的参与度：

  • 标普 500 20 日均线的参与度跌到了 29%，在周五的基础上继续出现下跌，也就是标普 500 现在 20 日均线的参与度已经进入了一个超卖的区间；
  • 纳指的参与度也是一样，跌到了 37%；
  • 罗素 2000 20 日均线的参与度也跌到了 38%。

所以现在都在一个中性偏悲观的位置，要接近于超卖的位置了。

在这种情况下，周五我们要等待 CPI 数据，下一周会有美联储的决议。CPI 数据基本上就能够决定了下一周到底美联储怎么去做。

有人问我：是不是应该对于周五的数据去做出一定程度的对冲？我认为完全没有必要。在当下情绪面已经在一个相对比较低的位置的时候，没有必要去做对冲。即使周五的数据不如预期、市场出现下跌，我认为下跌的幅度也是有限的。

三、半导体估值仍然便宜

参与度相对衡量的是一个比较短期的市场——它完全可以因为一两天、三四天市场的反弹就出现非常大幅度的反弹，也可以因为一两天市场的下跌就去到一个比较悲观的位置。

退后一步去看，市场的估值是一个更好的参考指标，或者是一个更好的"模糊正确"的指标。

SOX 半导体板块：

  • 我在六月底的时候，反复强调半导体板块的估值在 28 倍、29 倍，我们要去做一个移动止盈；
  • 七月底的时候，去到了 18 倍左右（稍微超过一点 18 倍）；
  • 经过半导体板块两天的反弹之后，截止到周二的收盘，半导体的估值来到了 19.7 倍。

19.7 倍，我认为仍然是在一个低估的区间。所以我今天发了一条 X，我说：整个市场虽然半导体出现了反弹，但是半导体现在仍然是便宜的。

最差的这种情况下，从现在的估值跌到今年 3 月份的低点，那就是 17 倍了。从现在这个位置跌到 3 月份 17 倍的估值，那就是往下 13% 的空间。如果到那时候的话，我认为基本上可以把所有的子弹、所有的现金全部打出去。我不是说不会跌到，但是我们知道如果跌到那个阶段的话，市场会相当的悲观。

四、贝森特喊话市场：我就是庄家

然后我们来聊一下贝森特。贝森特今天他在接受采访的时候，他说道他去怂恿那些交易员做空日元。他说："我现在就是庄家。"

哇，这句话真的非常的强硬。

他说：每当人们在说"美国财政部正在进行冒险"的时候，他会说，好吧，这就是我的梦想——我掌握了不对称的信息。他强调过很多次，这已经不是他第一次说"我掌握了不对称的信息"。就是：你可以和我对着干，但是我掌握了不对称的信息，你要和我对着干的话，你要小心。

他继续说道："我现在就是庄家。所以当我们在干预日元汇率的时候，我对日本人、日本央行及日本决策者的动向都有相当准确的了解。"

其实这就是他所谓的不对称信息。我认为他的意思就是说：我知道日本央行要加息。

通常来说，日本央行如果进行加息的话，将会使得日元出现上涨，或者日元兑美元将会出现上涨。从他的角度，他是不是关心日元兑美元出现上涨？他不关心。他关心的是：如果日元强势，应该能够帮助长期美债收益出现下跌。所以这就是他所谓的不对称信息——他知道日本央行会加息。

所以他最后说道：如果你想跟我赌，那就赌吧。

五、财政部回购规模值得关注

第二点是，在周三的早上，我们就知道美国财政部对于这一次回购的体量到底有多大。市场的预期是在 6~8 个 billion。上次贝森特说，起码是 4~6 个 billion 以上，就是 40 亿至 60 亿美金以上。

所以明天早上——周三早上，好像 11 点，我们将会看到这一次美国财政部回购的体量。

回购的体量如果非常的大，也会影响到周三起码美债市场这一块的走势；而长期美债市场这一块的走势将会影响到黄金；那黄金如果有波动的话，也将会影响到比特币。

六、Meta 推出 AI 智能体 Muse

OK，然后我们来聊一下这一次 Meta 所推出的新的 AI 智能体。

其实小扎在过去几次财报里边一直有聊到说，他们要出自己的 AI 智能体。这一次 Meta 所出的这个智能体，其实和谷歌 Gemini 的 Spark 是非常类似的——现在的智能体，它能够做到更加类似于一个个人助手：比如说帮你去进行购物，比如说帮你去整理自己的日志。

Meta 与谷歌智能体的出发点差异

但是他们的出发点还是有一些不一样的：

  • 谷歌 Gemini：更多的是整合在自己谷歌产品里面的一个智能体。因为谷歌现有很多 C 端和 B 端的产品，特别在 C 端这一块，Gmail、Google Map 等等。它更多的是为自己现有的产品去赋能——现有的产品如果以前是没有智商的话，现在给这个产品赋予了智商，原来的产品可以做到更多。
  • Meta Muse：有点不一样。它更多的是一个类似于长期运行的个人助手，并且已经强调，如果 APP 关掉的话，它也能够运行。

未来我相信苹果它也会推出自己的智能体，比如说 Siri，Siri 的话也会在年底之前应该也会进行一个大整改。

三家护城河的差别：数据类型不同

那这三者之间，差别到底在哪呢？差别其实就在公司原本自己到底掌握了多少客户的信息，包括他们所在的领域：

  • 谷歌掌握的是真实的数据和个人的数据。比如说你的 Gmail、比如说你的 Google Map 里面你每天上班的那些线路等等——它掌握了一些个人数据和实际的真实数据。
  • Meta 掌握的是个人的社交数据。

暂时来说，第一代 Meta 所推出的这个智能体，我并没有看到它展示的一些功能是谷歌没有办法做到的。但是未来我相信这个 AI 智能体会出现一个差异化，而这一个差异化肯定是来自于这两家不同的公司所掌握不同的数据，或者他们的护城河不同，通过这个护城河出发去做产品。

Muse 的落地示例

在今天 Meta 自己所举的例子里面，他举了一个例子：

你可以通过向 Muse 下一个指令："把 Instagram 里边我收藏的这个菜谱变成一个购物清单，并且记得我朋友那些忌口。"

那这就是一个非常好的把 Instagram 里面收藏的菜谱变成了一个购物清单，然后购物清单通过我们叫 agentic commerce（AI 智能体的商务）去解决。

另外一个我认为未来非常好的落地，比如说推荐餐馆：因为你在社交媒体上你点赞这个餐馆、你收藏这个餐馆，Muse 或者 Meta 知道每一个人的喜好到底是什么。所以它就可以非常好地去推荐你喜欢的这一类餐馆，无论是菜品也好、形式也好。同时还可以邀请朋友——它也知道你的朋友到底喜欢哪些餐馆，Muse 作为智能体可以帮你去推荐这个餐馆，同时帮你去邀请你的朋友，在其中可以直接帮你把定位这件事情直接做了。

另外一个落地就是制定旅游计划等等。基本上就我们在社交媒体上所分享的这些内容，Meta 可以从这些内容出发，最终这个智能体去服务这些内容，把这些内容去定制化。

Meta 的护城河与派发渠道

Meta 的护城河是什么？其实 Meta 的护城河就是数据，Meta 的整合就是它现有的这些 APP 里边的一些使用者，那这些使用者也变成了它的一个派发渠道。

当然啦，你也可以给 Meta 一些权限，让 Meta 去使用你其他手机里边的一些 APP，至于你愿不愿意给权限，这可能是取决于个人了，因为其实牵扯到个人隐私的这个问题。

所以未来我认为 Gemini 在 C 端这一块的智能体、Meta 的智能体，包括苹果的智能体，可能都会有自己的空间。最终谁能够跑出来成为在手机端使用频率最高或者占比最高的智能体，现在还不知道，完全就看应用场景。

但是起码站在当下，从 Meta 的角度，它现在做出来这个产品了，接下去就看它这个产品的落地。

定价模式：免费 + 订阅分级

那落地就要牵涉到你怎么去定价：

  • 现在它有一个免费版本，免费版本是给 token 的，好像一个月是给 100 万个 token；
  • 也有一个订阅版本。

当时我布局苹果的时候，我就说苹果这个智能体未来一定是有一个免费的版本，然后有不同的 tier——不同 tier 你付不同的订阅费，模型的智商是不一样的，可以帮你完成的事情的难度也不一样。

而 Meta 现在就已经在走这一步了，或者说 Muse 的定价就是在往这个方向去走。所以接下去可以去看 Muse 的接受程度。

七、高通 + 亚马逊合作：类似博通 + 谷歌的模式

OK，然后我们转一个画风来聊一下周二公布的高通和亚马逊之间这条消息。

我去看了下他们的公告，这个公告本身其实写得有点模糊，它并没有告诉我们高通和亚马逊之间的合作到底是什么。它只说：在多代定制芯片上提供支持。

我们知道亚马逊现在有自己的自研芯片 Trainium，也有自己的自研 CPU Graviton。那高通和亚马逊之间这个合作到底是什么呢？

我的判断：类似博通 + 谷歌 TPU 模式

经过一些调研之后，我个人的判断：我认为高通和亚马逊之间的合作，非常有可能就是类似于博通和谷歌之间的合作——也就是高通可能会授权他们的技术给亚马逊，共同去开发亚马逊新一代的 AI Accelerator（新一代的 AI 加速芯片）。

引用了高通什么技术？引用了高通的一个 HBC 技术。

什么是 HBC 技术？大家可以去搜一下。这个技术主要针对的目的是什么？目的就是为了去解决当下 memory 不够的问题。然后在这个基础上，还为亚马逊提供光互联的问题。所以基本上高通接下去和亚马逊之间的合作会非常紧密，那整套数据中心的设计上，包括提供 networking 上面都会有非常紧密的一个合作。

那然后在这一次公告里面还聊到了和其他另外的一家 hyperscale 也会可能有合作。那另外一家 hyperscale 是谁？无非就是两家之一：要不就是微软，要不就是谷歌。

合作的战略意义

这一次合作的意义，我觉得是在亚马逊对于高通 HBC 技术的一个背书。

虽然这个技术现在还在一个比较早期的阶段，最早好像要到 27 年的年终才会有一个 commercial（商业的）takeout，最终的量产可能要到 27 年底甚至于 28 年。但是它起码验证了未来高通在 AI 数据中心这一块可能也会有自己的一席之地。并且如果这个技术真的走得通的话，未来高通的客户会非常的多。

高通：C 端 + B 端 AI Agent 双重受益

而这只是在 AI Server 这一块。

我原本认为——因为以前一直有人问我："你介绍 AI Agent，C 端这一块的 AI Agent 最终有可能会利好哪一类的标的？有哪几个标地？"我一直聊：在 C 端这一块的 AI Agent，我看好几家公司：

  1. 一家是苹果；
  2. 一家是谷歌；
  3. 另外一家是 Meta；
  4. 剩下的一家就是高通。

所以这条消息出来之后，我经过仔细地对于它基本面的研究，包括整个行业的研究之后，我认为高通的基本面在转好。包括现在高通的估值又在一个合理的阶段——不算非常的便宜，但是在一个非常合理的阶段。所以配合加在一起，包括它 AI Agent 这一块的 telling，我认为高通现在是值得布局的。

那最后是我们今天的活动——微牛证券 (Webull)。大家对微牛证券应该并不陌生，他们在美国做得非常的好：

  • 美国市场（独家福利）：开户且入金 100 美金，只需要 100 美金就可以抽取 12 股免费的股票——最低价值 36 美金，最高价值 3600 美金。同时还可以获得一个月 Webull Premium 的订阅。
  • 加拿大市场：开户且入金，最高可以获得价值 250 加币的返现。

大家如果感兴趣的话，可以在置顶的留言里面找到这两个市场的开户链接。

那今天这期内容就到这边，我们下期见。

item.description:
## 一个让人意外的观察：贝森特的"庄家宣言"其实是在偷偷抄索罗斯的作业
大多数人听到贝森特那句"我就是庄家、我掌握不对称信息、你想跟我赌就赌"，第一反应是"这个财长真嚣张"。但如果你把这段话放到金融史里去对照——**这是一次结构性的角色互换**：1992 年是索罗斯用"不对称信息 + 央行政策路径推演"打爆英格兰银行，赢得"击垮央行的男人"称号；今天贝森特（本人正是索罗斯量子基金的前 CIO）在做的事情，是把当年**攻击央行的那套框架，反向装配到"防守 + 引导"这一侧**——他不是在跟市场博弈汇率，他是在**用汇率去操控长端美债收益率**。
这就是本期视频最容易被忽略的一层：**日元不是目的，日元是杠杆。** 他关心的从来不是 USD/JPY 的数字，而是"日元强 → 日本资金回流 → 抛售美债需求下降 → 长端收益率下行 → 财政部再融资成本下降"这条**跨市场传导链**。一个财长公开说"我知道日本央行下一步"，本质上是在把货币政策的信息不对称，变成财政政策的定价工具。**过去是央行为财政部背书，现在是财政部反向操盘央行叙事**——这是一次深层次的权力位移，值得单独警惕。

item.title: [Lex Clips] DHH on immigration: Response to critics of his political comments | Lex Fridman Podcast Clips
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个隐藏的镜像：DHH 的技术哲学与政治哲学是同一套算法

最出人意料的观察或许是：DHH 关于移民的论点，几乎是他 Ruby on Rails 设计哲学的政治翻译版。Rails 的核心信条是 "Convention over Configuration"——加入这个框架，就要接受这个框架的约定，而不是把每个人的偏好都拼进来做成一个平行系统。他谈丹麦移民时反复说的"assimilation vs. parallel society"（同化 vs. 平行社会），本质上是同一个架构决策：一个系统能承载多少异质性而不崩溃，取决于新成员是接受既有 convention 还是坚持自己的 configuration。他甚至在同一段访谈里同时抱怨"人们被塞进蓝色或红色的 bin"——但他对国家的想象恰恰是一种"更强的 bin"。这个内在张力他自己似乎没意识到。

丹麦的"元数据癖"是这场辩论存在的真正条件

他随口提到"丹麦人对移民保持极其细致的统计，我也不确定为什么"——但这个细节其实是整段论述的隐藏发动机。跨领域连接一下：这正是软件工程里的 observability 原则——What gets measured gets debated；what isn't logged, isn't a problem。瑞典和挪威没有这场辩论，不是因为他们更宽容，而是因为他们的国家仪表盘上根本没有这个字段。同样一批 Syrian 移民、同样的经济影响，在丹麦成了政治议程，在瑞典成了 taboo，差异不在现实，而在数据基础设施的选择。这提示一个更普遍的命题：一个社会能讨论什么，取决于它先允许自己看见什么——政治议题的生成是一个 telemetry 问题。

Harold Bluetooth 的双重讽刺，以及"被封入 bin"作为一种有损压缩

他提到 Harold Bluetooth——蓝牙协议以这位丹麦国王命名——用来强调丹麦血脉延续千年。但蓝牙技术存在的全部意义，是让异质设备无缝通信。也就是说，他用一个"消除差异、跨越协议"的技术图腾，来论证"保持差异、拒绝混合"的政治立场。这个命名讽刺他自己没提，但它非常精确地暴露了现代身份政治的核心矛盾：我们的日常生活运行在无边界协议之上，我们的政治想象却仍然停留在有边界王国里。

再连一层，Lex 后半段那个关于"blue bin / red bin"的抱怨，其实是在描述一种有损压缩算法：社交媒体作为编码器，把每个人复杂的观点向量强行压到一个 1-bit 空间。DHH 说"你选一个 bin 坐进去，系统就不再攻击你"——这不是政治现象，这是信息论现象：低维度状态在系统中总是更稳定，因为编码/解码成本更低。真正的代价不是被贴标签，而是说话前必须先自我压缩——所以最珍贵的信号（curious exploration）恰恰是这个信道最容易丢失的。

一个更深的悖论：他谈"言论成本"，用的却是"言论收益"的语法

他一边说"我不后悔一秒钟"，一边承认失去朋友、要更慎重选择议题、"我希望我不知道那个人的政治立场"。这是一种未完成的会计：他把 Overton 窗口的公共收益记在自己账下，把私人代价当成一次性成本核销。但如果每个像他这样有名气的人都做同样的账，社会总账未必是正的——你打开的窗口，可能同时关闭了一百个更温和的人参与讨论的意愿，因为他们看到了你付出的代价。他推崇的 Buckley × Black Panther 对话，之所以在 1970 年可能，恰恰是因为那个时代的 Overton 推动者比今天的 nudge 者更节制。这里有一个反直觉的结论：想要回到那个可以真诚辩论的世界，也许需要少一些像 DHH 这样直接推窗户的人，多一些愿意先修好房间空调的人。

📝 转录文本

Overton 窗口不会自己打开

Lex: You mentioned getting some criticism for Hamachi. So, uh let's walk further down that path of criticism. You have made some of your political opinions known. Um I guess you could broadly put in the category of immigration or illegal immigration or what—

DHH: —mass immigration.

Lex: Mass immigration. The role of demographics in the formation of a culture, of a society, of a nation. And you've gotten quite a lot of criticism for that and created a lot of drama. Do you regret any of that drama? What's your general thinking about—

DHH: Not for a second.

Lex: Okay.

DHH: And the reason I say that is that the Overton window does not open itself. It opens one nudge at a time by people risking a little. A little reputation, a little pushback, a little criticism, or maybe sometimes a lot of reputation or a lot of criticism, or a lot of pushback.

丹麦的早熟辩论：从 Mogens Glistrup 到 Bota Hill 的人口变迁

And I think the question of mass immigration in Europe was for many years this total taboo. And it still is in several European countries. Now, for reasons of maybe just chance and happenstance, they weren't in Denmark. The Danes started having discussion around mass immigration and the consequences thereof in the mid-90s. Really early. And some of it can be traced back to one man, Mogens Glistrup. Who was a very quirky character. I remember seeing him on the TV in the '80s talking about the dangers of mass immigration.

And this was at a time where I grew up in the '80s. And in the neighborhood I grew up in in Bota Hill in what was it? '84, 99% ethnic Danes. People who could trace their lineage back to Danes who'd lived in that country for a thousand years. The Danes have one of the oldest monarchies in the world all the way back to Harold Bluetooth—who literally has named the standard Bluetooth. So, well over a thousand years. There's a long lineage of people who lived in the same place. And 99% of the people lived in that neighborhood. And then early '90s, I think it goes to 5% or something like that. And then at this point it's down to around 60 something or 70% in Bota Hill. That's a big change.

And the Danes started noticing that this was not an undivided blessing—that there were downsides to mass immigration in about the '90s. And the debate really roared through the 2000s in a way that didn't happen in the neighboring countries. So, Sweden in particular just didn't have that debate at all. Total taboo. Same thing with Norway. Same thing with other countries in Europe. And suddenly now after some years after '15 where we had the big migration of a million Syrians walking up through the highways in Europe and Germany choosing to take a lot of them and 30,000 arriving in Denmark and so forth. It's gotten more of a focus.

"被允许注意到什么"：伦敦的一代人变化

And one of the ways I find that you can spot where sort of there's something that isn't right in the culture is: what are you allowed to talk about? What are you allowed to notice, actually, is how I should put it.

And what I noticed in an essay only a year and a half ago—I started coming to London in late '90s. At the time, whatever, it's 59, 60% ethnic Brits. And then 20 years later, we're down to 34% or something like that. That's noticeable. Literally just walking on the street, you realize, well, this is a different city from what it was when I visited 20 years ago. And if you went 20 years before that, you get back to similar rates to what the Danes have. So it's a country of ethnic Brits in the 85s, 90s percentiles. So that's a different country in a generation.

It's okay to notice that. It's also okay to think, you know what? I don't agree with that. I wish it wasn't that way. The last time I was in China was 2019. I was in Shanghai. It was all Chinese. If, when I go back there this October, I suddenly find that there's only 30% Chinese, and then there's 70% other people, I'd be a little weird. I'd probably be like, "What happened?" And I would not take offense if the Chinese in that instant would go like, "We don't like that."

So this idea that countries of Europe don't have the right to A, notice what's happening, and B, oppose what's happening, I find to be wrong. There's a moral argument for self-determination. And we invoke that argument all the time in other regions around the world—that all the people who live in that region have a right to self-determination for their country. And I think it's completely fair for say the Danes or the Swedes or the Norwegians to go like, "Well, we've been kingdoms here for a thousand years with a certain ethnic mix-up."

Merit-based 移民 vs. 大规模移民：丹麦的账本

I'm a big fan of immigration. I'm an immigrant to the US. Cherry-picked immigration where countries compete to attract the smartest, most talented people around the world is really good.

Lex: Legal merit-based immigration.

DHH: Merit-based is key here—because there's actually virtually no illegal immigration in most of Europe. Southern Europe has some illegal immigration, but most of Europe does not have a big problem with illegal immigration. The problem is with mass immigration of other kinds—you end up with demographics that are just totally different from what they were even a few short decades ago. And I think the countries of Europe would benefit from immigration.

In fact, one of the interesting things about the Danes is they carry meticulous statistics on immigration. I'm not entirely sure why they're so detailed. Maybe it's all the way back to Mogens Glistrup and his discussion in the '90s, but they do. And what's clear from those statistics is that when the Danes have folks from the UK, France, the US show up, on average, those immigrants are really beneficial to the Danish state. They contribute far more than what they ask of the state.

So the Danes should accept immigrants who do that—who contribute far more than they take. Then you look at other forms of immigrant groups. There was just a tally that came out last week from a Danish politician who had asked the finance ministry to do this tally with the latest numbers. What does it cost the Danish state to have the positive immigration cases I mentioned? For the whatever—France, UK, US—they were all clustered around the same thing: about $25,000 net benefit to the Danish state every year. I'm like, "Wow, that's very positive." That's average, right? And then at the other end of the spectrum, the most costly immigrants were Somalis. They ended up costing the Danish state on average $28,000 a year. I think it's fair for the Danes to go like, "We'd prefer to get more French, Brits, and Americans and not so many Somalis."

为什么这个话题激起如此多的仇恨

Lex: Why do you think you got so much hate on that post?

DHH: That's a very taboo topic in a lot of circles.

Lex: Some of it has to do with Overton window expansion.

DHH: I'm sure, but I also want to take the steel-man argument here. I do think that this can turn ugly. Is it possible for some of these things to just veer into overt racism that isn't founded in anything else but a hatred of other people? Yeah, that could happen. But that risk does not negate the need to have a discussion about the makeup of your country and what your immigration policy should be like.

And what I also find funny is—especially in Europe—it's so myopic that this discussion about whether Europeans should have a right to self-determination about what their countries look like, that standard seems to only apply there. No one is trying to tell the Japanese, "Hey, you're too Japanese." Whatever it's 98%—I think in Tokyo, that's ethnic Japanese. Is anyone trying to tell the Japanese that their Tokyo would be a much better country if they were down to London levels of ethnic Japanese, that it was whatever 37%? I don't think so.

So there's this weird almost self-loathing, in my opinion. I mean—Musk calls it "suicidal empathy"—that permeates this stuff to a degree that I still haven't fully unpacked. Like where's this coming from?

Regardless, I just noticed, "Hey, London looks different." I preferred the old London. As I would say I preferred the neighborhood that I grew up in in Copenhagen, how it looked in the '80s. I totally get how you can then jump five leaps and go like, "Okay, well, that's racist." And I also—I don't care anymore. This is a fair discussion to have.

白板论的实证失败与同化的意义

Countries and peoples have a right to set an immigration policy. And this notion that we shouldn't have any borders—or even worse than that, it's all just a blank slate, that all peoples are just the same, and we can take people from one place of the earth and place them in another place on the earth and everything's just going to work out hunky-dory—empirically not true. Europe has been running that experiment since the '80s. It hasn't panned out well.

And now there are forces in Europe who want to undo that experiment. Who want to end mass immigration as it's been run so far. And I happen to believe—and so do a majority of Danes and a bunch of other people—that, you know what? Yeah, it hasn't been working how we've been doing it. We got to make some changes.

And I don't think that means, again, zero immigration. Again, I'm an immigrant. The US generally speaking has benefited tremendously from immigration—but that's the kind of sleight of hand. Immigration depends greatly on who immigrates. And a country benefits when the people who immigrate are net contributors to the society and in most cases assimilate with the local culture.

If you come to Denmark and you want to become a Dane and you put in all the effort and you contribute to the society, I think most Danes would be quite happy to allow that in a reasonable number. If you come to Denmark and you don't want to assimilate and you are a net drain on society and you live in a parallel society, it's also fair for Danes to say, "Let's stop doing that."

美国的"可选式同化"文化

Lex: It's interesting that I'm not well versed on the immigration system of the United States, but as far as I understand, merit-based systems have not passed here.

DHH: And then also American culture is very different. This is a point I did not fully appreciate until living both places extensively. America has a culture of optional assimilation, where it is much easier and much more conducive for someone coming from Denmark or Ukraine or wherever to come to America, buy into the American set of values and norms and culture, and then be able to be respected as Americans by other Americans.

This is what's so funny to me when there's discussion like "America is such a racist country." I'm like, have you ever been anywhere? Do you know what other countries are like? If you think America is the most racist country, you are simply misinformed.

I mean, we're dealing with that—the time we spent in Denmark. My wife is American of Scandinavian heritage, but multiple generations in the US. Very difficult. Very difficult as a blonde, blue-eyed woman who's putting in all sorts of effort of learning the language and doing everything, still very, very difficult to assimilate to Danish culture. In a way where if that had been the other way around and she had been Danish and moving to the US, it would not have been that difficult at all.

Living in a country like Denmark with an American wife who is of Scandinavian heritage and has put in all the effort—and still realizing, man, assimilation is incredibly difficult even when you're 97% there. Holy smokes, must it be almost impossible if you come from a completely foreign culture and foreign norms and the rest of it. And of course, that's what the stats I just quoted bear out. The more dissimilar the culture is and the further it is, the less likely to be successful.

2020 年的大裂缝与失去的朋友

Lex: Has articulating that stance cost you friendships, relationships?

DHH: Yes, but not just that alone, I would say. It's more of the great divide that happened around 2020 where I think a lot of these political fault lines really opened up. The shorthand in the US, I think, is: were you woke or not? And clearly, I had a bunch of people that I thought I had good relations with for many years who, suddenly once that political fault line opened up, they were clearly just not anymore. And I think that's regrettable.

I've tried to put an effort into sort of understanding where that comes from—in part because I've changed my mind on several of these topics over the years. Sometimes you just change your mind after time; sometimes you change your mind after you get new information. There's all sorts of reasons and moments why you may change your mind, and we don't all change our minds on the same schedule, or at all.

So surrounding yourselves and interacting with people who don't think like you on every topic, I think it's quite healthy. I occasionally discuss politics with my brother. We don't quite see eye-to-eye on all these topics and sometimes the discussions can get a little heated, but then they'll also calm down and we realize, all right, okay, so we don't agree on this—and then we agree on a lot of other things. We appreciate a lot of the same things.

Basecamp 大爆炸后重新发现的旧规矩

Now, this was actually one of the things when we had our big blow-up at Basecamp, I came to appreciate in a whole new way this old-timey norm: that talking politics or religion or money with strangers or even acquaintances and certainly with colleagues was just not a good idea. That you had a much higher likelihood of being able to carry a good working relationship with someone if you're not rubbing your political differences up against each other all the time.

So I actually think liberals and conservatives should work together. I think the country would be much worse off if there's a complete separation between the tribes and there can't be any overlap or interaction. And that mingling is so much easier to do if you just don't focus on your differences all the time. Focus on what you like together. Some of the people I've unfortunately drifted from in tech—we had so much in common. So much shared love for say Ruby or other things. And that's unfortunate.

Buckley 与 Black Panther：一个失落的对话时代

Lex: I would like to live in a world where the differences are very interesting to also talk about. And not to be overly emotional about even radical differences—because in the differences, first of all, that's where interesting stuff is. And it's how you grow. It's a sign of health in a society if the differences are embraced and brought together into community where you can talk about it.

DHH: One of the great illustrations of that for me was when I watched a clip from William F. Buckley's show—I think it was called Firing Line or something like that—and he had a member of the Black Panthers on his panel. It was quite obvious that those two gentlemen did not share a lot of politics. They were able to carry a conversation for—I think I watched 25 minutes—and Buckley's just asking, "So what do you think about this? What do you think about this?" And the Black Panther would reply as you would expect the Black Panther to reply in the '70s. There was not a lot of conciliatory tones.

And I just thought, wow, that is so rare. If you had seen that show today, it would have been a shouting match. It would have been just accusations being hurled back and forth. The fact that Buckley was able to just have these conversations with people he vehemently disagreed with and still explore all the intellectual facets of their standpoints and letting them speak to those facets—it talks of a lost era that I'd very much like to get back to.

I always actually loved talking politics with friends that I trusted could talk about these topics in a way where it didn't have to be existential.

蓝仓与红仓：被迫选边的当代言论生态

Lex: But there's something about the current era where that's harder and harder to come by. And so what you just articulated is important to say regularly, to remind people of an ideal we should all strive for—to be able to have differences in a talk and talk about them.

Because politics is fun. I've gotten used to saying "I hate politics" at this point, but what I really mean is: whatever the system that's currently happening where there's certain topics… I just know—we know all the phrases you can say that somehow put you in a bin of blue or red. And that creates drama versus a conversation.

I could think of a lot of harmless statements I could make analyzing the situation in the world that would trigger everybody to say, "Oh, that guy's a leftist piece of shit," or "right-wing fascist." Objectively, if I wasn't paying attention to the internet, I would be—and I have been—shocked. I haven't been paying attention to the internet deeply, but reading and preparing a lot, for example, for the war in Ukraine. I have been shocked how certain statements from me can come off as one way or the other and they get viciously attacked for it.

But what that attack is doing is it's saying, "Hey you, [] who thinks he could just move about and think freely, pick a bin and sit in that [] bin. Put on that blue shirt or red shirt." And then—actually what I've realized is things calm down. The system doesn't pick on you if you just say, "I'm a blue person or I'm a red person." But if you're just curiously exploring the world and reasoning about the world, the system punishes you. And I hate that, because I want to get back to the Buckley and the Black Panther discussion.

DHH: Yes.

Lex: You were just saying opinions. But then looking pragmatically at the situation, I have realized not to mention politics unless I really care about an issue, because I realize there's a cost. They'll put you in a blue bin or red bin. So you have to be more deliberate about choosing.

说话的代价，与一个可能正在缓慢好转的时刻

DHH: Yes. And I have been trying to be more conscious of that too. When I do choose to speak up about it, it's usually because I have deliberated and I think, "You know what? This is worth it."

Now, I say that and then I also catch myself thinking the opposite all the time—that I follow some person or another for whatever their technical work. And then I learn their political standpoint and I often do think, "I wish I didn't know that." So it's hypocritical to think that of other people and then go like, "Well, occasionally I will chime in on a debate that's controversial." And then you have to accept that there's a price to that. And I do think you should—and more people should be—somewhat conscious about that.

Again, we're both contradicting ourselves here by saying: wouldn't it be nice if we could talk about politics in a more free and open forum and just intellectually turn ideas around. Yes, it would. Is that currently possible in the climate of social media and so forth? It's quite difficult.

Now, some of it could simply also be a moment—and we could get past that moment. Maybe there is some way to get back to Buckley's conversation with the Black Panthers even on social media in a way where those discussions don't lead to the vicious mob cancellation nonsense drives that we've had.

I actually think we're closer there now than we were 5 years ago. The tribalism and the sanctions those tribes were able to exact on heretics in 2020 was way greater than it was in 2025. Certainly within tech. Now, I know if you're in academia—try going into the sociology department at, I don't know, Harvard and mention some right-wing ideas. I don't think it's going to go over very well and I don't think you're going to recover from it quickly. But in tech and many other business domains at least, it is now possible to have an opinion that does not square with what the consensus was in 2020. That's for sure.
