item.description:
## 一、"缺陷"的相变：Linux 悖论的反转时刻
DHH 提到的这个洞察其实是一场哲学级的反转：**Linux 那些"过度具体、极度晦涩的错误信息"——过去二十年被视为它对普通用户最不友好的地方——在 AI 到来的瞬间从最大劣势变成了最大优势**。
这里发生的不是"AI 帮我们读懂 Linux"，而是一次**受众的悄然置换**：错误信息的目标读者从人类变成了模型。当读者变了，同一段文本的"质量"评价就完全颠倒——对人越晦涩、对模型越具体、越能定位。Windows/macOS 那种"抱歉，出错了"式的友好错误，反而在 AI 时代变成了**信息稀薄的负资产**。
这让我想起一个跨领域的对照：**基因组测序数据也曾是"垃圾"**。ACGT 的四字母长串对人类完全不可读，被嘲笑为"没有信息的信息"。直到算力和模型追上来，这堆"乱码"才突然成了医学最珍贵的诊断金矿。Linux 的 stack trace 正在经历同样的相变——**从噪声到信号的临界点，不在数据本身，而在读者的认知带宽**。
## 二、多智能体的"意外副作用"：并发即混沌工程
DHH 顺口提了一句极其关键但没展开的话

item.title: [Business of Sport] Does the British Media Hate Successful People | James Haskell
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：Haskell 其实是"英国媒体逻辑"最完美的产物，而不是受害者

他花大量时间抱怨英国媒体如何"捧杀"名人、如何嫉妒成功者。但仔细听他的叙述会发现一个悖论——他的所有商业成功（书籍、播客、代言、DJ 事业）恰恰是建立在"被误解"这一情感杠杆上的。他自己说了："我一周会收到三四次'我以前觉得你是个混蛋，现在改观了'的私信。"

这意味着："先被讨厌"是他商业模式的入口漏斗。如果英国媒体真的像美国媒体那样对成功者友好，Haskell 就没有那个"人格反转"的戏剧曲线可以卖了。他愤怒地抱怨的那个系统，正是他所有非橄榄球收入的定价机制。这就像鱼在抱怨水太湿——他把生存环境错认成了敌人。

跨领域连接：橄榄球的溃败 = 传统媒体的溃败 = 同一种"业余治理精英主义"的病

他讲的那个 RFU（英格兰橄榄球联盟）故事有一个让人震惊的细节：理事会成员被要求投票决定是否解散自己的职位。他们当然否决了。 这不是橄榄球的问题，这是一个跨越所有百年机构的通用病理：

  • BBC、《卫报》等传统媒体也是被"业余治理者"（60 岁以上、不理解社交媒体、以"传统"为身份认同）把持
  • 大学的终身教职委员会
  • 大多数国家的中央银行治理结构
  • 医学专业协会

Haskell 无意间描述的是"自我延续型精英治理"的通用溃败模式：一个组织当它的治理层由"以'守护传统'为身份"的业余者组成时，这个组织无法进行任何威胁到治理层身份的改革。你看到的不是橄榄球病了，你看到的是任何以"业余精神"为道德优越性的机构，在专业化经济中都必然崩溃。 Full Contact 被 Netflix 砍掉这件事之所以成为完美的隐喻，是因为它揭示了：这些机构宁愿死，也不愿被看见真实的自己。

隐藏的系统性真相：Haskell 的整个人生哲学是一个"疼痛货币化"引擎

注意他讲话的节奏和主题的隐藏结构： - 身体（10 万英镑修复、睾酮从 3 恢复到 25） - 童年（父亲的操纵、17 岁开始的治疗） - 职业（受骗签约、被低薪、诉讼 68 万英镑） - 关系（离婚、父亲留下的财务烂摊子）

大多数运动员在退役后会尽力掩藏这些伤口。Haskell 做的完全相反——他把每一次疼痛都转化成了一个内容产品：书、演讲、播客话题、纪录片素材。

这里有个惊人的洞察：他其实是英国最早期的"创伤经济"从业者之一，只是他自己没意识到。他反复说的那句"你可以骗所有人，但骗不了自己"——这不仅是他父亲的教诲，这是内容经济时代的核心资产。在一个"真实性 = 稀缺性"的注意力市场里，愿意公开承认自己被父亲坑了 10 万英镑的前橄榄球国脚，比一百个完美的品牌大使更有价值。

他抱怨自己"没坐过私人飞机"——但真正的问题不是他赚得不够多，而是他还没有意识到自己已经从"橄榄球运动员"进化成了一个"人格 IP 运营者"，而后者的定价模型完全不同。 他还在用运动员的账本算内容创业者的收入。这就是他"下一个突破"的所在位置。

📝 转录文本

开场：关于金钱、诚实与英国媒体的自白

I'm not one of these bitter old rugby players that doesn't want people to earn. I'm mercenary in lots of areas. I love money. I love working hard. I work very hard. Do I think players should earn more money? Yes. Is there more money in the game? No. And that's the biggest problem.

My dad taught me a very valuable lesson when I was younger, which was: you can lie to everyone else, but you can't lie to yourself. There was lots of things probably that I didn't get right to start with.

I was tragically underpaid at Wasps for five years that I was there. I was the lowest paid player in the England squad. And what they used to trade off was the fact that great culture, unbelievable players would win everything. But they never invested in the squads, they didn't have the money, they underpaid people, people took pay cuts to come and win stuff.

Rugby turned the greatest opportunity and balls it up to the point where they cancelled it before the second season even came out. And that is all you ever need to know about rugby, because they don't know what they're doing.

We're actually not that happy for people to do well over here. Our media is the worst media in the world. Every celeb or every sportsman says it, because they'll build you up and then they will go out of their way to **** you over.

Business is fun. Fascinating.

见面寒暄：礼服、领带与训练后的身体

主持人：James, I'm so excited for this. My favourite thing is someone who has an opinion and stands behind it. Not that common, I find, today, but I think we'll do just fine here.

Haskell：My pleasure. I mean, I'd like to say I dressed up for the occasion to appear more corporate, but I'm actually going to the Gentleman TV series premiere this evening, and I realised, as per my diary management, that I didn't have enough time to get home. So I showered, spruced myself up, come in. So I'm killing two birds with one stone.

主持人：I just love the fact that you actually put the tie on for the show as well.

Haskell：Also, yeah, I didn't need to, but then I don't know why, I just finally did my top button up. And that one itself was quite hard because I trained this morning. I did some boxing training which was pretty intense, and being a slightly sort of muscle-bound individual trying to access your own tie in a tailored shirt while trying to put your… my hands don't physically get around there. So once I did it, I was like, I'm into it now, I'm not going to around.

身体的代价：伤病、手术与 10 万英镑的自费维修

主持人：Can I ask, how broken is your body?

Haskell：Pretty broken, yeah. From my perspective, I'm not one of these rugby players that at this point in time — touch wood — that I have any sort of cerebral issues or mental issues. I played a very physical position and my approach to my training and the way I worked was very, very intense. A lot of my teammates and coaches would say I was one of the most professional players they'd seen in terms of nutrition, training, working with other people, accessing other sports, talking to different individuals.

I reinvested a lot in myself, so I never accepted what the club offered me wherever I was. I'd always get my own physio, own nutritionist. I would do what they wanted me to do, but I would always think there was a better answer.

Because if you look at the NFL, for example — if you're paying Patrick Mahomes 450 million over 10 years, if he breaks down, that is a massive issue, and they have high level quality of staff and people to look after. If the best rugby player in your squad is paid — I mean today it's slightly different — but say paid 350, 400 grand a year, the budgets of a medical and everything else like that are not the highest. So you're not going to get access to the best people. Sometimes you do have amazing people, but often you'll get some average care.

And so having finished playing, I've had probably four or five operations since I retired. I had a discectomy on my back, I had a screw taken out my wrist, I had my bicep reattached, I had my ankle cleaned out, and then I ultimately had my ankle fused about a year ago. I'll get no insurance to pay for it — all myself. I reckon I've done probably 100 grand on injections, physio, medical fees, pilates. I've tried Ayurveda, Reiki — I've tried everything. Even when I went to Fiji, I saw something about my ankle, like a witch doctor. He wrapped my foot in leaves. I'll do anything to feel better.

But I've always — I see a wellness doctor, I work with a testosterone company. I had my testosterone test the other day: it was three. It starts at a healthy level about 12. So I was really low. I'd obviously shot myself to pieces with kind of training and tiredness. So I've got that back up to about 25.

I've always looked to get my bloods done. So everything I do is science-based information. It's not gym wisdom where a meathead says, oh, you want to take this. Because like anything in life, the cheque's always in the post. If you drink and smash it up now, it's not now you're going to worry about — it's when you're older. When you smoke now, it's not a problem, it's when you're older.

So my body's pretty wrecked, and sometimes having a low level of pain in my back, my neck, my ankles, my feet — waking up, feel like you've been hit or been put through a tumble dryer. But I do look after myself.

唯一的遗憾：42 场比赛与麻醉针

I have no regrets. The only thing that I would have done differently in my career was I would have taken more rest. We shouldn't have played as many games as we played. And I wouldn't have played injured. Well, I was injecting anaesthetic into my ankle — not me doing it, but the doctor was doing it in bits, trying to get through games. There's just no need to do that.

主持人：How many games are you playing a year?

Haskell：Oh well, at my peak, I played 42 games a year. Yeah, and I used to play 80 minutes as a back row player. And I would then practice my tackling every day.

So at some point, would I say that I am someone that would be in a place that could potentially have dementia or Alzheimer's? I've had a brain scan as part of a medical with a company called One World Beck, and there was some stuff on there, but nothing that you would think.

Actually, because bizarrely, my dad, who's passed away — I think he wasn't completely… I want to say English, but he wasn't. There was something going on with his genetics because he had bigger cast than Trevor Leota. His two of my fingers would be like one of his fingers. Massive joints, big lips. So I don't know what my grandma was up to, but he had some genetics. When I've had DEXA scans, which does your bone density, my bone density is massive. So I think I've got pretty hard bones, pretty hard head — but obviously your brain still rattles around, so I would be susceptible for that.

关于 Sam Warburton、法国联赛与"活在当下"

主持人：Can I just ask on the number of games? We had Sam Warburton in a few years ago. He was talking about when he got to play in Wales domestically and then when he got offers in France. The big challenge with France was: yes, fine, good money, but the demand to play would be more, he would have then had to compromise what he then did for Wales. So did you have to make choices between where you would put that focus? Because 42 games a year for the intensity that you had to play at your full potential for England and Wasps — is that virtually impossible?

Haskell：I mean look, I love Sam. As an aside, I think he's become a brilliant commentator. If you'd said to me Sam Warburton was going to be one of the most accomplished commentators and sort of orators around our game, I wouldn't have said so, because personality-wise he's quite quiet — great leader, unbelievable player, but I didn't know he had that kind of media stuff in him. So I'm always supremely impressed by him.

I never thought of it like he thought of it. I never came into question. I live very presently. I got therapy from the age of 17 to last week around — to start with — consistent performance, addressing criticism, bits and pieces. And through that journey you obviously find out you've maybe got some blind spots you need to work on. I didn't have any sort of conditions per se, so I live very much in the moment. If you can't control it, I wouldn't worry about it. So I never thought about that.

I played, I would be professional — sleep, train, not drink, rest, recover, and put my best out there. Would 42 games — would I have underperformed for England? I don't think so. It never crossed my mind. It was never considered. I never had to make any compromises. It made me a better player going to Stade Français, playing with Sergio Parisse, Dimitri Szarzewski, Pierre Rabadan, Juan Hernández — some of the best players in the world.

I'd come back to England camp, you're looked after. In those days when I was in France, I never missed an England game. I was playing under the coaching staff, Martin Johnson and John Wells — great guys, great coaches, but not like Eddie Jones. Eddie Jones' environment was light years ahead and better. I had five England coaches in my career; Eddie Jones was a million miles away from that.

Sometimes those sessions under those guys are draconian and long and purposeless and really a bit like, what the hell are we doing here? So maybe some of our performance did — but actually, no, I never did that.

Travis Allen 的教训：训练太多，比赛太少

I would say my biggest thing about my performance was doing too much off the field by extra training. So I was doing, not necessarily in France, but when I was in England, I was doing wrestling at London Shoot Fighters to help with tackling, takedowns. I was doing extra conditioning. I was seeing Margot Wells, a sprint coach. I was doing extra weights to help rehab injuries. And I was then trying to pursue a career and hustling in business and entrepreneurial spirit.

To the point where one of my friends, a guy called Travis Allen, who's a Kiwi — he's a specialist in certain training techniques and treatments — he sat me down and was like, "I don't understand why you're setting records in training and lifting all these weights, doing all this extra fitness when no one gives a shit. It's all about the performance on the weekend."

I remember it quite clearly. We had this meeting at High Road House in London. He said, "I want to sit through and go through a game with you." He sat and went through a game with me and he's like, "Look, you're playing inside yourself. You look like you're scared of the ball. You don't want to make mistakes. You turn up to training tired."

And I sat there and I thought, "What the fuck are you talking about? I know you're a Kiwi, so you immediately think you know more about rugby than everybody else." But he was a mate of mine. I've always been very good at listening to feedback. I don't necessarily like it at the time, but I have very much a level of self-awareness in terms of how I am as a person, what I say, how people view me. I watch people's body language all the time. I'm very in the moment. I never get too down. I don't look backwards.

And so I went away from that meeting going, he's right.

父亲的教诲：你可以骗所有人，但骗不了自己

And my dad taught me a very valuable lesson when I was younger, which was: you can lie to everyone else, but you can't lie to yourself. And when someone says, for example, you've got a drink problem, or you're late, or you're lazy, or you're tired, or you don't behave, or you're not a good parent — you can listen to it and you can have all the excuses. But that moment when perhaps when you go to bed, when you switch your phone off just before you close your eyes, everything hits you. And then you're like, maybe there's a bit of truth in this.

And that happened twice in my career at that point. And also, the day before my first day at Wasps, my dad said to me, "I know you don't like tackling. You're a bit of a fucking pussy. You don't tackle properly. You tackle up high, you're going to get found out if you don't learn to tackle properly." I was like, shut up, dad. Anyway, I had a row.

Went into Wasps next day and I was like, he's right. I don't really like this, I'm technically not very good at it. And I went up to Joe Worsley, who I regard as the best tackler in the world. I said, "Joe, nice to meet you." And he thought my name was Jonathan, which is my dad's name, for the first three months. I didn't have the balls to tell him it was something different. So he said, "Lawrence Delalia." I went, "Joe, his name's James." And Joe looks at me: "Why don't you tell me?" I was like, "I'm sorry, sir."

I went up to him, said, "Listen, I can't really tackle. You're the best tackler I've ever seen. Come with practice every day." For nine and a half seasons, I practiced my tackling, bar team run days or game days. But I would practice it, and it became one of my greatest assets, and I became a very physically dominant player. Was that necessary in my nature? Not really.

Same thing with this conversation with Travis. I went away and I was like, "You're right." So I said, "Listen, I've lost my way." I was probably, I don't remember, maybe 40-odd caps or 50 caps at the time. Help me or talk to me about something. So we worked on it, and that was just before I toured Australia, where I played what people perceive as my best rugby for England. And then I went on the Lions tour, and it completely changed the way I did things.

So I had to listen and I had to have self-awareness and also put your ego in check. And because of all the therapy and all that kind of stuff, I go from day to day. If I can't control it, I don't worry about it. I don't overthink things.

I've worked very hard, particularly from the start of this year, on doing what I did when I played. If you've got negative thoughts, concerns and fears, sit. You can change your thinking, visualisation — all these really important elements. And I just sit in the day. Like last night, I knew what I was doing today. I woke up this morning, did what I need to do. I haven't looked at tomorrow. I haven't looked at what I did yesterday. I'm on it today.

And so Sam's mindset about those compromises — no, look, going to France is hard. They train you hard. It's a bit mad over there. It's Wild West. It can be quite political in terms of what they do in coaching and clubs, and they're very passionate. But actually, if you have the mentality I had, you just live in the present. So I never concerned myself.

关于评论区、Henry Ford 与 Tom Holland 的哲学

主持人：You said the top earner in a team. And people hate me often in the comments because I just go to money quite often.

Haskell：You're good at it. You're very good at it, man. I wouldn't worry about it. If you went to money and you didn't have a pot to piss in, I'd be like, what are you talking about?

主持人：Seriously, you should read the comments — there are some bangers.

Haskell：Don't ever read the comments. I tell you why. Would you change what you said if you did? And I saw a great analogy…

主持人：It does hurt me though.

Haskell：Don't look at it. It doesn't matter. Who cares? You don't know him. If I tell you — so two things I thought were interesting. Noel Gallagher said — well, three things. Henry Ford, who invented the car, he said: if you'd asked people at that time what they wanted, they would have said a faster horse, not a car. So they gave him a car — he don't need a horse anymore.

Noel Gallagher said: nobody wanted Oasis. No one gave him Oasis — they wanted something else. Who cares what they want, give them what you believe in and test it. And obviously, if there is some popularity, stick with what you do.

And Tom Holland, Spider-Man, said that if you've got a problem with him or a comment with him, text him. And if you haven't got his number, you don't know him well enough to text him.

I do not give a shit about people's comments. Now, does it still hurt if you see them or people talk about them? 100%. Because we're programmed like that. People who say, "I don't care about other people's opinions" — of course you do. But I don't look, because it's a form of self-harm.

If you believe in what you're saying, then you shouldn't worry about people who haven't met you, who aren't informed, who have no context. Social media does not work because it takes all the context away. How could you relate to somebody who's a single mother of three from a different country, who has had no money — you're never going to. Whose political background is very different, who sees the world in a completely different space. You're not meant to. That's why it's caused more agg than anything else, because contextually we have no background, no knowledge, no understanding.

So when you put stuff out there, if you say, "I like milk, I love cow's milk," people go, "How fucking dare you? You're destroying the environment. What about almond milk? You shouldn't drink milk." You're like, I just said I like milk. Relax.

So I post now, I don't look. And I've got a video guy that does stuff with me and I go, look, if you said something outlandish, or something that is provably wrong, then you've got to step back and put your hand up and say, "I've got that wrong." But what people want or don't want — the fact they're commenting is brilliant, because you want now to create interaction.

And every time I do something, I want people — because that's what life's like — to equally like or dislike me. If people have no reaction to you, what are you doing in life? It's creating conversation. Negative or positive is brilliant.

演讲、领导力与观察人的能力

So when I do content with brands — and the hardest thing I do is I do a lot of corporate speaking about mental health and mindset and performance and resilience — because I've played, I don't know how many games I've probably played in my career, but I've worked with some of the best environments, the best people. I spend a lot of time personally looking at my leadership, other people's leadership. I work very hard on my own self-awareness.

I said to you all the time, I'm reading people's body languages, and sometimes I like to be destructive and play up to it. Sometimes — we did this dating show — and I could go and sit on dates with girls and I could see them instantly. They'd already made up their entire minds about me and everything else. The reason I left Wasps was: it took me two years to negotiate my contract with three different MDs. All of them subsequently left. The club was sold. The new owner came in. It took me two years to get to a point where I was still underpaid, but I would have accepted the offer because I was indoctrinated because Wasps won everything.

And what they used to trade off was the fact that — shit facilities, great culture, unbelievable players would win everything. But they never invested in the squad because they didn't have the money. They underpaid people. People took pay cuts to come and win stuff. That's great. When you stop winning stuff, you're suddenly confronted by terrible facilities.

We used to have a training pitch called the Fox Shit Minefield, which if you got tackled, you basically would fall in a piece of fox shit and then that'd be a session over. I think they ended up having some council and they shot 200 foxes on that thing at night. They were just shitting all over the place. This is a high-level premiership-winning team, and your training session would finish when you fall into fox shit because you've got it in your eye and you go blind. Then we went up to Broad Street, which, again, they said they'd done all this investment. The pitch was waterlogged. We had to go and train on Astroturf at school, all this kind of stuff.

Once that glory finishes, you then have to go about your salary. The new owner came in, got 10 of us in a room who were out of contract, slid envelopes across the table, said, "We're not paying agents' fees. And you've got 24 hours to decide. These are the latest offers." And the offer they gave me was exactly what they'd offered me two and a half years ago.

So I said to everybody, got everyone in a room and said, "Right, remember Friends, TV series?" They all got together and said, "If we negotiate as individuals, we'll get caught out. They can't lose all of us. Let's stick together." One guy folded straight away because they offered him the captaincy. So I was like, fine, if that's what you want to do. And most other guys left, because we just stayed staunch. Wasps then had a massive decline.

主持人：What was the offer they gave you?

Haskell：£140,000. No, no, sorry, 120 grand is what it was. And I was playing for England at the time. Look, that is a lot of money for people. But as a pro in the England team — when the club are leveraging your commercial rights, you are giving up your medical health and body. You are expected to… I think some people think rugby players were like, "Oh, is it just a Tuesday, Thursday night?" It's a seven-day-a-week thing. You're putting your body in jeopardy. You're training hard, you're travelling, you're working. It's a privileged environment, I get it, but it takes a lot to do that.

You were never allowed — if I was sponsored by Under Armour, you were never allowed to post anything about Under Armour during England time. And it just, the whole thing was flawed in rugby, really. It was kind of very odd. It was just the generations of, "I remember Davey, 2007 to 2015" — team first, humble, don't ask, don't fight, don't question, do as you're told, take the money, this is it, don't worry about this.

You used to get 25 grand a game for England. Some of it is image rights, some of it was playing contract, and the image rights would be some of the money that you would get used for that. Now in life, because of social media, it's not just watching the event. They want to know what you're like, what you're doing behind the scenes, what your family's like, what kind of parent you are, what you go on holiday, what you drive, what you eat. That's why At Home with the Furys — it's not just him. It's him and his kids and his wife. People want to know. What events? What do they drink? What do they go out? That's where life's going. We want to look behind the curtain.

So against all the odds, rugby had an opportunity with Full Contact on Netflix, right? To suddenly — with all the other stuff, the tennis and everything else that had been developed — to make something mega.

And all we did was squabble about what we're being paid. I don't know what the fees were, but you know, "We're not going to do it, do it." Everyone was so worried about cameras in the rooms. What was the fear? "We need editorial approval." And then we do one season. I never watched it, but it was pretty boring. They got a second season. They cancelled the second season before the first season had even come out.

We managed to fuck up the greatest opportunity rugby had to transform its worries because somebody was worried that someone might have "changed" them — see, you call someone a see-you-in-T or do something.

And what rugby forgets is: in life, in anything, the silence you leave, the void you leave, people will fill it with opinions and thoughts and everything else. Show them it. Show them the rawness. You wouldn't let have the cameras in the changing rooms.

Rugby turned the greatest opportunity and balls it up to the point where they cancelled it before the second season even came out. And that is all you ever need to know about rugby. Anyway, Alex almost had a nervous breakdown because they were hammering him the whole time and he was seen as the adult was a group, because I've been to court three or four times. I'd had legal stuff. I'm no push over. So I was very veteran in this. Alex is much more amenable, placatory than me. I was very firm.

So they basically stopped messaging me, just started dealing with Alex. They then told Alex halfway through that it was going to go because 750,000, not 250,000. Never told us. Never wrote to us client care letters, said they were going to do it. We managed to get security of costs against them, went all the way through to the end, and the day before court, they pulled out. And obviously in UK law, you can't counter. So we either had a choice: do we pursue them, or do we just take our ball home and do we just deal with whatever they want? I think we had to give an apology — some bullshit that we did.

And then the answer was, we then had a bill of 750 grand. Which we thought the new company we were working with had been servicing the bill. Turns out Alex was getting calls every day because we owed him 500 grand and no one had paid it. I said, "Alex, I'll deal with this." Called him up with one call and said, "Stop calling him. There's no money. You're hounding him. Let's stop calling." I said, "Well, you should have sent me in there anyway."

We then had to fire our lawyers, our own lawyers, because they had not told us. So it's like me coming around to your house going, "Could you prune my rose bushes, which I imagine you've got? Could you do this? Could you don't do the topiary on the extensive lawn — right, on the bushes?" And then building your swimming pool and coming back over: "You I'm a million quid for swimming pool." You're like, "I didn't order a swimming pool." "Like we've built it now." And that's basically what they did. They never told us what they were doing.

So me and Mike, I explained: if you could show us what you told us it was going to go out, money will pay. So they obviously couldn't, because their lawyers — we ended up having a row, they took some money off the bill. It cost us probably about 680 grand in total we didn't have to pay. Luckily, the business made that money. But Alex almost had a nervous breakdown. It almost destroyed our relationship with other people.

But the podcast basically launched and became profitable and has carried on. So we've gone from the phoenix in the flames, through the ashes, had all this drama. I've been cancelled twice doing it. I upset various people. And so it's been really tough. And we actually, for the first three years, we earned nothing out of it.

遗产、离婚与"未来 200 万的机会"

主持人：Did you ever just feel like, I just can't take this anymore?

Haskell：No. I don't know why. I just don't have that mindset.

But I actually think — I spent a bit of time this year, I have moments like that, when you go, "Fucking hell, this is tough. Woe is me. This is hard." Because there's lots of stuff with my dad passing away. He left a shit show, financial disaster. My mum's going to sell our house. My brothers are great, but he's a bit of a lost soul. I have a divorce. I've got a child. I've got 10 things that I do as businesses. I work with some people. I'm obviously slightly controversial, not intentionally. I have media scanners. I have dramas. It can get on top of you.

All the work that I've done through the therapy helps me, but there are moments of course you go, "Fuck this." But then I generally spent a lot of time going: actually, I know it sounds woo-woo, but the way you talk about stuff and how open-minded you are and what you talk about in your own head about how you sell and how you're going to view things — is I then just go back, "Right, what is it I can do? What are the solutions? What can I control? Who can help me? And why not put the energy into that?" Figuring out who do I speak to, a lawyer?

I remember there's a story where my dad basically tricked me into signing a — it said it was for something, it was basically a personal guarantee. And it was about 75 grand. I thought it was like four grand. And people came to the door, knocked on my door, and he'd gone to court, lost it and I owed 90 grand and they gave me 10 days to pay. Every lawyer I spoke to said, "You sign a guarantee, you can't get out of it." I went to someone else, the guy that was a bit more rogue, and we found a solution and got out of it. Now, if I'd taken all the professional advice that everyone told me, I would've had to pay. It was nothing to do with me, because I signed a guarantee.

主持人：How do you feel about your dad getting you to sign that?

Haskell：I don't know. It's a hard one. It's not ideal, but there's lots of things like that that have happened to me. But I just think, again, I have this excitement for life and this desire to perform. I want to be successful. I also know my limitations.

Unfortunately, I'm bright in certain ways, in social situations. I'm relatively articulate. I'm a good learner. I don't have that business — I'm not great with figures. So I know my limitations. I work with people that do. And obviously, because of the way I've conducted myself, not intentionally, I'm not always the most brand-friendly person. I'm not probably what the zeitgeist of what's going on now wants — not too collective, but you want them to a focus, right? For an 18-plus type brand, you're pretty good. If you want to be the family and friends brand, they're not going to come to you. But that's great. You know what you want.

Also, I don't want to ever pretend to be something I'm not, because you get caught out. If you read in the papers that James Haskell's sworn and done something and pushed someone down the stairs, you go, "Oh, that sounds probably a bit like him." It's when someone goes, "Oh, my God, you know, James Haskell" — I'm like, they're hugging babies and kissing children, and then suddenly you get found out. James Haskell's seen with almond milk. You're like, "What? What a guy. I feel betrayed."

But again, I think for me with a lot of this stuff, it is challenging and I do have those moments of woe. But I have worked so hard recently on trying to reframe things and trying to understand this. And look, there are times when stuff really gets on top of you. But again, I try to have the emotional reaction, which you should be entitled to — kick your toys, throw your pram, swear, lost, desperate, "What am I going to do?" And then you've got to go, "Look, there's got to be a way out of it." And sometimes there isn't. And sometimes you have to take your medicine.

But I think ultimately, if you go back again to what you can control, who can help you, how can you get help, and what's the plan to get you out of where you're going to go. And also talking about having an open mind, being positive, and going, "Look, there is…" Because we can always complain about stuff. But I get annoyed and jealous of people doing things that I want to do and earning money that I want. But then actually when I sit back and look at my life and I go, I've got a great life and I work with cool people. I get to do stuff like this.

Be grateful for what you've got, not what you haven't got. Because you're only fighting against yourself. And I know it sounds like rhetoric you'd hear online, but it is true. I'm as happy as ever with a good cup of coffee, mate. What's the problem?

三人组合、员工问题与代际工作观

主持人：Did that experience in the media bit, did that make you, Alex and Mike stronger together?

Haskell：Yes, it did. We very rarely row. We row during those bits because we have different approaches. We're in different parts of our lives. Alex is a brilliant guy, consummate professional, one of the best presenters out there. But he's got family, he's got kids, he's got bills, kids go to eat and it's expensive. He doesn't want to blow that up, he doesn't want to have that. I have a thicker skin because I don't mind those challenges, but we're ultimately in the game to make money.

And we get on very well together. We've had a couple of rows over stuff, but actually, I think I'm a very good judge of character. And a lot of people that I called out with these guys — I'm not going to sit on here, but we've been stitched up on a couple of things where I told these guys, "I told them point blank, lads. You are going to get…" Because I basically said, "I don't trust them. I don't care. Until you put a contract, shareholding agreement thing, I'm not interested in doing it. I'm not having my word." Take my word. Don't take anyone's word. I trust no one. Really. I see human nature for exactly what it is. Before someone to a corner, they'll do whatever they need to do. And people, if they can get away with it, we'll show, after you cheat and whatever.

So I said to him, and lo and behold, the lads got fucked. And we all three of us got fucked by somebody or something. It's like, "Lads, you've got to play nice and be respectful, but ultimately you have to do what needs to be done." So I think we do get on really well, and actually we're able to have conversations. But we are three very different people with three different experiences. But we love what we do. We love the audience that we've got. We love talking and having the passion, and it doesn't ever feel like work and it's never a chore.

The only time it was a chore was the court case and trying to manage other people we work with. And as soon as you get to business, you've got staff. Staff's the biggest issue for any business, because no one cares about your business as much as you do. And you've got to go through — kiss a lot of frogs to find a prince or princess that's prepared to work hard and do what needs to be done.

And this modern generation, they want it all for nothing and don't want to work, aren't prepared to commit, don't want to work weekends, aren't prepared to sacrifice. And people say to me, "Well, it's different for you." Why? Why am I different? I have an argument with producers. "Oh, can you come in here?" I was like, "No, I've got to take my daughter to school. I've got to do this." "Well, you know, what other people can." I mean, here's my diary. Turn my laptop around. "Look at that. Look what I did." "Well, I've never seen anything like it."

This is life. You either meet me or we don't do it. And he goes, "Well, I'm working on weekends." "Well, I'm 0-0-0." "What do you fucking mean you're 0-0-0? I'm representing the business. Why is there no one from our business working? Why am I going to a GBR event and no one I can get hold of?" It's not how it works. You work and you work hard and you do what needs to be done. Now, you need to get work-life balance. But if you're not prepared to work and sacrifice, I'll find someone else who is.

"Oh, you can't do that because you can't fire anyone these days. You can't tell anyone the shit. You've got to go, 'What do you stop doing, start doing, keep doing? Here's a formal letter.'" I understand about employment, but there needs to be some protection over some things.

But I think the issue is that, like in life, in a friendship group — I said to you earlier, there's always people that are going to pull together, help you, and be good energy givers or energy sappers. Same thing with business. There are people that see this as a career and want to work, but there are people who are 9-to-5ers, or nine-to-threes, and that's all they want to do. And you're like, fine, but that's not what I want. Just because you don't want to meet me halfway, I'm not here to listen to you or stop you. Go at your pace, you work at my pace. You can't take the pace, go away. And that's what I believe in all this stuff.

一周的节奏：混乱、结构与享受

I think when I was a player with all the stuff I did, I probably got the work-life balance wrong a little bit. So I had to run it back, had to listen to Travis, do less, be better for weekends, peak at the right times. Did I go through the openings of envelopes? Did I go and meet everyone that would have a coffee with me to talk about business? Was a lot of it a waste of time? Could have been an email, could have been a Zoom. Yeah. Now I'm ruthless on all that stuff.

But life's for living and fun. I was in France for a week. I flew back to London on Saturday night, DJed on my own event I did in Shoreditch from 2 till 11 with some guest DJs, flew back to France Monday. I had a France all week, flew back Sunday, took my ex-wife and my daughter for food, DJed Sunday night, woke up at five, got home at 12, woke up at five, flew to Toulouse, interviewed Antoine Dupont, did an Adidas campaign, flew back Tuesday, had work, here today, two DJ sets. And I've got all the admin work bits, stuff. I've got a PA, I've got stuff to help me. But that's how I want to live my life.

I like the chaos, I like the structure, I like doing it. I've got Thursday, Friday, two days with my daughter, just focused on her. I'm taking her, I'm going to physio, she'll come with me, I'll take her for food, I'll play with her, all that stuff. Saturday, Sunday, I play with her all day, DJ sets balance. That's me, that's balance. That's how I want to do it. I don't want to be sitting at home, I don't want to retire, I just want to keep working. So when I go to a restaurant, I can have a bottle of Montrachet and enjoy myself, or have a Cohiba Robusto and enjoy myself, and that's it. And I'm prepared to do it.

快问快答：品牌、嘉宾、球员与遗憾

主持人：Should we do a quickfire round? What brand do you not work with today that you would most like to work with?

Haskell：Oh, that is a very good question. AP, I quite like. I'm not a big watch man. I like my watches, but the Royal Oak — there's a rose gold and black one that I think is fantastic. It's big. They've got big watches. Arnold Schwarzenegger used to wear it. They've got big ones. Their feet suit me. I think they're really cool.

I would love to — I don't think it'd be great for my health, but the Cohiba brand, a cigar brand, stuff like that. Because I do like that. Someone said, "Oh, you can't talk about smoking. You shouldn't put it out there." Well, whatever. Arnie used to do it. So why not? The Rock smokes. So I think AP would be right up there.

主持人：Favourite person you've spoken to on GBR?

Haskell：Oh, I've had some amazing ones. I thought Jason Fox I really enjoy. Bobby Skinstad, he was great. And Eddie Jones, I think. They're all up there because they're all very different. Because that's the beauty of the show is one day it's emotional. Like when Nigel Owens came on, he talked about him trying to take his own life. I've known him for years and the question of his sexuality and stuff. And you just think, that's how terrible, how difficult that would have been. And next week you're then laughing with Billy Vunipola or something else. I love the rollercoaster.

主持人：Who did you most dislike playing against? Could be feared, could be fucking nightmare to mark. Individual players.

Haskell：Any massive Polynesian or sort of Pacific Islander — it was always going to be a tough day in the afternoon. Guys like — I remember the biggest hit I ever got hit on me was Sam Tuitupou, who played for the All Blacks and played for Sale. Hit me. I wasn't even looking, hit me and basically put my ribs through the other side of my head. The fridge with legs. Yeah. Henry Tuilagi — you always knew that I was going to be, I played Sevens once against Henry Tuilagi. I mean, there's a lot of space for a huge man, and like trying to tackle him around the leg. So that was always quite tricky. Any of those guys, you just knew that it was going to be a tough afternoon and that you're about to get levelled.

主持人：What have you not done yet that you'd like to?

Haskell：What have I not done? I've never been on a private jet.

主持人：What? No, no.

Haskell：Sorry, brother. I'm a former rugby player. I'm not — I know I come across…

主持人：Listen.

Haskell：What? I'm divorced. Listen, I'm divorced. I have to earn a lot of money. I've got fucking two houses, one and a half houses to pay for. Cars, things, everything. Divorce, bits, travel. I need to earn more. I need to earn way more than I'm earning. I've got a Range Rover, but then some drug dealer crashed into me the other day with my daughter in the car, snapped the wheel off and then legged it. But luckily he was insured. And he got arrested. He was an insured drug dealer.

主持人：Yeah, mental, conscientious, isn't it? Road safety.

Haskell：Less likely to get pulled over.

主持人：Less likely to get pulled over, exactly.

Haskell：Yeah, because that's how stupid it would be if you've got like a gram of gear in the car, you get pulled over for not insuring. Like a moron.

主持人：You have your opinions, you're confident in yourself. Is there anything that you regret?

Haskell：Oh, good question. There was something I regretted the other day, actually, I thought. I'd rather let my dad manage me at the time — only because he didn't have any experience and I think he probably created part of the myth around Brand Haskell and all that kind of stuff that wasn't me. I'm actually not as big a prick as people think I am. So that I think would probably be something I wish I hadn't done, because it changed our relationship. Even though I still loved him at the end and we knew he loved it. I made the conscious choice to look past everything just because you only get one dad. So that wasn't a problem. When he passed away, I was very content and I knew he loved me. So that wasn't a problem and vice versa. But I think him managing, I think, what else would I have not done? I think I'd say that one.

I think most things, regrets — I don't give a lot of time for it. There's things that I cringe at that I've done. I'm like, "Oh, why did I do that?"

主持人：What goes through your mind then?

Haskell：I don't know, just some ways I dressed before and I turned up and like, I don't know. Yeah, just little bits. But mostly I'm pretty happy because everything shaped me to be the person I am today. And again, when I said about, when things get tough, I always think that if you are so focused on what you want and what's happening, you actually step back and go: if I'm receptive and open and happy, things fall into lap. I find when I'm like that, stuff, people knock on my door, connections — and what you're doing is it's not what you wanted it to be. You want two million quid deal, but then we actually looked at it, if you were present, you go, "Oh, that adds to that and that and that's coming," and before you know it, you're actually in a good place. And so I've tried to do a lot more of that and not regret stuff too much.

营养建议、素食主义者与 Padel

主持人：If you could only give someone one piece of nutrition advice, what would it be?

Haskell：Worry about your protein, always. Where's your protein source coming from? It should be the most important part of every meal. If you look at your plate and you can't see where your protein is, you're fucked before you even start it.

主持人：Don't go vegan.

Haskell：Not for that. Well, I mean, vegan — I wouldn't, because it doesn't work for everyone and the amount of supplementation you have to have. And I also think the best meals are medically improving — animal proteins with plant-based as well. So I would have plant-based food. I would try lots of things. I'd have variety. Always colour on your plate. Not one is better than the other. And everyone thinks about The Game Changers. People were winning way more Olympic medals ever than not being a vegan. It's like, "Look how amazing these people are doing it." I was like, "Yeah, but they were doing it, lots of other people are doing loads of other things."

主持人：So I wonder what they're worst… You can just say you dislike vegans.

Haskell：I don't. I like vegans. Some of my best friends are vegans. I probably know more about veganism than anyone else. Them and Hyrox people, you know all about them, because they fucking don't show up.

主持人：You never do Hyrox?

Haskell：No, not because I don't like — dislike a brand. It's just I can't run. My ankle fused and I don't want to run around doing stuff like that.

主持人：So you haven't fallen down the padel train either?

Haskell：No, I've played padel. I've not seen a little boy on the TV show — a vegan and a vegetarian run off a cliff — who hits the ground first, or who wins? Who wins? Society. Sorry, but padel — yeah, I love padel. I've had six lessons, played four times. Love it. For a bigger gentleman, want to play more.

主持人：Six lessons played four times? It's not great.

Haskell：No. So six padel lessons played four actual games.

主持人：Not — you to the slowest, the classes you're right, you know?

Haskell：Too literal. Yeah, exactly. Too literal, just cut the nerds loving life. Well, one super nerd, one front-of-house. The front-of-house nerd. Yeah, less nerds, more palatable. Well, what more money are you earning? Get back in there, wait until the fucking deal's signed.

想采访的人、结束语与 OnlyFans 玩笑

主持人：Who have you not had on the pod who you'd most like to have on?

Haskell：Oh, I really want to interview — guys like Ricky Gervais I want to really speak to. The Rock, I think, would be great. And Arnie. I think his business acumen — look at Rock in terms of all the stuff he touches, how smart he is. For America, he swears a bit. He's a bit edgy. Nothing bad, but he's just a big character and I love it. He's gone from Arnie, weightlifter from Austria, to governor of California. That's stuff that people write in books. That's stuff people write in dream journals that never happens. Tindall's — Wakefield to Windsor. From Corgis to Coalmines. Oh, Coalmines to Corgis. That's unheard of.

Rock — from wrestling to the highest-paid movie star of all time, selling brands, bits, millions and millions and millions of pounds. Interesting guy, kept his personality, seems to be a great, good family man. Like, really interesting.

主持人：James, dude, you've been amazing. I think we should go on a private jet.

Haskell：Yes. Can we make some money together?

主持人：I don't know how to do it.

Haskell：Yeah, yeah. You sound like you've got enough, so just share it around. How can I make some more? Because I need it.

主持人：As I'm hungry, what do you need to do?

Haskell：I'm not doing anything too… Well, on that note, follow James' OnlyFans.

主持人：It's out of action. Shut that down.

Haskell：Follow me on Instagram. If you like music, you can follow me on SoundCloud. I've got a Facebook page. I'm not — cross-heading under James Haskell or Haskell Music. Very simple. Buy my books. What a Flanker. Ruck Me. What a Flanker. Basically What a Flanker. Ruck Me. I've written another book.

主持人：No, I did get it. Well, you say that. You shouldn't laugh as loud as I needed you to.

Haskell：How much money did you make out of it?

主持人：A lot. Not a lot. Not as much as I should have.

Haskell：Dude, you're a star.

主持人：My pleasure. Cheers, lads.

item.description:
## 一个反直觉的观察：Haskell 其实是"英国媒体逻辑"最完美的产物，而不是受害者
他花大量时间抱怨英国媒体如何"捧杀"名人、如何嫉妒成功者。但仔细听他的叙述会发现一个悖论——**他的所有商业成功（书籍、播客、代言、DJ 事业）恰恰是建立在"被误解"这一情感杠杆上的**。他自己说了："我一周会收到三四次'我以前觉得你是个混蛋，现在改观了'的私信。"
这意味着：**"先被讨厌"是他商业模式的入口漏斗**。如果英国媒体真的像美国媒体那样对成功者友好，Haskell 就没有那个"人格反转"的戏剧曲线可以卖了。他愤怒地抱怨的那个系统，正是他所有非橄榄球收入的定价机制。这就像鱼在抱怨水太湿——他把生存环境错认成了敌人。
## 跨领域连接：橄榄球的溃败 = 传统媒体的溃败 = 同一种"业余治理精英主义"的病
他讲的那个 RFU（英格兰橄榄球联盟）故事有一个让人震惊的细节：**理事会成员被要求投票决定是否解散自己的职位。他们当然否决了。** 这不是橄榄球的问题，这是一个**跨越所有百年机构的通用病理**：
- BBC、《卫报》等传统媒体也是被"业余治理者"（60 岁以上、不理解社交媒

item.title: [Lex Clips] Will AI kill most jobs? | DHH and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、AI 并没有杀死工作，它只是给早已死去的工作开出了死亡证明

DHH 抛出的最尖锐观察是：Graeber 那 30% 的"狗屁工作"数据早在 AI 出现前十几年就已存在——AI 不是凶手，而是验尸官。这里有个反直觉的推论：疫情后的过度招聘 + AI 叙事的爆发，恰好制造了一场资本层面的"体面下台阶"。管理层需要一个不必承认自己招聘失误的理由，而 AI 恰好提供了这块遮羞布。换句话说，AI 当前最大的经济价值，可能不是自动化本身，而是作为一种"合法化裁员的意识形态"——一种类似 20 世纪 70 年代"效率工程学"的话语工具。

二、F1 的隐藏教义：人类文明本质上是"仪式化的过剩劳动力吸收器"

DHH 把 F1 描述为"深度无聊的活动"，但他没走到最深那一步。让我把这个跨领域连接推到底——F1 与中世纪造大教堂是同一种社会技术。当基本生存问题被解决后，任何文明都必须发明一套"看似必要但本质上是奢侈仪式"的巨型工程，来吸收剩余人口的时间、意义感和身份认同。哥特式尖塔的空气动力学优化，和 F1 尾翼上那毫米级的调整，服务的是同一个心理刚需：让智力过剩的猿类相信自己的生命值得被投入。这意味着后 AI 时代的挑战不是"发明新工作"，而是发明足够多、足够昂贵、足够神圣的新型仪式。这不是经济问题，是神学问题。

三、生育率崩塌是理解 AI 焦虑的隐藏变量——一个时间贴现率的数学诡计

对话最后突然从 AI 跳到生育率，看似跳跃，实则击中了一个被主流讨论完全遗漏的数学结构：经济学中的时间贴现率（discount rate）在没有后代时会趋近于无穷——一切超出你自己寿命的未来都被折现为零。这解释了一个奇怪的现象：为什么最焦虑 AI 取代工作的群体，往往与生育率最低的群体高度重合。它们不是两个独立问题，而是同一个"时间视野塌缩"的两个症状。DHH 说的"nihilism sneaks in"其实可以形式化：当你不再有 30 年后仍在乎的人，AI 带来的"渐进式繁荣"在你的效用函数里变得毫无价值，而"渐进式痛苦"却是全部由你承担。

四、一个反 DHH 的补充：卢德分子的类比其实反证了他自己的乐观

DHH 用卢德分子论证"进步值得当下的痛苦"。但仔细看这个类比会出现一个令人不安的裂缝——卢德分子被替代后，他们进入的是纺织厂里更糟糕的工作，用了整整三代人才等到工业化红利真正惠及底层。也就是说，"进步的补偿"在时间尺度上远远超出个体寿命。把这个规律套用到当下：如果 AI 转型的社会补偿也需要三代人，而我们又同时面临生育率崩塌——补偿的对象可能根本不会存在。这是整段对话中被两位讲话者都刻意绕开的黑洞。

📝 转录文本

On Toby, and how AI reshapes work inside companies

Toby is such a fascinating human because he's running a large company, so I would love to get insights of how AI is being incorporated effectively in companies. Because — okay, for me, humans are pretty slow, and so there's a temptation to like use AI for basically, you know, AI running inside Slack, for example, or inside Basecamp, whatever. You know, AI running and, like, collecting all the information about the human interaction, basically hand-holding the humans to speed up as much as possible.

And, like, and then at a certain point, you're like: wait, what is this human, what are each of us doing that's not replaceable by AI? It's not replaceable by AI. And that becomes like a scary kind of conversation, because a lot of work is kind of replaceable.

The "bullshit jobs" thesis — and why AI is just an excuse

The irony here is: it already was. So the number of fake email jobs that currently exist in this world is an absolute epidemic. And this, by the way, is not a new thesis. David Graeber wrote this wonderful piece, Bullshit Jobs, back in — I think it was maybe early 2010s — based on a poll he did in the UK asking people at that time, would... I think the question was something like, would it make a difference if you didn't go to work, for humanity, mankind? And something like 30-some percent answered no, it wouldn't. That a third of workers thought that their job was fake, that it did not produce any worthwhile valuable outcomes, neither for the community or society or maybe even the economy at all.

And this was my argument since day one with startups. This was why we stayed a small company. This was why we didn't want to take VC. Because I was so skeptical of the idea that you could get hundreds of programmers, thousands of programmers to do something productive as a collective group.

And I think what we're seeing right now with some of the layoffs is a testament to that — not AI. It's just that during the pandemic, a bunch of over-hiring went on, and now AI is a convenient excuse to slim down. But I do also think AI is going to expose some roles as just not being productive ways for humans to spend their time. And therefore, we must come up with new ways of spending their time.

The Formula 1 parable: frivolous work as the future of employment

And the one — again, I'm quoting Toby for the third time here — but an anecdote that he shared with me: our observation was, okay, let's say we lose half the jobs that are currently happening right now. Do you notice Formula 1 employs literally tens of thousands of people just to run cars around in a circle for spectators? That whole circus has no intrinsic value to society, besides the spectacle it produces of amusement and entertainment.

We just decided it would be really fun for these 12 manufacturers to create these vast cars and constantly tweak the little aero improvements. And we will watch it, and we will spend literally billions of dollars doing it, and employ tens of thousands of people towards an ultimately deeply frivolous activity.

So if we are liberated from a bunch of drudgery and fake email jobs, maybe we all get employed as F1-style engineers and drivers and mechanics and masseuses and the other 1,500 jobs that are involved in that. And we come up with new things.

We are terrible at imagining the future — but the future is already here

I think humans are very poor at imagining what exactly the future is going to be like. Yeah, imagine a future a hundred plus years from now where we look back at this whole span of history — thousands of years — where humans worked.

Funny thing is, we're already doing that, right? Like, the number of fake email job people who sit on a chair all day long and type into a machine, who don't have hard physical labor, would be unimaginable to folks in the 1800s, right? So the future is always already here — it's just not evenly distributed.

The suffering of transition, and empathy across time

Unfortunately, as is always the case, the transformation of society required to go from one step to the other is going to have a lot of suffering. Yes. And potentially political turmoil and all that kind of stuff. Because — can you imagine how many white-collar jobs might be lost in this process?

Yes. And I don't think you should make light of that. I don't think it's funny. But I also do think it's a necessary component of progress. And I think if we look back upon the Luddites or the folks working the fields — separation has a tendency to reduce empathy. So we have high empathy right now because we know people and we are people who are facing these challenges. But what is our empathy for the Luddites of the early 19th century?

Would we wish that all garments were still made by hand weaving? No, we wouldn't. We want the comfort and accessibility and convenience of being able to buy clothing off the rack. So we must suffer in the moment for future generations to live more prosperous.

And that's always been true. I think that's actually the trick: is to push for progress but have deep compassion for the people who have to suffer. Yes. And that's many of us. The suffer — the transformation required to achieve that progress. And sometimes, too often, in places like Silicon Valley or so on, you can over-focus on a kind of utilitarian view of things and look at the progress. But, you know, considering deeply each individual human that suffers because of that progress is important.

Falling birth rates, nihilism, and skin in the game

I do think that suffering becomes more meaningful when you are suffering for a future someone in particular — like your kids. And I think this is one of the great tragedies of the moment: is the falling birth rates are making it more difficult for people to be excited about a more prosperous future that is difficult to get to.

Because if we're planting trees of which our children will not sit in the shades — I don't know, maybe we should just make some lumber and burn it all down, right? I think there's a nihilism that can sneak into society much more easily when we are not DNA-invested in the future, when we are not liable to our own offspring to propel forward.

So I think these are bad trends to merge at the same time — that we have these falling birth rates and these problems with coupling. And the fact that we need to keep our chin up about the future and be — I mean, you don't even have to be excited about it in this literal ecstatic sense that I'm portraying here — but I think you should be hopeful. And I think you should be working towards that hope. And I think it's much easier to do so when you have literal skin in the game.
